spots.desc: Serves British-style food made by a Japanese guy. One of the signature dishes is a burger that has pieces of apple inside.

spots.name: Tama Zoological Park
spots.desc: Like its better-known counterpart in Ueno, this park is run by the Tokyo municipal government. While it's not spectacularly large, the conditions seem more humane than at the older Ueno Zoo, which many western visitors find downright depressing. Directly across the street from the entrance to the Tama Zoo is a small train museum (Keio Rail Land), including a very large model train set.

spots.name: Tama Center
spots.desc: "Tama Center" is the central commercial area for the huge Tama New Town districts, not a single mall. A major shopping area, and if you're this far from central Tokyo, it's probably worth your while to do some shopping here before making a special trip all the way to Shinjuku or Ginza. Musicians, jugglers and other performers often play at the station, and the malls are illuminated for Christmas…

spots.name: Tama Chuo Koen
spots.desc: A park with a lot of nature and a pretty big pond. It's nice to see people reading books, talking, and sitting on the grass.

spots.name: Grand Cru
spots.desc: A cake shop. The cream-filled rolled sponge cake is popular.

spots.name: Cross Garden Tama
spots.desc: Buy miscellaneous goods, clothes, furnitures, and accessories! There are some restaurants, too.

spots.name: Izumi Tenku no Yu Haneda Airport
spots.local: 泉天空の湯 羽田空港
spots.desc: Indoor and outdoor public bath overlooking the Tokyo area skyline. It has luggage storage, rest area and a restaurant.
spots.price: Adult (including high school students) ¥4800, child (age 4 to elementary school) ¥2000. Late night surcharge…

spots.name: AKB48 theater
spots.desc: AKB48 is a home-grown, all-girl idol group — their name comes from Akihabara — which started in 2005 and quickly became the best-selling female group in Japan. They perform 6 days a week. If you are into J-pop music and cute girls all rolled into one (and are lucky enough to win the ticket lottery), don't miss this.

spots.name: Kanda Myojin Shrine
spots.desc: Akihabara's own temple. You can buy a multi-piece charm for ¥1,000 which will protect your electronic devices from evil. It's mostly noteworthy for the festival it organizes around May. On this occasion, a massive shrine is traditionally carried through the streets of Akihabara, providing an interesting contrast with all the high-tech to say the least.

spots.name: GiGO
spots.desc: Formerly run by Sega, four locations in Akihabara. As of July 31, 2025, the first store of gigo was closed.

spots.name: LaOX Duty Free
spots.desc: LaOX Duty Free specializes in export products and has multilingual staff on hand.

spots.name: ONODEN Tax-Free Department
spots.desc: ONODEN specializes in overseas electronics. Multilingual staff.

spots.name: Radio Center
spots.desc: Radio Center is an unbelievable two-floor warren of tiny shops, each specializing in (for example) LEDs, voltage meters, ceramic capacitors or miniature cameras. Heaven for the do-it-yourself electronics aficionado, and these days a flashback to the Akiba of yesteryear.

spots.name: Yodobashi Akiba
spots.desc: Electronics giant Yodobashi's massive 9-story flagship store selling anything that beeps or clicks, from PCs to games to cameras. Many languages spoken, tax-free and credit cards no problem, and their famous Gold Point Card system gets you credit worth 10% of your purchase, usable for two years starting the next day. Or you can have your purchase tax-free.

spots.name: Melon Books
spots.desc: In the basement of Taito HEY, it is mostly a mind-boggingly huge selection of fanart (Manga heaven, in a way).

spots.name: Animate
spots.desc: Seven floors - plus one basement level - of pure otaku goodness. From DVDs and manga to character goods and games, the variety of merchandise on offer is mind-bogglingly vast and will make anime/manga fans wish they were made of money.

spots.name: Comic Toranoana
spots.desc: Looking for dōjinshi? This is the place to head for. Look next to the Taito Station.

spots.name: Book-Off
spots.desc: About 8 or 9 floors of all books. The thing that sets this book-off apart from others though is that the top two floors are dedicated exclusively to manga. There is a small section for dōjinshi as well but selection is limited.

spots.name: Mandarake
spots.desc: An 8-floor second-hand shop dealing manga, dōjinshi, video games, toys, and collector's items. To buy toys from these show cases you need to find a slip of paper and write down the code of the toy you want, then take the paper to the counter and the attendant will retrieve the toy for you. It's easy and effective, although the stores can becomes quite busy at times. Check their online floor guide.

spots.name: K-Books
spots.desc: Only two floors. First floor is half adult manga/hentai while the second floor is half dojinshi. There is plenty of space though to browse around and they have tons of doujinshi there. Some cheap figures and a whole row of shelves dedicated to body pillow cases. If you want regular manga they have that on both floors as well.

spots.name: Radio kaikan
spots.desc: This is Akihabara's cartoon, anima shop, with several separate stores on each floor. You can buy various figures and anime related goods.

spots.name: Don Quijote
spots.desc: Japanese discount store chain offering an incredibly wide range of items at low prices, from snack food to clothing to gag gifts. The Akihabara outlet also has well-stocked costume and adult toy departments to cater to the local crowd. About half way up as well there is an arcade. If you want to play rhythm-based games like DDR or Jubeat it has the cheapest machines in town.

spots.name: Gachapon Hall
spots.local: ガチャポン会館 Gachapon kaikan
spots.desc: An entire store full of gachapon: capsule toy vending machines. Put in a few coins, turn the crank, and out pops a capsule containing a random trinket. The small toys and figurines, some of which attach to your keys or phone case, are of fairly high quality, and many are collector's items.

spots.name: Yoshinoya
spots.desc: Chain fast food restaurant selling gyudon beef bowls. Meals start from around ¥400-500

spots.name: Traveler's Dining Pushup
spots.local: 世界一周旅ダイニング居酒屋秋葉原駅店
spots.desc: A tiny place, convenient for anyone staying there. Serves Japanese and foreign food. The owner, Yuki, is a former backpacker and will happily give advice on choosing the right sho-chu from a selection of 60 kinds. Try the raw octopus (tako) in tomato sauce or the kimchi risotto.

spots.name: Marugo tonkatsu
spots.desc: It is a donkatsu shop in Akihabara. It sells high-quality donkatsu even if there is a small amount of money.

spots.name: @home cafe
spots.desc: This maid cafe has card games, drinks, food, and young women dressed up as maids to serve you. If you order an omelet, they'll draw a picture of a cute animal on the top in ketchup. In addition to this shop, there are 3 branch stores elsewhere in Akihabara.

spots.name: Cure Maid Cafe
spots.desc: The original and not quite as over-the-top (or expensive) as some of the competition. A long line can form on weekends.

spots.name: Neko JaLaLa
spots.desc: A 'cat cafe': you play with the shop's (very clean) cats while drinking tea. You'll be asked to remove your shoes and wash your hands on entry. You'll also be gently pressured to order one of their drinks. It's a different experience.
spots.price: ¥500 for first 30 minutes; ¥150 for each ten minutes; drinks ¥300 to ¥500

spots.name: Spa LaQua
spots.desc: One of Tokyo's largest spa complexes, using water pumped from 1,700m below Tokyo. Outdoor pools, saunas, beauty salons, restaurants and more across 5 floors. No tattoos or children under 5. Children under 17 can only enter with an adult and must leave before 6pm.
spots.price: ¥3,230/2,640 adult/child on weekdays, weekends +¥990, nights +¥2420 after 1am

spots.name: La Qua
spots.desc: La Qua is a new shopping mall with some attractions attached. It opened in 2003, replacing a section of the amusement park at Tokyo Dome City. There are boutiques, a grocery store, restaurants, a hairdresser, massage salon, and gym. In addition a roller coaster runs along the roof, and there are other amusement attractions including a water slide and a concert stage. Among all these, the main…

spots.name: Seijo Ishii
spots.desc: The supermarket chain has a store in La Qua, with many imported foods and wines. Many frozen products are sold in restaurant packs.

spots.name: Fire House
spots.desc: A popular hamburger restaurant decorated with American memorabilia.

spots.name: Hantei
spots.desc: Serves kushiage (deep fried skewered food) in a rare old wooden building.

spots.name: Komatsuan
spots.desc: Obsessively perfectionist handmade soba noodles for connoisseurs, made using only buckwheat from a certain village in Hokkaido and rolled on the thighs of virgins — or at least that's what you'd expect from the price. Their famous sakurakiri soba, available only from Apr-Jun, has real cherry blossom leaves mixed in.

spots.name: mAAch ecute Kanda Manseibashi
spots.local: マーチエキュート神田万世橋
spots.desc: A historic train station that's been converted into a shopping mall. Besides interesting shops and cafes, there's also a library and history exhibits about the station, including a large diorama showing the area around the station as it was in 1912 when it opened.

spots.name: Bic Camera
spots.desc: A huge, six-floor electronics store in front of JR Yurakucho Station, selling everything from household appliances to contact lenses. There is even a small movie theater on the 7th and 8th floors showing lesser-known Japanese and foreign films. Perhaps a good place for a one-stop shop if you are not able to spend time exploring the streets of Akihabara.

spots.name: Maruzen bookshop
spots.desc: It may be your best bet to look for English books in Tokyo, including a "Books on Japan" section. If you don't find what you are looking for here, you probably won't have much luck looking elsewhere.

spots.name: KITTE
spots.desc: The former Japan Post headquarters have been renovated into a trendy building with many shops and restaurants. The top roof is an open garden giving an amazing view on Tokyo Station, perfect for watching bullet trains come and go.

spots.name: Peter
spots.desc: Restaurant with amazing views of Imperial Palace and excellent service. Lunch seems the best value. Kobe beef from ¥23,500. Dress code: casual.

spots.name: Yamaya
spots.desc: For lunch you should get a bowl of rice with mentaiko (semi-spicy red fish eggs). Their specialty for dinner is motsunabe (tripe hotpot).

spots.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
spots.desc: The Outer Market of the Tsukiji Fish Market contain a bewildering array of shops. One shop carries nothing but dried seaweed, another knives, another is just bowls of all shapes and sizes! After you've had your sushi breakfast, wander around these shops and pick up something interesting.

spots.name: Ramen Cooking Tokyo
spots.desc: English-only small-group cooking class (maximum 8 participants) where visitors prepare ramen and sushi in a 3-hour session, with a sake pairing of three varieties. Located in Tsukishima, a short walk from the monja-yaki district.

spots.name: Sho-Chu Authority
spots.desc: This humbly named shop stocks over 3,000 varieties of the Japanese tipples shochu and awamori.

spots.name: Oshio Honten
spots.desc: The original shop of one of the better-known chains here, with half a dozen restaurants. Try the mentaiko-shiso monja with cod roe and perilla, which tastes oh so much better than it looks.

spots.name: Sushisay Main Store
spots.desc: Over 120 years old, this is now a large chain, but the head shop is in Tsukiji and it is well-reputed.

spots.name: Sushizanmai
spots.desc: The self-proclaimed "King Of Tuna", this is now a large chain but they originate from here in Tsukiji, where they have at least 7 locations and this three-story Honten. Prices are per roll and range from ¥100-500, or order a set meal for ¥3000. They have an excellent English menu.

spots.name: Tamahide
spots.desc: In business since 1760, perhaps the oldest in Tokyo. This restaurant specialises in Oyakodon, literally "parent-child bowl", made from spiced chicken with scrambled eggs (hence the name) and sweet sauce on rice. A popular comfort food with surprising complexity. Expect long queues.

spots.name: Tsujihan
spots.local: 日本橋海鮮丼 つじ半 日本橋本店
spots.desc: It is a Kaisen-dong store located near Tokyo Station. It is characterized by pouring stock with a little rice left.

spots.name: Meguro Parasitological Museum
spots.desc: One of a kind and oddly popular with couples on dates, although you might want to skip lunch before (or after) your visit here as the exhibits and pictures can be rather graphic. A compact two-story building, the most famous exhibit inside is an 8.8-meter-long tapeworm, with a matching string for you to take the measurement.

spots.name: Meguro Gajoen
spots.desc: A luxury hotel and wedding hall, with restaurants, cafes, and banquet rooms. One of the most popular attractions, though, is the spectacular public restroom.

spots.name: Gohyakurakanji
spots.desc: This temple contains over 300 statues, all with different facial expressions. They were all carved by the same monk from 1687 to 1695.

spots.name: Kameyamannendo
spots.desc: This Japanese-style confectionery shop was established in 1938.

spots.name: Wara
spots.desc: There are many kinds of kimono which is gathered all over Japan. Money pouch (巾着) and bag which are made by cloth of kimono are popular. In this shop, you can learn how to put on kimono.

spots.name: Sweets Forest
spots.desc: This is a mall dedicated to desserts. Multiple shops and cafes.

spots.name: Nana's Green Tea
spots.desc: This cafe has a lot of sweets and drinks made with powdered green tea and adzuki bean. Taste four kinds of Japanese tea. Try the Maccha chocolate latte.

spots.name: Hara-Donut
spots.local: はらドーナッツ 目黒店
spots.desc: Organic donut shop. Seemingly oxymoronic healthy donuts are made with soy milk.

spots.name: Tonki
spots.desc: Possibly good place to go for tonkatsu (breaded deep-fried pork cutlets), and popular with foreigners.
spots.hours: Closed Tue and third Mon of the month

spots.name: Junkadelic
spots.desc: Though the building looks a little old, this Mexican restaurant has some great Tex-Mex cuisine. The menu is not very large, but what it has is worth eating. Portions are reasonably sized, so consider getting an appetizer along with the main dish. For drinks, there are several Mexican beers and Mexican tequila available.

spots.name: Shutters
spots.desc: Try the apple pie a la mode. Popular dishes here are the odd combination of spare ribs and apple pie. You can eat many flavors of tender spare ribs such as soy sauce, basil, and mustard. You can choose from sauces on your apple pie: cinnamon, blueberry, raspberry, chocolate and caramel--with vanilla ice cream too.

spots.name: Jiyugaoka Burger
spots.desc: Domestically-sourced, organic and thick burgers in a lush balcony setting.

spots.name: Kochoo
spots.desc: Specializes in sundubu, a Korean stew which actually has roots in Los Angeles. All-you-can-eat banchan, which is common practice in Korea but rare in Japan!

spots.name: Mangetsu Korean Cuisine
spots.desc: Korean-run establishment with an intimate atmosphere, great for an evening date. Good chijimi!

spots.name: British Restaurant CLASH
spots.desc: Formerly known as The Meguro Tavern. A British-style pub with plenty of draft beers and football on the telly.

spots.name: Rakuya
spots.desc: Spacious, classy but casual restaurant-bar with live music every night.

spots.name: Speyside Way
spots.desc: Hundreds of whiskeys fill every available space. Hundreds. Short selection of micro-beers is also available.

spots.name: Japan Traditional Crafts Aoyama Square
spots.local: 伝統工芸 青山スクエア
spots.desc: Gallery and shop for handicraft products from all over Japan.

spots.name: Tokyo Cruise
spots.local: 水上バス 東京湾クルーズ (waterborne bus Tokyo Bay cruise)
spots.desc: Plies the Sumida River and Tokyo Bay between Hamamatsucho, Odaiba, Asakusa and other points.

spots.name: Japan Sake and Shōchū Information Center
spots.local: 日本の酒情報館 nihon no sake jōhōkan
spots.desc: This four-story complex run by the Central Brewers' Union sells anything and everything related to sake, including cups, glasses, books, hydrometers and, of course, the nectar itself. \315/515 gets you a taste of 3/5 sakes that change daily.

spots.name: Kua'aina
spots.desc: Hawaiian hamburgers, order-at-the counter from a picture menu with English.
spots.price: Meal sets are available for ¥1000, higher after 17:00

spots.name: Worldstar Cafe
spots.desc: Popular with business people or singles during lunchtime. Meal sets are ¥980–1200, comes w/ main, salad, drink; main being spaghetti, etc. Useful for a late night spot to hang around, since they're open until 06:00.

spots.name: Gonpachi
spots.desc: This lively and popular izakaya, with a spectacular spacious interior and high-profile location, has served luminaries such as George W. Bush and former Prime Minister Koizumi, and was the model for the battle scene in Quentin Tarantino's film Kill Bill. (The owner turned down the director's request to use the place itself.) Apart from this, it is a chain, so prices are reasonable food is not…

spots.name: Sarashina
spots.local: 麻布永坂 更科本店
spots.desc: One of the most famous restaurants for soba (buckwheat noodle). Try the various noodles they have, for instance egg noodles, with different colors. Their factory is still across the road despite sky-rocketing real estate prices.

spots.name: Tony Roma's
spots.desc: Step out of Japan and into the United States; the bilingual staff and English-only menu might make you forget you are in Tokyo. The restaurant features their trademark ribs, worth the price which starts at ¥1880. The Texas Mud Pie is the cure for tiny Japanese desserts.

spots.name: Nodaiwa
spots.desc: Perhaps the best spot in Japan to be served unagi, or freshwater eel. Famous for always using naturally grown eels, never farmed ones. In the business for more than 200 years, Nodaiwa remains as popular as ever.

spots.name: Anniversaire Cafe
spots.local: アニヴェルセルカフェ
spots.desc: This is a fashionable cafe of Paris style. You can enjoy elegant mood with seeing a row of houses and street of Omotesando. You can also choose fish or meat for lunch. Has another branch at Minato Mirai in Yokohama.

spots.name: Daigo
spots.desc: Exquisite vegetarian or vegan "shojin ryori" cuisine. This is the traditional Buddhist spin on kaiseki. Gracefully served by attentive kimono-clad staff. Small private dining rooms look out onto Japanese gardens. Very expensive, but a top-class experience.
spots.addr: Atago 2 chome 3-1, Atago Green Hills Forest Tower, 2F, Atago

spots.name: Narisawa
spots.desc: Ranked among the world's best restaurants and with two Michelin stars. Expect a blend of classical French techniques with the finest Japanese ingredients. Narisawa also has a commitment to sustainability, which expresses itself at the table.

spots.name: Ristorante da Nino
spots.desc: Within easy walking distance from both Tokyo Midtown and Roppongi crossing, owner chef Antonino Lentini offers fine and fresh Sicilian dishes. Good wine selection.
spots.price: Weekday lunch courses from ¥1400 (Saturday lunch courses from ¥2800); dinner courses from ¥8000

spots.name: Baishoin
spots.desc: 51 weeks of the year, this is just a small, unimportant and uninteresting temple connected to an equally uninteresting park / playground. But during one week in the year, in early April, this is where Nakano celebrates hanami. There are lots of white cherry trees on the way there already, and some more sakura can be seen on the grounds. At this time, there are also lots of food stalls and even a…

spots.name: Nakano Shiki-no-mori Park
spots.desc: Medium-sized park in the northwest of Nakano station, with a water playing area added in summer. Adjacent buildings (confusingly named Nakano Central Park) has many restaurants and fast food outlets. Shiki-no-mori means "forest of four seasons". Opened in 2012.

spots.name: Various Eateries
spots.desc: While you probably won't find any outstanding restaurants in Nakano, there's lots of options if you get hungry while there. There are lots of restaurants (mostly chains) in Nakano Sunmall and dozens of eateries and izakaya in the side streets next to it. There's something for every taste, e.g. ramen, sushi, soba, curry, pizza, and burgers.

spots.name: Marui's Restaurant Floor
spots.desc: A couple of typical department store restaurants, offering both Japanese and overseas food. Also has a good food section in the basement.

spots.name: Tamagawadai tumulus
spots.local: 多摩川台古墳群, Tamagawadai Kofungun
spots.desc: Zenpō-Kōenfun tumulus (前方後円墳). Built during the 4th and 5th centuries, many tumulus can be seen throughout several parks around Tamagawa station. A free small museum shows replicas of swords and other objects found in the graves, get the free English pamphlet before going around the tumulus, as you might miss them: they just look like small hills.

spots.name: JAL Sky Museum
spots.desc: You are allowed to enter the building only at the reserved time. They will first let you explore JAL Museum with exhibits, try on JAL pilot or flight attendant uniform, followed by brief video information session about Haneda airport and JAL operations. They will also go over safety rules before going on a guided tour to the maintenance hangar. Whole experience takes about 2 hours.
spots.hours: Tours runs on Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat and Sun at 09:30, 10:45 and 14:45 (increasing to Mon, Tue, Thu-Sun at 09:30, 10:45…

spots.name: ANA Blue Hangar Tour
spots.desc: Upon arrival, you will sit in a seminar room and they show a video about Haneda airport, ANA maintenance operation and safety rules. Afterwards, you can try out their business class and premium economy seats. The guide will take you to the ANA maintenance hangar. After the hangar tour, you can explore ANA museum for approximately 30 mins before boarding the free shuttle bus that takes you back to…
spots.addr: ANA Component Maintenance Building, 3-chōme-5-5 Haneda Airport

spots.name: Tamagawa River
spots.desc: It stretches from Haneda Airport to Kawasaki city and beyond. A great place for a jog or a bicycle ride with the locals. Best time to see it is in spring when all the cherry trees are in bloom.

spots.name: Kamata Onsen
spots.desc: Ota has the most number of onsens within Tokyo 23 wards. This particular onsen is famous for having black hotspring water from plant organic matter dissolving into the water.
spots.price: 12 years old and up ¥450, 6-12 years old ¥180, under 6 years old ¥80

spots.name: Granduo Kamata
spots.desc: Inside JR Kamata Station and split into East and West buildings, Granduo is a typical department store that has some good and reasonably priced restaurants and take-home food on the top and basement floors.

spots.name: Don Quijote
spots.desc: A 24-hour discount store that sells everything from grocery items to clothing, bicycles, electronics, jewelry, and gag gifts.

spots.name: Select Bar
spots.desc: One of the most popular 'standing bars' and frequented by Japanese and foreigners alike. All drinks and food is priced ¥300. They serve great meatloaf which fits well with a couple of beers.
spots.hours: Opens at 17:00 daily, closed on Sundays and public holidays

spots.name: Shot Bar St. Elmo's
spots.desc: A low-key bar in Omori serving excellent drinks, free traditional bar snacks are usually served.

spots.name: Setagaya Art Museum
spots.local: 世田谷美術館 Setagaya bijutsukan
spots.desc: Houses works by artists from the Primitivist School, such as Henri Rousseau.
spots.hours: Tue-Sun 10:00-18:00, last entry 17:30, closed at New Years
spots.price: Adults ¥200, college students ¥150, children and senior citizens ¥100

spots.name: Tamagawadaishi
spots.desc: A Buddhist temple, and a branch of Kawasaki Daishi. It isn't very large and the location is in a nondescript residential area, but its curious attraction is hidden: an underground passageway that snakes its way under the building. There are statues and altars with lighting at various points, but much of the tunnel is in absolute darkness. It symbolizes a passage through the intestines of the…

spots.name: Setagaya Park
spots.desc: A public park with a pool, tennis courts, baseball grounds and so on. There is a mini steam train and a retired full-size steam locomotive for children to play on.

spots.name: Saitama's Apartment
spots.desc: Real-life inspiration for the house where Saitama from the One Punch Man manga lived.

spots.name: Okuraland
spots.desc: Here you can go bowling or practice your golf swing. There are also batting cages.

spots.name: Kuhonbutsu River Green Street
spots.local: グリーンストリート・九品仏川緑道
spots.desc: Take a date, canine friend, or both for an afternoon stroll from Jiyugaoka to Kuhonbutsu. Lined with cherry trees (wonderful in spring), benches, shops and sidewalk cafes.

spots.name: Ex
spots.desc: Sells artistic designed stuff like photo stands, postcards, clocks, accessories and so on.

spots.name: Setagaya Boro-Ichi
spots.desc: A flea market that's held on the 15th and 16th of December and January each year. It's been drawing shoppers from all over Tokyo since it started in 1578. The main attraction is used clothing (such as kimono) and antiques.

spots.name: Tamagawa-Takashimaya S.C.
spots.desc: The original anchor, now renovated to keep up with its reputation as a fashion center, is home to many of the same international brand name boutiques you'd find in Ginza, Omotesandou, or Roppongi Hills. Many of its annexes are connected via pedestrian bridges or garden walkways.

spots.name: Futako-Tamagawa Rise
spots.desc: A complex of shopping centers and offices on the eastern end of the station. Rakuten Corporation has their headquarters right outside the station. Also has a bridge connected to a park.

spots.name: La Befana
spots.desc: Good pizza from wood-fired stone oven, something you will be missing if you are staying for a long time in Japan. The lunch menu is excellent.

spots.name: Setagaya
spots.desc: A famous ramen restaurant. Also has a branch at Haneda Airport Terminal 3.

spots.name: Shiro-Hige’s Cream Puff Factory
spots.local: 白髭のシュークリーム工房
spots.desc: Bakery specializing in adorable Totoro-shaped cream puffs, cookies and cakes.

spots.name: Village Vanguard Diner
spots.desc: Hamburger shop that has many kinds of very delicious hamburgers. Run by Village Vanguard, a chain of variety & bookstores.

spots.name: Ushi Tora
spots.desc: Two bars. One with tables & chairs, allows tobacco smoking, and accepts a credit card. One space over, a standing bar with more beers on tap, is non-smoking, and takes only cash.

spots.name: Kua'Aina
spots.desc: Branch of the Hawaiian-American burger joint found in on both sides of the Pacific.

spots.name: Moti
spots.desc: Moderately priced Indian food with a great view. Vegetarian options.

spots.name: Starbucks
spots.desc: While its ubiquity usually negates any need of mentioning, this particular location somewhat breaks from typical cookie-cutter mold through its unique seating arrangement and indoor garden setting.

spots.name: Jiyugaoka Burger
spots.desc: Domestically-sourced, organic and thick burgers in a lush balcony setting.

spots.name: Jiyugaoka Sweets Forest
spots.local: 自由が丘スイーツ・フォレスト
spots.desc: Cheerfully themed modern food park of sorts that brings together all kinds of kawaii-inspired sweets in one place.

spots.name: Kochoo
spots.desc: Specializes in sundubu, a Korean stew which actually has roots in Los Angeles. All-you-can-eat banchan, which is common practice in Korea but rare in Japan!

spots.name: Bear Pond Espresso
spots.desc: World-class espresso (very short ristretto with “sticky” texture) and excellent coffee, in a stylish, NY-style space. Ok to buy cupcakes from across the street. Ask before taking pictures.

spots.name: Mother
spots.desc: Multi-ethnic food and an interesting selection of imported beers, in a cave-like, Gaudi-inspired setting. If you come for food, make sure you have time to kill, as the kitchen works at a rather leisurely pace.

spots.name: Center Gai
spots.desc: The narrow street leading away from the station to the left of the giant video screen, it's famous as the birthplace of many of Japan's youth fashion trends. Center Gai is jam-packed with clothing stores, music stores, and video game arcades. This is a great place to stroll and feel the Shibuya vibe.

spots.name: Moyai statues
spots.desc: Another popular meeting spot, this time on the south side of the station, the two Moyai statues here are a spin on Easter Island's famous moai, made from volcanic pumice on Niijima in the Izu Islands far south of Tokyo. This, not the originals, was the inspiration for the 🗿 emoji.

spots.name: Bunkamura
spots.desc: Bunkamura-dori. A complex featuring an excellent art museum, in addition to theaters for film and stage plays. On the basement floor there's an art and design bookstore as well as a branch of Paris' famous Les Deux Magots café.

spots.name: Hikarie
spots.desc: Hikarie is a massive building on the east side of Shibuya Station with many restaurants, galleries, and theaters. Opened in 2012.

spots.name: Myth of Tomorrow
spots.local: 明日の神話, Ashita no shinwa
spots.desc: A huge mural by famous artist Tarō Okamoto, it commemorates the Hiroshima atomic bombing. A human figure in it burns and others appear to run from flames. The mural is at the entrance of the Inokashira line, 100 m from Hachikō. It was built in Mexico, found there in 2004 and brought to Japan in 2005. Under repair from Oct 2023.

spots.name: Mandarake
spots.desc: Massive shop devoted to manga, anime, hentai, dojinshi, figurines and collectible offshoots.
Department store with all of the usual high-end brands. Closed in 2022 for re-building, reopen due 2026.

spots.name: 109 Building
spots.desc: Teenage fashion. Worth an escalator trip. The name is a wordplay on Tokyu, its owner company: 10 is toh and 9 is kyu in Japanese.

spots.name: Disk Union
spots.desc: Used and new record dealer with floors each specializing in punk, rock, jazz and dance music.

spots.name: RECOfan
spots.desc: Good shopping for second-hand music in this cavernous hall: all records are categorized and alphabetized for quick browsing, and prices start at ¥100.

spots.name: Tower Records
spots.desc: For a while the largest record store in the world, now merely mind-bogglingly huge. Good selection of English books and magazines on the top floor, in addition to 6 other floors of J-pop, Western rock, jazz, classical and DVDs.

spots.name: Hands
spots.desc: Long known as Tokyu Hands, acquired by another company in 2022. Promoted as "Creative Life Store", Hands has everything from do-it-yourself, interior, hobby, crafts, outdoors to stationery and more. The Shibuya store spans eight floors.

spots.name: Loft
spots.desc: Loft is Seibu's answer to Tokyu Hands, also offering a large array of products related to interior, hobby, crafts and gifts, but with less strong emphasis on do-it-yourself. The Loft Shibuya branch consists of seven floors.

spots.name: Kujiraya
spots.desc: The specialty and only food here is whale meat dishes, which are very rare elsewhere. Human consumption of whale meat is controversial and has been denounced by detractors on grounds of wildlife conservation, toxicity, and animal rights. The restaurant hands out pro-whaling propaganda pamphlets.

spots.name: Murghi
spots.desc: Founded in 1951, when the owner decided to serve the kind of curry he had enjoyed in Burma before World War II.

spots.name: Tokyu Food Show
spots.desc: A superb food section in the basement with enough free samples to make a full lunch, if you don't mind not having a place to sit.

spots.name: Gonpachi
spots.desc: Trendy foreigner-friendly eatery specializing in soba, with a separate sushi bar in the back.

spots.name: Restaurant Kinoshita
spots.desc: Kinoshita makes eating French food in Japan justifiable. Some say that with its underpriced menu, dinner courses for ¥3800-¥7000, and weekday lunches for ¥1800, this restaurant is considered one of the best kept secrets in Tokyo. But in fact it is popular, and reservations are mandatory. Menu in French and Japanese.
spots.hours: 12:00-14:00, 18:00-21:00, closed Mondays and the third Tue of each month

spots.name: Udon Shin
spots.desc: Although it is Shibuya in terms of address, it is a udon store closer to Shinjuku. It is cost-effective and features homemade udon noodles.

spots.name: Mikore Sushi
spots.local: 江戸前割烹 三是寿司
spots.desc: It is a sushi restaurant located in Shibuya, but close to Shinjuku Station. The lunch special features cost-effectiveness.

spots.name: Cafe Apres-Midi
spots.local: カフェ・アプレミディ
spots.desc: Jazzy cafe with 1960s decor in moody lighting. Excellent food, try the quiche, although portions are small.

spots.name: Beat Cafe
spots.desc: Small cafe-bar-restaurant catering to the young alternative rock crowd. While showing constant videos from VH1 Classic on their TV, the easy drinking, simple eating crowd is about as friendly as they come. If you can't talk in your own native language, you can always discuss music.
spots.price: Cash only and drinks range from ¥500-1000

spots.name: The Aldgate
spots.desc: Down to earth smoke-free British-style pub, with a large number of Japanese and international beers on tap and a large collection of British Rock music on vinyl.

spots.name: Bar Ishinohana
spots.desc: Acclaimed high-end bar serving up drinks that are more works of art than cocktails. You may reserve seats from the English webpage.

spots.name: Camelot
spots.desc: Multi-room nightclub that plays a mix of hip-hop, r&b, and techno/house in their different areas. Most of the clientele is of a younger crowd (ages 20-25). Friday's entrance fee is only ¥1000 (including two drinks).
spots.addr: 神南1-18-2 神南坂フレームB2/B3

spots.name: Club Atom / STUDIO-A
spots.desc: Owned by Vanilla, this club houses three dance floors with music ranging from psychedelic trance to hip-hop.
spots.price: Entrance fee is only ¥1000 before midnight

spots.name: Harlem
spots.desc: Large two-floor all hip-hop club. Foreigners may not be admitted unless they bring along a Japanese friend.
spots.price: ¥3000, occasional discount if you enter before midnight

spots.name: Womb
spots.desc: One of Tokyo's largest clubs, designed by the people behind New York's Twilo and the setting of a scene in Babel.

spots.name: Oto
spots.desc: Upscale club of mostly locals that have live jazz bands and DJs. Music ranges from jazz, electro, to Euro rock.

spots.name: Rock West
spots.desc: A smaller, friendly club that specialised in underground techno, fairly well hidden on 7F of an office building. It's certainly one of the cheaper spots in the area.
spots.price: Cover charge of ¥1000 and most drinks around ¥500

spots.name: Showa Neon Takamura Kanban Museum
spots.local: 昭和ネオン高村看板ミュージアム
spots.desc: The sign company Showa Neon has a museum with shop signs from the Edo and early Meiji periods. Reportedly all descriptions in this museum are in Japanese. Closed in June 2023 for renovation; reopen due in March 2025.

spots.name: Aqua Park Shinagawa
spots.desc: Aquarium with dolphin and seal shows and hundreds of species of fish. There is also a carousel ride.
spots.price: Adults ¥1,800; Elementary and middle school students ¥1,000; Kids over 4 years old ¥600

spots.name: Takanawa Catholic Church
spots.desc: This modern church rebuilt on a historic site is handicapped-accessible and has Sunday Mass in English on the fourth Sunday of each month at 13:00.

spots.name: Ōi Horse Race Course
spots.local: 大井競馬場, Tokyo City Keiba
spots.desc: The best racecourse affiliated to National Association of Racing, the umbrella organization for local horseracing operators. Tokyo Dai-Shoten race in December is rated as international Grade I. Many restaurants and food stands. Night races from March to December are decorated with beautiful illuminations.

spots.name: Coffee Roast Sai
spots.desc: Roasts beans while you wait (30-60 min), usually with a wonderful free cup of coffee. For true connoisseurs.

spots.name: eCute Shinagawa
spots.desc: A small food court and take out restaurants featuring a couple of dozen food stands and bakery or sweet shops on the first level. This is also a very comfortably air-conditioned place to wait for a train connection. There are some full-service restaurants on the upper level. A few examples of shops include:.
spots.hours: 08:00-22:00 for most shops, some open earlier

spots.name: Andersen
spots.desc: If you are making an early departure for Kamakura or points south pick up sandwiches to go

spots.name: Kongariya
spots.desc: Select from a wide range of onigiri with interesting fillings like squid and kimchee, miso or shoyu grilled riceballs, or even ones wrapped in Indian naan and baked.

spots.name: Atre Shinagawa
spots.desc: A collection of restaurants grouped around a Queens Isetan grocery. Dean & Deluca, on the second floor, has a take-out sandwich and coffee bar which is convenient for supplies to get you through a long Shinkansen ride. The fourth floor has the Lounge Foodium restaurant complex including Grand Central Oyster Bar.

spots.name: Royal Host
spots.desc: Popular "family restaurant" chain with surprisingly good coffee but little else that stands out.

spots.name: Tsubame Grill (Shinagawa-ekimae)
spots.local: つばめグリル 品川駅前店
spots.desc: Tsubame Grill chain is famous for its "hamburg" dish. Contrary to belief, lunch special only costs ¥1150 — a bargain for the excellent quality of food. The "hamburg" dish comes piping hot covered completely in an aluminum foil.

spots.name: 82 Ale House
spots.desc: Very convincing Victorian style British pub run by the same company as another popular pub chain, HUB. Largish drinks menu which includes single malt whiskeys, real ale and Guinness on tap for ¥900 a pint.
spots.hours: Last orders are at 22:45 on Saturdays and Sundays

spots.name: Shinjuku-sanchōme and related red-light districts to the east of the station
spots.desc: It is perfectly safe to walk around here during the day and marvel at the photo billboards of various male and female escorts on offer as well as the live gangster-types acting shady. While it probably shouldn't be done with children, for adults the result is far more "cultural interest" than sleaze.

spots.name: Tokyo Toy Museum
spots.local: 東京おもちゃ美術館 Tokyo omocha bijutsukan
spots.desc: An old school filled with toys and fun small houses. Accompanying adults won't get bored, thanks to the variety of toys.

spots.name: Suga Shrine
spots.local: 東京四谷総鎮守 須賀神社
spots.desc: It is a shrine located around Shinjuku. It is a small shrine, but the stairs in front of it are famous as the background in the animated movie Your Name.

spots.name: Karaokekan
spots.desc: Karaokekan is a large chain of karaoke shops. They have rooms available from one person up to a large party. All you can drink set menus are available.

spots.name: Shinjuku Piccadilly
spots.desc: The newest movie theater in Shinjuku. It features stadium seating and "platinum" seating. Platinum seating ranges from a semi-private room, including a private lounge (¥5000 per person) to a private room, including a relaxation room (¥30,000 for 2 people).

spots.name: Wald 9
spots.desc: Part of the new generation of movie theaters in Tokyo. It features stadium seating, a small gift shop, and clean theaters.

spots.name: Cinem@rt Shinjuku
spots.desc: 335 seats total. Mondays are Men's Days, when men can watch movies for ¥1000. Wednesdays are Ladies' Days, when ladies can watch movies for only ¥1000.

spots.name: Marui
spots.desc: Marui is well known department store known for focusing on the 16-32 year age group. Spread out around Shinjuku Sanchome, the main building is next to Shinjuku Gyoen. The men's building is north of the main building and Marui Young is west of Isetan.

spots.name: Mylord
spots.desc: Cloths department store run by Odakyu, targeted at younger age group.

spots.name: Bookoff
spots.desc: Bookoff is a well-known second-hand book store. They also offer various albums, games, and movies.

spots.name: Books Kinokuniya
spots.desc: Books Kinokuniya is the best book store for foreign language books. The Main Branch is the older of the two, however, the Southern Branch has a greater selection of foreign language books.

spots.name: Book 1st
spots.desc: The largest bookstore on the west side is hidden underground. Navigation inside may be a pain for its unusual layout. English books are in the C3 area.

spots.name: Bic Camera
spots.desc: Second-largest electronics shop in Shinjuku. While not as big as Yodobashi Camera, prices and product range is roughly the same. The East side shop, next to Books Kinokuniya, is bigger than Yodobashi's East side shop, but still smaller than the West side location.

spots.name: Yodobashi Camera
spots.desc: Yodobashi is the largest electronics retailer in Shinjuku. The main building is their multimedia centre. They also have a dedicated building each for Games, Camera, Travel, Watch and Mobile/smartphone (with a liquor section in the basement). Yodobashi also has a branch on the east side of Shinjuku, across from Lumine EST.

spots.name: Disk Union
spots.desc: You can get music, movies, and music books. Another branch at Shinjuku 3-17-5 specialize in specific genres or used goods. Great for music enthusiasts.

spots.name: HMV
spots.desc: HMV is one of the bigger record stores in Japan with a good selection of music and movies. Another store at Shinjuku Alta 6F.

spots.name: Tower Records
spots.desc: Tower Records is one of the biggest record stores in Japan. They have any CD or DVD you can imagine, and if not, you can probably order or reserve it.

spots.name: Nishi-Shinjuku 7-chome
spots.desc: Packed with music shops specializing in various genres such as punk and heavy metal. Many sell nothing but bootlegs and collectibles.

spots.name: West Exit Square Event Space
spots.local: 西口広場イベントスペース
spots.desc: An area hosting a rotating series of stalls or exhibits. These have included various local foods from around Japan, furniture, art prints and information about various government projects around Tokyo. The underground area around it is a great place to find takeaway food and fast food outlets - named Keio Mall, Odakyu Ace and Shinjuku Delish Park (temporary location for Odakyu's depachika).

spots.name: Blumare
spots.desc: Pizza and pasta restaurant. The building is full of restaurants all run by Sapporo Beer.

spots.name: Suzuya
spots.desc: This tonkatsu restaurant is famous for its green tea tonkatsu, which is salty and filling. It also serves other types of tonkatsu and katsudon.

spots.name: Martiniburger
spots.desc: This restaurant serves hamburgers and martinis. The large juicy hamburgers are made with high quality ground beef, which is very hard to find anywhere in Japan. Though uncommon, the combination of hamburgers and martinis is surprisingly nice.

spots.name: Acacia Shinjuku
spots.desc: Specialises in cabbage rolls. Also has a set menu with hashed rice and pork sauté. Has a branch at Haneda Airport.

spots.name: Botejyu
spots.desc: Botejyu is an okonomiyaki shop that sells a variety of okonomiyaki. They also have various yaki-soba dishes. Beware that at times, this restaurant can be busy with wait times of up to 30 min.

spots.name: Kappō Nakajima
spots.desc: Specializes in sardine dishes. Yanagawa teishoku is deep-fried sardines with scrambled eggs on rice (it tastes better than it sounds).

spots.name: Hokkaido
spots.desc: Enjoy the view while dining on seafood and other specialties of Hokkaido. Got another branch near Shinjuku station (9F 110 Building).
spots.addr: 53rd floor of Tokyo Opera City (see above)

spots.name: Yanbaru
spots.desc: Now occupying the whole of a three-story building, there's nothing pretentious about this restaurant specializing in Okinawan food, which emphasizes pork and vegetables that are unusual even to Honshu Japanese. Recommend is beni imo korokke (¥480), tempura-style sweet potato; and hechima misoni (¥620), an eggplant-like vegetable served in a strongly fermented miso sauce. A picture menu is…

spots.name: Din Tai Fung
spots.desc: Tokyo branch of the renowned Taiwan dim sum restaurant; speciality is the xiǎolóngbāo (小籠包) soup-in dumplings.

spots.name: Nabezo
spots.desc: An all-you-can-eat Shabu Shabu restaurant with another branch in Shinjuku and many other places. \3850 gets one person 100 minutes, including unlimited meat, veggies, and ice cream. Drinks cost extra, but water and Gobo cha are free. If 100 minutes isn't enough, extend 30 minutes for additional \550.

spots.name: Onegiya Shinjuku ten
spots.desc: Excellent traditional but modern Japanese restaurant. Plenty of dishes to order but you need to like leeks.

spots.name: Zauo
spots.desc: Indoor fishing and restaurant combined at dinner time...(click the link and see photos). No fishing on weekday lunch time.

spots.name: Torafugu-Tei
spots.desc: Specializing in the infamous fugu (blowfish), it's one of the huge number of seafood restaurants in Kabukichō (see below). Set dinners go for around ¥5000, featuring fugu prepared five or six ways, fresh from the tank. Has another branch nearby (at 1-3-15 Kabukicho).

spots.name: Araku
spots.desc: Australian-run, considerably larger and can be less intimidating than many other Golden Gai establishments.

spots.name: Hair of The Dogs
spots.desc: Punk rock with a dash of Mexican Luchadors. Good cocktails and beer at an average of ¥700 a drink. The owner, Tohru, is very welcoming to anyone who loves to rock. Cover charge lets you sit at the bar and choose music from a menu split into various Punk Rock styles (UK, USA, Japan, Hardcore, Goth, Oi, Mod, Post Punk, 70s, 80s etc). Movies like Taxi Driver and Sid & Nancy are played from a cheap…

spots.name: Bar Albatross-G
spots.desc: Casual cocktail bar with Burgundy painted walls, chandeliers and no-frills mixology. Cover charge includes a small snack of either noodles, miso or whatever's brewing. Most drinks are around ¥700. Space includes a second floor "attic" accessible by a thin staircase with more fixtures and local artists' creations. Also visit the original Albatross bar in Shinjuku Omoide-Yokocho.

spots.name: Rock Bar: Mother
spots.desc: Has an extensive collection of Punk and Metal CDs for those looking for some alternative rock.

spots.name: New York Bar & Grill
spots.desc: One of the main sets for Lost in Translation, this slick joint on the 52nd floor has dark decor and floor-to-ceiling windows with jaw-dropping vistas, with live jazz nightly. Eating a steak here would cost you well north of ¥20,000 per head, but you can nurse a beer for a mere ¥1000 or, "for relaxing times", try out Bill Murray's Suntory Hibiki for ¥3,500.

spots.name: Casablanca
spots.desc: A two level nightclub and lounge with a large dance floor and darts. The DJ normally spins hip-hop, R&B, reggae, and house, and there are live house performances periodically through the night.

spots.name: Loft/Plus One
spots.desc: Performance art space meets bar run with a simple concept: different people and groups rent a block of time and do whatever they want to. The end result runs from stand-up comedy and lectures to porn star photo shoots and incredibly violent live S&M. Erotic shows 18+ only (ID required).

spots.name: Tokyo Loose
spots.desc: Small bar full of men. It's not easy to find, so call for directions.

spots.name: AiiRO Cafe
spots.desc: Cruisy open-air bar with a torii gate at the entrance. Crowd spilling onto the street makes it feel like a block party.

spots.name: Arty Farty
spots.desc: Among Nichō's most well-known pubs, with a thumping dance floor. A hand stamp upon entry will also get you into sister bar The Annex.

spots.name: Dragon Men
spots.desc: Masculine gay pub with a dance floor. Rebuilt after a fire, the place is popular among male and female foreigners, and with Japanese men.

spots.name: Gold Finger
spots.desc: Primarily lesbian bar with all-female staff, and karaoke for the multinational patrons. Interior themed like a 1970s motel. Saturday is strictly women-only; Monday is FtM night.

spots.name: Doutor
spots.desc: Doutor is a relatively "salary man" coffee shop. You will see lots of business men within this shop. Non-smoking, with some shops equipped with smoking booths.

spots.name: Excelsior Caffe
spots.desc: Excelsior Caffe and Doutor are run by the same company, however Excelsior Caffe caters to a younger, more feminine crowd and one-notch upscale. Generally non-smoking, with bigger shops have separate smoking rooms.

spots.name: Pronto/Di Punto
spots.desc: Pronto is a very relaxed cafe/bar that is a cafe during the day. They offer premium style drinks.
spots.hours: Cafe style opens in the morning and closes around 17:30. Then bar opens within minutes

spots.name: Segafredo Zanetti Espresso
spots.desc: Segafredo is a somewhat upscale Italian style cafe that has various locations near Shinjuku. Segafredo tends to have a darker atmosphere akin to Pronto and offers many kinds of alcoholic drinks too.
spots.addr: 3 locations near Shinjuku Station and another in Tokyo Opera City

spots.name: Canal Cafe
spots.desc: In the far east of Shinjuku City in the Kagurazaka district. With views remarkable for Tokyo, Canal Cafe consists of a separate restaurant and cafe situated alongside a canal. The open-air cafe has great ambiance. At the restaurant figure ¥6000-9000 for dinner, but at the café, which is a long patio-like dock, drinks and snacks are purchased at the bar and can be quite reasonable.

spots.name: Tokiya
spots.desc: Japanese sweets and drinks. Famous for dorayaki, drum-shaped cake with red-bean paste inside.

spots.name: HUB
spots.desc: Popular chain of cash-on-delivery English pubs. Have some fish and chips with your pint at one of four Shinjuku locations. "82 Ale House" pubs are run by the same company with wider selection of whiskeys.

spots.name: Marone
spots.desc: Tucked away in this tiny cubbyhole of a space is one of the most interesting small bars in Tokyo. A country western theme with Chet Baker and Nat King Cole pouring from the stereo. The food is cheap and superbly done (think chili nachos and the like); beer and spirits are also available. The place is tiny but it attracts a great mix of young groups of friends and office workers. Some nights…

spots.name: Vagabond
spots.desc: A great little pub with two floors. The first floor is a little more private while the top floor is a very cozy jazz bar with live music and a good selection of finger foods cooked right at the bar for you. Caution to taller travelers: it's a little cramped at the bar. Cover charge and drinks are ¥500-700. The pub usually closes around 23:00 to 23:30 leaving you with plenty of time to get the…

spots.name: Suginami Historical Museum
spots.desc: It is small but has some interesting findings from the prehistoric and historic times.

spots.name: Namisuke
spots.desc: Namisuke is Suginami's official character and can be seen in posters on walls and loaves in convenience stores.

spots.name: Myōshō-ji Temple
spots.desc: Myosyoji Temple built in 1325, then rebuilt in 1646. Myosyoji park and Myosyoji river are nearby.

spots.name: Myōshōji River
spots.desc: The Myoshoji River starts from Myoshoji Pond in Myoshoji Park, then passes near Myoshoji Temple and finally meets the Kanda River. Cherry trees bow gracefully along the river.

spots.name: Myōshōji Park
spots.desc: Myoshoji Park is bigger than most other parks. One highlight is Myoshoji Pond, which has a fountain.

spots.name: Suginami kōkaidō
spots.desc: Suginami kōkaidō is a building that was built in 1957, then reconstructed in 2006. Many kinds of events take place here, including the coming of age ceremony for 20-year-olds.

spots.name: Omiya Hachimangū
spots.desc: Built in 1053, the shrine is sometimes called "The Navel of Tokyo" because the center of Tokyo Metropolis lies there. It is said praying at the shrine brings easy delivery of your child.

spots.name: Zenpukuji Park
spots.desc: Near Tokyo Women's Christian University. There is a lot of greenery. This park is well-known for water lily in the pond. You can take a boat and see them blooming in late May to early July.

spots.name: A-san no niwa
spots.desc: A small Ghibli-studio like garden with a cute house for an urban escape within the city itself.
spots.addr: 5 Chome-45-13 Asagayakita, Suginami City, Tokyo 166-0001, Japan

spots.name: Kōen-ji
spots.desc: Has many used clothing and other shops and restaurants, as well as "live houses" where bands play all genres of music. After the war many temples and shrines were moved here and now there are many walking tours to visit them.

spots.name: Tokyo Kōenji Awa Odori
spots.desc: The Tokyo Kōenji Awa Odori is held yearly on the last Saturday and Sunday in August. About 1.2 million people show up to eat, drink and watch 188 groups (or 12,000 dancers) perform Awa dance to lively music and parade through the nine routes set up along the Shotengai station-front street. It is the second largest Awa Odori festival in Japan, after Tokushima.

spots.name: Wadabori Park
spots.desc: A large park in Omiya that runs along Zenpukuji River. It is a popular place for groups and families to barbecue. There is a small pond, restaurant, and fishing tanks. There is also a children's park for bicycle training in a safe area with street signs and traffic signals. There is a traditional thatched roof house near the park as well. Kingfishers have their habitats in this area which is very…

spots.name: Baan-Esan
spots.desc: A trip to Thailand just a minute's stroll from Koenji Station's south exit. Located on the Koenji shotengai, they serve good-sized portions of traditional Thai food but not at Tokyo prices. Most dishes are ¥580 and great for sharing. The service is less than stellar, but the Thai woman in charge of the kitchen makes the wait worth it.

spots.name: Miyagawa
spots.desc: Another yakitori-ya. It is small but has outdoor seating for about eight, and is some of the best yakitori you can find. Decorated with rock and blues paraphernalia spanning from the 1940s, it's got friendly staff, good prices and great food.

spots.name: Taishō
spots.desc: A popular open-air yakitori restaurant. Cheap and good, it's crowded late into the night with the young and old working on tomorrow's hangover. Just look for the big red sign and tables made from milk crates. Two other locations of Taishō are also near the station: one about 100 m west of the station adjacent to the train tracks out the same exit, and another about two blocks straight north of…

spots.name: Ebisu Yakitori
spots.desc: Don't let the glitzy photos on the website fool you. This branch consists of a sometimes changing string of tiny storefronts, kiosks, and rickety tables in the alley running west from the south exit of the station. Get ready for a raucous and very crowded and chaotic but fun experience.
spots.price: Per piece from as low as ¥90

spots.name: B-Glad
spots.desc: A large restaurant-bar just north of the intersection of Ome-Kaido and the main street leading to Kōenji Station. The menu is a blend of Japanese and Western dishes (pasta, salad, pizza, yakitori) ranging from ¥450 to 1200. Located in the basement, it's extremely spacious by Japan standards, with comfortable seating, free billiards, and two electronic dart boards. Highballs are ¥550 and beer…

spots.name: Rad Bros Cafe
spots.desc: Clinical white & gray lab serving up fine coffee, both espresso and drip, and Basque (burnt) cheesecake. The most intriguing item on offer is a frozen cheesecake pudding served Mont Blanc style with freshly squeezed chestnut threads on top (¥1600, large enough for 2).

spots.name: Tokyo Solamachi
spots.desc: Tokyo's largest commercial complex, with over 300 shops and restaurants, plus an aquarium and a planetarium, at the base of Tokyo Skytree.

spots.name: Chanko Tomoegata
spots.desc: One of Tokyo's oldest chanko joints, operating for over 100 years, specializing in a slightly unusual miso-flavored soup. Lunch sets at ¥840/1260 weekdays/weekends are just about the cheapest chanko you'll find anywhere and a good option for the solo traveller. Dinner starts from ¥2940/person for the Tomoegata (miso) or Yahazuyama (dashi) set and goes up to ¥8400 for the aptly…

spots.name: Popeye Beer Club
spots.desc: Popeye's is an excellent place to try Japanese microbrews. There are 70 beers on tap, which cover the full range of beers from familiar ales to barley wines and rauchbiers. The food menu is interesting, try the avocado and blue cheese. English menus are available. Not English friendly if you have problems asking about the menu or bill. Not a standing bar, you have to be seated and charged for…
spots.price: Pints of beer are around ¥900, half pints and a sampler set are available

spots.name: Asakusa Smile Bar & Cafe
spots.local: 浅草スマイルバー&カフェ
spots.desc: Founded by a Tokyo resident returning from abroad. Located across the Sumida river from the Asakusa tourist district. Clientele has many expats and English-speaking Japanese. Periodically hosts an English-language comedy show.

spots.name: SCAI The Bathhouse
spots.desc: A small gallery showing the work of contemporary artists, the building is a former sento, or bathhouse.

spots.name: Iwasaki's Ganso Shokuhin Sample-ya
spots.desc: Make your own replica food or sample food (sampuru) out of wax. This shop, in Tokyo's Kappabashi restaurant supply district, offers onsite workshops and at-home DIY kits to make food from wax. Workshops are usually conducted in Japanese. If you don't want to make it yourself, then you can buy the company's readymade options from the store, or order some of the more elaborate pieces for delivery.…

spots.name: Kappabashi
spots.desc: A more offbeat shopping option, it is best reached from Tawaramachi station on the Ginza line. This is Tokyo's restaurant wholesale district, which sells plastic food, metal spatulas, deep fryers and an immense variety of affordable crockery. Some shops sell only in wholesale quantities, but many are happy to sell single items and factory-made Japanese pottery (which to the casual eye is…

spots.name: Dengama
spots.desc: A particularly good boutique specializing in handmade Japanese pottery. The discount racks outside are downright cheap at several hundred yen a pop, but more expensive items on the second floor may run into tens of thousands of yen. Don't miss the trays of wacky decorative chopstick holders.
spots.addr: at the corner of Kappabashi-dori and Asakusa-dori

spots.name: Kiwa Seisakusho
spots.desc: 5 floors of plastic baubles of all shapes and sizes. Three shops in Asakusabashi alone, the largest near exits A4 and A2 of the metro.

spots.name: Chaho Kanekichi-en
spots.desc: An old-school tea shop near the entrance to Yanaka Ginza, just follow the smell of roasting tea. They prepare their own blends, which are uniformly excellent: try the slightly bitter Snow Plum (雪の梅 Yuki-no-Ume, ¥600 per 100g) or the unusual Yanaka Midori (谷中みどり, ¥600-1000 per 100g), a mix of roasted tea stems (the cheapest tea) with tea-ceremony grade matcha (the most expensive tea). Ask…

spots.name: Gotō no Ame
spots.desc: A traditional Japanese candy (ame) shop at the very end of Yanaka Ginza, everything sold here is made on premises and quite cheap (¥100+).

spots.name: Aoi Marushin
spots.desc: Tempura, Tempura, Tempura. Aoi Marushin is the largest tempura restaurant in Tokyo!

spots.name: Bentenyama Miyakozushi Souhonten
spots.desc: This is a very small, very expensive sushi restaurant in Taito. If you are a sushi buff this is that place for you, with fantastic sushi and great ambiance.

spots.name: Cigars & Cafe LWAN
spots.desc: A cigar bar that serves coffee, alcoholic drinks, and desserts. There is a large cigar selection, in particular from the Dominican Republic.

spots.name: Zakuro
spots.desc: Located in the heart of the traditional Yanaka neighborhood, this Persian/Turkish restaurant goes all-out on the "dining experience": you sit on the carpeted floor, they make you wear middle-eastern garb, and dessert includes a hookah (water-pipe) to puff on! And all the while, the owner wanders from table to table making wisecracks in Japanese. The set dinner course (¥2000) is guaranteed to…

spots.name: Honmyōji Temple
spots.desc: This temple is known for a fire called Meireki-no-Taika, an inferno 400 years ago which killed over 100,000 people. It is said that this fire broke out in Honmyōji. There are also some tombs of famous people in this temple. A Japanese swordman Chiba Shūsaku and a political office leader Tōyama Kinshirō, for example.

spots.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Theatre
spots.desc: Offers various exhibits and concerts behind the impressive glass facade.
spots.addr: on the west side of the Ikebukuro train/subway station

spots.name: Tokyo Shaheed Minar
spots.desc: A beautiful monument, symbolizing love to the mother language. It is based on the mother language movement, that originated in Dhaka, Bangladesh in 1952, followed by the UNESCO declaration of International Mother Language Day (21 February). It was a present from Bangladesh to the Japanese people, in 2005, recognizing Tokyo Boishakhi Mela (Bangladesh New Year Festival), organized every year in mid…

spots.name: Ikefukurō
spots.desc: A statue of an owl (fukurō) near the east exit. Many people use this as a meeting spot.

spots.name: Manten
spots.desc: There is a planetarium called Manten (meaning "full sky") in Sunshine City. This planetarium shows three types of programs and repeats them in a day. These three types of programs are called The Planetarium Program, The CG Planetarium Program, The Healing Program. The Planetarium Program shows some themes of programs with Japanese famous musicians. The CG Planetarium Program shows science…

spots.name: Mandarake
spots.desc: One of the Mandarake chain of used anime/manga goods stores, the Ikebukuro branch specializes in doujinshi, in particular doujinshi for girls.

spots.name: Bic Camera
spots.desc: This discount retailer's flagship store on the east side of the station, with several branches nearby.

spots.name: Sugamo
spots.desc: Popularly known as "Grandma's Harajuku" (obaachan no Harajuku), and indeed most shops in the area do seem targeted towards an older clientèle. For the (rare) tourist, however, this means a plentiful supply of tea, pottery, kitchen implements and clothes in styles that went out of fashion 50 years ago. The area is at its liveliest on the 4th, 14th and 24th of each month when a street market is…

spots.name: Maruji
spots.desc: Probably the most famous and successful shop in Sugamo, Maruji specializes in one thing: red underwear (赤パンツ aka-pantsu). By energizing a pressure point below your navel, Maruji's crimson panties, boxers and long-johns will keep you warm and fill you with vigor — or so they say.
spots.addr: Sugamo 4-21-11 and three other outlets nearby

spots.name: Konaya
spots.desc: The original shop of restaurant chain renowned for its curry udon noodles. The noodles are cut by hand, the special curry stock is brewed for two days, and ¥1210 will get you some mighty fine tasting udon.

spots.name: Fight Gyoza
spots.desc: Famous for deep-fried gyoza. So many people stand in a line in front of the restaurant.

spots.name: Souten
spots.desc: High-end yakitori. Five stick set from around ¥1,600. Do try the chicken sashimi--outside the comfort zone for many visitors, but you may be pleasantly surprised. Extensive selection of nihonshu featuring Kozaemon. Its website has some English info.

spots.name: Tobu and Seibu basements
spots.desc: Urban Japanese keep their grocery stores beneath their department stores. If you go to the B1 and B2 levels of the massive stores flanking the Ikebukuro station, you will find endless acres of raw and prepared food. Buy a bunch and take it back to your hotel fridge.

spots.name: Shakey's Pizza
spots.desc: Down Sunshine-Dori on the way to Sunshine 60, on the left, there's a Shakey's Pizza. There are lunchtime buffets with great pizza the way only Japanese like to serve it.

spots.name: Ghiottone
spots.desc: Excellent pasta and salads, in portions that are ample for two. The crab spaghetti is very popular. No non-smoking tables.

spots.name: Malay-Chan
spots.desc: A small Malaysian restaurant on the west side of the train/subway station that is a little hard to find. Halal food.

spots.name: Al-Flah
spots.desc: A halal supermarket and restaurant that sells halal food, including vegetarian curries. The store also conveniently has a bollywood-movie section.

spots.name: Namja Town
spots.desc: Namja Town has some big food shops in Sunshin City– the gyoza studium, the ice cream city, and the dessert empire of Tokyo. Gyoza is a kind of Japanese food. The gyoza stadium collects gyozas of many famous gyoza restaurants in Japan. The ice cream city collects many kinds of ice creams in the world. The dessert empire of Tokyo collects some famous cakes. And it has events regularly. For example…

spots.name: Sakura Cafe Ikebukuro
spots.desc: Opened in 2008, one of Tokyo's largest open-air-terrace cafes with easy-going and relaxed style located at 1st floor of "Sakura Hotel Ikebukuro" which welcomes guests from over 110 countries every year. International atmosphere with 60 beers from around the world from ¥550, monthly changing snacks and meals from ¥300 also from a wide variety of countries, and coffee for ¥180.

spots.name: Ohori Park Japanese Garden
spots.desc: This beautiful, small Japanese garden is right next to Ohori Park.
spots.hours: Tue-Sun 09:00-17:00, closed Mondays and Dec 29 - Jan 3

spots.name: Kego Koen
spots.desc: The park behind Solaria Plaza, Kego Koen, is a great place to go to experience Tenjin's youth culture and do some people watching. Don't be surprised if some of these kids try to approach you for a bit of random conversation.

spots.name: Asian Art Museum
spots.desc: This gallery hosts temporary exhibitions from Kyushu and all around Asia. It has a good shop.

spots.name: Bayside Place Hakata Pier
spots.desc: For a view of the bay, check out the Bayside Place Hakata Pier:a marine terminal for the regular service ferries for Tsushima Island and Hakata Bay cruise boats. The terminal building has an 8-m-tall aquarium, with 6,000 fish.

spots.name: Fukuoka City Science Museum
spots.desc: Cotains Robosquare on its 5th floor. You can see and play with different kinds of robots and watch some of the engineers at work. Despite the imposing sounding name, Robosquare is one medium sized-room with a few robotics exhibits and some toy robots and is primarily aimed at children. Some English explanations are now available.
spots.price: Free but ¥510 adults/ 310 high schoolers / 200 children each for 5F exhibition room and 6F planetarium

spots.name: Ichiran Ramen Museum
spots.desc: Ichiran is one of the largest chains of Hakata ramen restaurants, with locations all across Japan and in several other countries. At this factory, you can learn about the ramen-making process and view their factory where they make noodles. At the end is a small restaurant with a weekly special dish. The museum is entirely in Japanese.

spots.name: Marine World Uminonakamichi
spots.local: マリンワールド海の中道
spots.desc: It is an aquarium and you can watch shows of various marine life, and there are also various hands-on activities, such as feeding dolphins. There is also a park outside the aquarium.

spots.name: Noh theatre
spots.desc: A cultural experience that some may not want to miss. There is a Noh theatre in Ohori Koen. Many of the performances are free, get more information at the Rainbow Plaza (IMS building 8th floor). Don't worry, if you fall asleep during the play, it's almost expected. It's all part of the Noh experience.

spots.name: Hakata Dontaku
spots.desc: Japan's largest festival, drawing well over 2 million people during the Golden Week holidays. The name "Dontaku" comes from Dutch "zondag" meaning Sunday. The festival features traditional dance.
spots.hours: May 3–4, with a pre-ceremony on May 2

spots.name: Hakata Gion Yamakasa
spots.desc: Fukuoka's second-largest festival, drawing up to a million spectators, is famous for the Oiyama parade float race. The elaborately-decorated yamakasa floats, around 5 m tall and weighing up to , have no wheels; they're picked up and carried by teams of loincloth-clad men, each team representing one of the seven historic districts of Hakata. The race takes place on July 15; teams line up around…

spots.name: Nokonoshima Island Park
spots.desc: Has several well manicured gardens and fields of flowers that vary by the season.

spots.name: Nishidori
spots.desc: It is easy to find thanks to the Apple store on the corner with Kokutai Dohro. The area to your left is Daimyo, full of funky little boutiques and shops. There are also a countless number of restaurants, lunch time being a great time to try out their specials.

spots.name: Nakasu Kawabata shopping arcade
spots.desc: A long, old-fashioned shopping streets with a variety of shops selling traditional Japanese goods among other items. Good for picking up souvenirs and other randomness.

spots.name: Hakata City
spots.desc: Another large shopping area is the Hakata Station area. It includes over 230 shops, restaurant floor, and roof observation deck. With regards to gift-giving, if you're pressed for time, take a quick look around the craft and boutique stores in Hakata Station before leaving. Many carry the white clay Hakata dolls that are unique to Fukuoka. Prices range from under ¥1,000. Prices comparable to…

spots.name: Yodobashi Camera store
spots.desc: For cameras, computers or other electronics, there is a huge Yodobashi Camera store right outside of Hakata station. Go out to the eastern side of the JR station (Chikushi Gate), go down 2 blocks and it will be on your right.

spots.name: Konoha Mall Hashimoto
spots.desc: While perhaps not worth a special trip all the way there, it's worth a look if you happen to be anywhere near the area.

spots.name: ¥100 shop
spots.desc: Don't miss out on the ¥100 shop. A great place to shop for souvenirs (although many items are made in China), dishes, toys and everything else you didn't think you needed. There is one located in the bus centre building next to Hakata Station. Another is in Daiei, in Tenjin behind the MINA building.

spots.name: Amu plaza Hakata
spots.desc: It is an integrated shopping mall in Hakata. There are various brands and there are also many good restaurants.

spots.name: Nagahama
spots.desc: Famous for Hakata's Nagahama ramen, with stalls (yatai) that get set up daily to handle the locals who are proud of their ramen. You will most likely smell it before you see it, and if you want a true Fukuoka experience is definitely worth a look if not a full meal.

spots.name: Daimyo
spots.desc: A few places offer Happy Hour from 17:00-19:00, if you are looking for some refreshment before dinner.

spots.name: Ichiran
spots.desc: A well known ramen chain, dedicated solely to perfecting tonkotsu. Buy a ticket from the vending machine outside (just hit the big top button) and take a seat at the counter. Each seat has a curtain in front and dividers on the side, so nothing distracts you from the noodle experience that awaits. Cellphones, children or conversation are not allowed. Hand over your ticket, receive a questionnaire…

spots.name: Ramen Stadium
spots.desc: This celebration of ramen offers 8 restaurants with every style of ramen between Kyushu and Hokkaido. Ballots collected at the center determine a monthly favorite.
spots.price: Place your order by purchasing a food ticket from the vending machine before entering the restaurant

spots.name: Yama-chan
spots.desc: Tasty ramen and late night hours off the streets of Oyafukodori. Cut through the park behind the police box and you're sure to find it. Yama-chan is the owner.

spots.name: Tetsu-Nabe
spots.desc: There is another restaurant of similar name located in Nakasu, but the Hakata one seems to be the most popular. Be aware though that when you enter, you will be expected to be quick with your order as the place is usually very busy.

spots.name: Sancho Panza
spots.desc: Has a fabulous lunch menu, most dishes around ¥700-800. Tasty wrap tacos and other Latin-American style food is on available. On weekends, there is often live guitar music in the afternoon. In the evening the restaurant also opens the floor to dance: salsa, bachata, merengue and the cha-cha-cha all make their appearance at some point. Usually a ¥500 charge.

spots.name: RingerHut
spots.desc: A chain restaurant that does Champon (a kind of Chinese noodle dish with seafood and vegetables). Some branches have a system where you put your money in a machine, push the button under the dish of your choice and give your ticket to the staff. Other branches you just order from the menu.

spots.name: Hitokuchi Gyoza Taketora
spots.desc: It is a restaurant that specializes in alcohol snacks such as Japanese gyoza dumplings and gopchang.

spots.name: Usagiyorikame
spots.local: ウサギよりカメ もんじゃ焼き 春吉
spots.desc: It is a restaurant that sells monjayaki and okonomiyaki in Chuo Ward. Indoor smoking is available.

spots.name: Umeyama tetpei shokudo
spots.local: 梅山鉄平食堂 本店
spots.desc: It is a restaurant that sells Japanese home-cooked meals. You can enjoy Japanese home-cooked meals at an affordable price.

spots.name: Menya Ishi
spots.desc: This is a udon restaurant located around Hakata Station. It is famous for its udon and pollack udon.

spots.name: The Craic and The Porter
spots.desc: A beer bar for beer-lovers. Features numerous, hard-to-find American and European imports by a very interesting American expatriate. An entertaining time is guaranteed for all.

spots.name: Off Broadway
spots.desc: Run by a friendly American expatriate and is a favorite with navy personnel passing through the region. Serves a great hamburger, but don't expect it to come too quickly. Happy hour from 18:00-20:00 everyday.

spots.name: The Dark Room
spots.desc: The de facto hang-out for foreign rock bands playing in the area. The proprietor, Moses, ensures a good time in this multi-level indie hangout. Also has an 8th floor beer garden, which is a great place to kick back on summer evenings. Thursdays are ¥300 Corona beer night.

spots.name: Happy Cock
spots.desc: Ignore the suggestive name; this is a popular crowded spot for locals and gaijin alike. The British expat owner is very friendly.
spots.price: All drinks ¥500; all-you-can-drink or all-you-can-eat-and-drink specials available early evenings and some nights…

spots.name: Morris' Black Sheep British Pub
spots.desc: Does Happy hour from 17:00-19:00. Guinness, Old speckled Hen ¥590 a pint, and cocktails are half price. Fish and chips. Around the corner from the KFC on Nishidori. Open from 17:00. One of four Morris pubs in the same part of town.

spots.name: Bar Bliss
spots.desc: Bar/restaurant is a great place to meet interesting locals, variety of shochus and a wide range of western style foods. Guinness is served on tap. Eclectic mix of local Fukuokans.

spots.name: Zenrin Map Museum
spots.local: ゼンリン地図の資料館, zenrin no chizu no shiryōkan
spots.desc: The Zenrin company, whose head office is in the black segment of the Riverwalk complex, is a major local employer which pioneered mapping software in Japan. This location has been chosen because a famous Edo period mapmaker, Ino Tadataka, started making his map of Kyushu here. The views of the city and Kanmon straits from the museum on a fine day are excellent.
spots.hours: Mon-Fri 10:00-17:00, closed at weekends and on national holidays

spots.name: ChaCha Town
spots.desc: A shopping and amusement center with an IMAX movie theater, game center, food court, clothing stores, a grocery store, and a very big ¥100 shop. On weekends there are concerts and other attractions in the amphitheater- usually a kids' dance group, a magician, or a local musician. The shopping center's large red Ferris wheel isn't the biggest, but it's kind of a fun way to see the city at night.

spots.name: Aru Aru City
spots.desc: Easily reached from Kokura station, Aru Aru City is Kitakyushu's center of otaku culture, hosting frequent events per year, eight stories of anime-, manga-, and game-themed shops, game arcades, a manga kissa, and the Kitakyushu Manga Museum. While obviously not as huge as Tokyo's Akihabara or Osaka's Den Den Town, it is far more specialised than those two and has the obvious convenience of having…

spots.name: Tobata Gion
spots.local: 戸畑祇園大山笠, Tobata gion yamagasa
spots.desc: Designated an important intangible cultural asset of Japan and dates back to 1802. It involves the carrying of large floats called Yamagasa by about 100 men who shout "Yoitosa" to keep in time. Fourth weekend in July.

spots.name: Wasshoi Hyakuman Summer Festival
spots.local: わっしょい百万夏祭り, Wasshoi Hyakuman Matsuri
spots.desc: Early August. Many dance groups. Ends with a parade and firework display.

spots.name: Booties
spots.desc: Irish pub, Japanese-run, Guinness and pub food available. Big screen for viewing sports.

spots.name: Kurume City Art Museum
spots.desc: Next to the museum is a traditional Japanese koi garden which is open to the public. And there is the Kurume public library.

spots.name: Kurume Azalea Festival
spots.desc: 300,000 azaleas of 150 varieties on display. There are also bonsai trees, potted plants and various other displays.
spots.addr: 839-0827 福岡県久留米市善導寺町木塚214-20（くるめ緑花センター特設会場）Kurume Ryokka Center Special Venue (South Side of Michi-no-Eki Kurume)

spots.name: Kagoshima Prefectural Museum of Culture
spots.desc: Beautiful museum with nice expositions retracing the origin and evolution of the first habitants of the southern Kyushu area till the Meiji restoration. Generic information is available in English but for more details about the different pieces contained in the exposition, a Japanese reading friend should be brought to fully enjoy all the information available.

spots.name: Shiroyama Park
spots.desc: Mountain park in Kagoshima. You can see the panoramic view of Kagoshima including Sakurajima from the observatory.

spots.name: Yakusugi Museum
spots.local: 屋久杉自然館, Yakusugi Shizenkan
spots.desc: There are photos, movies and hands-on exhibits showing the island's natural wonders and the history of the logging industry. You can also hug a section of a 1660-year-old yakusugi. English explanatory pamphlet provided. A short walk away is the World Heritage Conservation Center.
spots.hours: 09:00-17:00 daily, last admission 16:30, closed 1st Tue of each month, closed Dec 29-Jan 1

spots.name: Yakushima Fruit Garden
spots.local: 屋久島フルーツガーデン, Yakushima Furuutsu Gaaden
spots.desc: Walk among the hundreds of tropical fruit trees and plants, with seasonal fruit like papaya, mango, guava and starfruit available to eat or drink.

spots.name: Shitogo Gajumaru-en Banyan Garden
spots.local: 志戸子ガジュマル園, Shitogo Gajumaru-en
spots.desc: There are 300-year-old Banyan trees and a variety of sub-tropical plants in a park setting.

spots.name: The Shiratani Unsui Gorge
spots.desc: A map and suggested routes based on your time constraints are provided at the trail head.
