spots.desc: This athletic center is just west of downtown (close to Hon-Hachinohe station). It has an old, but functional gym (¥100 per hour, showers ¥60), with treadmills, stationary bikes, free weights, nautilus machines, and a table tennis area. There is also an outdoor running track (free), several playing fields, an outdoor ice rink for winter skating, and facilities that offer a variety of classes. The…

spots.name: Movies
spots.desc: There are a movie theaters located in Cino and also at the Shimoda mall. Check the schedules for special discount days (ladies' day, men's day, couple's day, etc.) where tickets are only ¥1000.

spots.name: Pia-do
spots.desc: Shopping mall including Xebio (sporting goods) and Sunday (home improvement/general store) where you can look at puppies! Next to the mall are also a Toys R Us and an electronics store, Yamada Denki. The food court has a McDonald's.

spots.name: Hasshoku Center
spots.desc: the big food market hall of Hachinohe. A few minutes apart from the centre (¥100 bus from Main Station available), with a lot of different stands of food (fish, sweets, restaurants, liquor). The belt conveyer sushi restaurant here is a bit expensive, but oh so delicious. Also, there is a restaurant where you can grill your own fresh fish you buy from the market. You simply pay a fee to rent the…

spots.name: Greenhouse
spots.desc: A great outdoors store near Hon-Hachinohe Station (exit Hon-Hachinohe station and take the street on your right headed away from the station, it's just past the gas station on the left). The store features brands like the North Face, Patagonia, Columbia, and MontBell. Hiking, trekking, camping, and other outdoor activity gear and clothing are available. The Japanese lines of the clothing are…

spots.name: Aeon Mall Shimoda
spots.desc: Large shopping mall with many stores, restaurants, food courts, movie theaters, a bowling alley. It also has two large sporting goods stores - Sports Authority is attached to the mall & Takeda Sports is located across the street. Takeda Sports usually has an English speaking staff member working to service the many American customers who come from nearby Misawa Base. If you spot the American…

spots.name: Kaldi
spots.desc: This chain grocery store sells many international products. Pastas, sauces, Indian foods/spices, olives, pickles, various sweets & candies, Mexican ingredients (taco shells, salsa, etc.), cheeses, wines, even frozen bagels can be found. They hand out free coffee upon entering the store. The fresh ground coffee available for purchase is terrific!

spots.name: Bon
spots.desc: Located in an alley behind Concert Hall Pachinko. The 'Master' Kappa has some of the best food in town. There is a mix of Japanese, Western and other Asian Cuisine. There is an English menu, plus Kappa has excellent English too.

spots.name: Pore Pore
spots.desc: This Indian restaurant in Lapia shopping center features an amazing lunch buffet for around ¥1200. The naan bread is delicious!

spots.name: Kantaro Sushi
spots.desc: This upscale kaiten-zushi restaurant offers fresh sushi. The flagship Kantaro is in Hakodate, so there are Hakodate posters and scenic dvds playing on the restaurant flat screen TVs. There is also a variety of Hokkaido sweets for sale at the register.

spots.name: Izakaya Row
spots.desc: Located in the center of downtown on the main street is an alleyway of tiny izakayas. They serve up cold beer and tasty food. It is a great place to mingle with locals and business travelers.

spots.name: Tenryu
spots.desc: A small restaurant that serves local cuisine at very reasonable prices. It's conveniently located near the main train station.

spots.name: Bar Saude
spots.desc: This is a tiny, but fun Portuguese restaurant. The owners are a very nice young married couple (Yuko and Takashi) who are learning English. Yuko serves and handles the bar, while Takashi whips up delicious small bites in the kitchen. It is great to watch him cook while sipping a glass of the many fine wines available.

spots.name: Hirosaki Tourist Center
spots.desc: On the other side of the park, Oteman Square contains Hirosaki's tourist information center and showcases more beautiful Neputa stuff including Japan's largest drum, diameter 4.5m wide and big enough for 50 people to bang on at once.

spots.name: Shinteramachi
spots.desc: A slightly newer set of temples affiliated with the Nichiren sect.

spots.name: Former Ito Residence
spots.desc: The Ito family were a doctor family for generations during the feudal era. They operated out of the house, so even though it is located in the samurai district, it is not actually a samurai residence. Nevertheless, the architecture closely resembles that of a samurai residence.

spots.name: Neputa Festival
spots.desc: Hirosaki's biggest event is this yearly festival, held in the first week of August and quite similar to Aomori's Nebuta Matsuri (note slight difference in spelling). The festival is famous for its extravagant and colorful illuminated floats and accompanying dancers, and accommodation in the area is booked tight in season. In contrast with Aomori's huge Nebuta festival, Hirosaki's Neputa is known…

spots.name: Bunpuku Chagama
spots.desc: This ramen shop has many flavors of ramen, and the old woman who serves you is an interesting character. It also sells ice cream.

spots.name: Tsugaru Akatsuki no Kai
spots.local: 津軽あかつきの会, Tsugaru Dawn Club
spots.desc: At some distance from the center of town, this organization was formed to preserve the traditional cuisine of the Tsugaru region. With advance reservations (by phone, Japanese language only), they will cook lunch for groups of four to ten people.
spots.addr: 青森県弘前市石川字家岸４４－１３

spots.name: Kajimachi area
spots.desc: It's the area around the castle. If you can't find it, just look for the giant bowling pin downtown. If you're looking for an "American style" bar, try 'Ash', 'Gumbo', or 'Garcom de Bar'. This is where you'll find the best nightlife in Hirosaki.

spots.name: Nishihiro area
spots.desc: There are a lot of cheap bars and izakayas there because of the nearby colleges. They are going to be harder to find than the bars in the Kajimachi area.

spots.name: Visitor Centre
spots.desc: Entry is free, but the IMAX movie on the park (shown 5 times a day) costs ¥200. Open around the year.

spots.name: Irimizu Cave
spots.desc: Another cave, 6 km away from Abukumado Cave. This undeveloped cave is for the hard-core adventurer. Its 3 interconnected courses follow a 10 °C stream as its snakes its way through darkness. The water height is rarely higher than your ankles and not swift. Water drips from the ceiling so light raincoats or even wetsuits may be a good idea. A hard hat with light is highly recommended.

spots.name: Tadami Line Scenic Railway
spots.desc: The Tadami Line is a scenic railway in western Fukushima and neighbouring Niigata Prefecture, winding through remote mountain valleys, forests and riverside villages. Its bridges over the Tadami River are particularly famous for their spectacular views, especially during autumn foliage and winter snow.

spots.name: Bridge for Fukushima
spots.desc: The organization offers tours specially designed so that the visitors can get first-hand impressions from areas affected by the great Tohoku earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear accident. The participants can experience, how local people and businesses are coping with the recovery from the disasters. The tours start and end in Tokyo and include accommodation in Iizaka hot spring near Fukushima.

spots.name: Samurai Residence
spots.desc: A preserved samurai estate featuring a teahouse, magistrate's office, a warehouse, and a rice mill in addition to the Aizu chief retainer's house. There is also a restaurant and a gift shop, and visitors can participate in a variety of hands-on activities throughout the year.

spots.name: Hideyo Noguchi Seishunkan
spots.desc: A former hospital built in 1897. It's where Hideyo Noguchi's hands were treated at age 16 that gave him full use of his hands for the first time. When he was one year old, he suffered a burn that caused his left hand to remain clenched. The doctor's ability to return his hand to normalcy is said to have been what inspired him to study medicine himself. The buildings today has a museum dedicated…

spots.name: Hideyo Noguchi's Baptism Spot
spots.desc: This is the original spot where Sakaemachi Church stood when Hideyo Noguchi was baptized. He also learned English and met his first love here.

spots.name: Aizu Shinsengumi Memorial Hall
spots.desc: Located on the 2nd floor of an antique shop, the museum features artifacts from the Shinsengumi, the battles they fought in, and art and documents related to them.

spots.name: Hajime Saito Grave Monument
spots.desc: The grave of the leader of the Shinsengumi in the grounds of Amidaji Temple.

spots.name: Byakkotai Museum
spots.desc: A private collection of exhibits related to the Boshin War and the Byakkotai.

spots.name: Byakkotai Legendary Museum
spots.desc: Over 5000 artifacts are on display from the Byakkotai, Shinsengumi, and Boshin War.

spots.name: Tonoguchi Weir Cave
spots.desc: It looks like a small spring, but is actually part of an ancient irrigation tunnel. It took over 50,000 men over 3 years to dig here from Lake Inawashiro. It is best known today as the tunnel used by the Byakkotai to escape after their defeat from the Battle of Tonoguchihara. Upon emerging from the tunnel, they saw smoke around Tsuruga Castle and believed the entire domain had fallen.

spots.name: Byakkotai Hara-kiri Memorial
spots.desc: A statue and monument built over the sight where the 20 Byakkotai soldiers saw the burning castle and committed ritual suicide however, it is believed that only 16 of them succeeded here. Three of them are thought to have died later either in battle or suicide elsewhere and one was rescued as he was attempting to kill himself here and nursed back to health. It was this survivor who recounted the…

spots.name: Byakkotai Graves
spots.desc: Graves for each of the 19 boys who committed suicide on October 8, 1868 (the date written reads August 23 which is from the old lunar calendar used at the time. It coincides with October 8 on modern calendars) when they believed their castle had fallen to the enemy. Villagers hid their bodies in a nearby temple so that they would not be defiled by the Western Army and later returned to Iimoriyama…

spots.name: Monument from the City of Rome
spots.desc: A monument made from the pillar of a temple that was uncovered from the ruins of Pompeii dedicated in 1928 by Benito Mussolini who found the story of the Byakkotai inspiring. It reads, "Rome, Mother of Civilization, pays its undying respect to the brave Byakkotai by displaying the axe of the Fascist Party symbol, representing the authority of ancient Rome, and commemorating the thousand-year-old…

spots.name: Byakkotai German Monument
spots.desc: A monument gifted to the city by Hasso von Etzdorf, a diplomat from Nazi Germany who was inspired by the story of the Byakkotai and felt it spoke to the German condition of the time. It reads, "To the young samurai warriors of Aizu". The monument was removed by occupying American forces after WWII however, it was returned after the 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty restored sovereignty to Japan.…

spots.name: Former Takizawa Honjin
spots.desc: A resthouse that was used as a headquarters during the Boshin War. The Byakkotai left here to fight in the Battle of Tonoguchihara.

spots.name: Akabeko Crafter Bansho
spots.desc: One of Aizu's most famous souvenir, the Akabeko, is produced here, and they offer visitors the opportunity to paint their own Akabeko. Alternatively, you can paint a bell of the town's mascot, Aka-bee. No reservation necessary. They also have a shop where you can buy Akabeko and other Aizu souvenirs.
spots.price: ¥1300 to paint your own Akabeko or Akabe

spots.name: Tokaichi Market
spots.desc: A New Years tradition for over 400 years, the market center's around purchasing Okiagari Koboshi.

spots.name: Higashiyama Onsen Oyukake Festival
spots.local: 東山温泉お湯かけまつり
spots.desc: Geisha from Higashiyama Onsen, known as geigi, are carried in portable shrines and throw water from the onsen (oyukake) onto onlookers.

spots.name: Aizu Festival
spots.desc: Events are held around the castle along with a parade in the town

spots.name: Nozawa Mingei
spots.desc: A shop where many local craft products are produced. You can buy 3 different sizes of Okiagari Koboshi, 8 different sizes of Akabeko, Aizu Tenjin dolls, masks, and other products. They also have their own unique varieties of traditional goods such as an Edvard Munch "The Scream" Okiagari Koboshi and a "Handsome Blossom" variant of Akabeko which was featured in the NHK drama Yae no Sakura.

spots.name: Yamada Mingei Kojo
spots.desc: Self-advertised as an Okiagari Koboshi producer, they have the traditional varieties as well as versions that look like Doraemon, Pikachu, etc. They also offer visitors the option to paint their own Okiagari Koboshi for ¥800.

spots.name: Agemanju
spots.desc: "Age" means deep-frying and "Manju" means Japanese style bun stuffed with adzuki bean paste. Therefore, Agemanju means deep-frying Japanese style bun stuffed. It is a traditional sweet in Aizuwakamatsu and it is sweet and soft, but it has high calories because of frying. It is especially popular among children and older people. There are a lot of shops which sell Agemanju about ¥100.

spots.name: Sumire Shokudo
spots.desc: A popular restaurant, offering ramen, udon, and sauce katsudon sets.

spots.name: Marumo Shokudo
spots.desc: A ramen and sauce katsudon restaurant conveniently located near Aizu-Wakamatsu Station.

spots.name: Iwaya-Kannon
spots.desc: Iwaya-Kannon has sixty Buddhas carved into the rock face of Mount Shinobu (信夫山) and offers a decent place to take a look down at the city.

spots.name: Fukushima Racetrack
spots.desc: If you feel like betting on horses then this is the place to go in Fukushima. Live races only happen during certain times of the year (usually April, July and November), but video races are available on weekends year-round.
spots.price: Entry costs ¥100 (free for video races), plus whatever you bet on wrong horses when inside

spots.name: Shiki No Sato
spots.desc: Discover agricultural activity in this park with an animals area, a watermill, crafts, restaurants and hot springs

spots.name: Waraji Festival
spots.desc: This festival involves tons of dancing, parades, food stalls, and a huge waraji (Japanese sandal).
spots.hours: First Fri and Sat in August

spots.name: Azuma dori
spots.desc: pedestrian street with restaurants, izakayas, and craft beer bars.

spots.name: Neo
spots.desc: Neo is the other club in Fukushima. A smaller smoky room with decent music and young clientele.

spots.name: Shiramizu Amidado Temple
spots.desc: Shiramizu Amidado is the oldest building in existence in the Iwaki region and was Designated a national treasure in 1952. It was built on the orders of Tokuhime the widow of Norimichi Iwaki, a feudal lord of the Iwaki area in 1160 at the end of the Heian Period. Surrounding the temple is a beautiful Japanese garden where visitors can relax and enjoy the peaceful temple grounds.

spots.name: Aquamarine Fukushima
spots.local: アクアマリンふくしま
spots.desc: This aquarium focuses on the ocean off the coast of Fukushima, specifically the meeting of the warm Kuroshio Current from the south and the cold Oyashio Current from the north. Other highlights include the touching pool, walk-through glass tunnel as well as tropical botanical gardens and marine mammals.

spots.name: Misaki Park
spots.desc: Located on the eastern side of Onahama Bay lies a headland that rises 46 m above sea level and is home to Misaki Park. The park's main features are the Shiomidai Lookout and the Marine Tower, which features an observation deck approximately 60 m high providing a bird's-eye view of the surrounding coastline.

spots.name: Iwaki City Coal and Fossil Museum
spots.local: いわき市石炭化石館 ほるる
spots.desc: This museum provides a comprehensive overlook at the history and development of the Joban coalmine. Displays include a replica of the living conditions of the miners as well many interesting fossils found from within the city. One of the featured displays is a dinosaur fossil known as the Futaba Suzuki Ryu, a kind of plesiosaurus, which was discovered in the Futaba strata group, a layer that…

spots.name: Nakoso Barrier
spots.desc: According to ancient records, this was the sight of the Kikuta barrier gate. The name 'Nakoso' means 'do not enter' and the barrier gave the impression to the Michinoku (the people of the north), that they were not welcome. Ancient Japanese people had a tendency of being afraid of the unknown in northern Japan. This image of divided people, lovers and even seasons made the Nakoso-Barrier popular…

spots.name: Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing
spots.local: いわき市役所 暮らしの伝承郷
spots.desc: Reproduced traditional houses, household goods and villages from the late Edo to the early Meiji period are on display. Experience first hand old style Japan at this village.

spots.name: Iwaki City Sea Dinosaur Centre
spots.local: いわき市海竜の里センター
spots.desc: A mini theme park. Futabasaurus suzukii is a Late Cretaceous long-necked plesiosaur discovered by a high school student Tadashi Suzuki at a riverside outcrop of the Ohisa River in Itakizawa, Ohisa Town, in 1968. This is so far the only known specimen of this species, and (as it was later found out) it had been bitten by sharks. The fossil and a reconstructed skeleton is on display in the National…

spots.name: Iwaki City Ammonite Centre
spots.local: アンモナイトセンター
spots.desc: The Ammonite center was built directly at a giant ammonite fossil excavation site. On weekends (excluding the third Sunday of each month) 10:00-11:30 and 13:30-15:00 the visitors can take part in ecavations just outside of the ammonite center. The field work may be cancelled due to bad weather.

spots.name: Spa Resort Hawaiians
spots.local: スパリゾートハワイアンズ
spots.desc: This amusement complex is a huge indoor and outdoor hot spring resort featuring a large waterpark, waterslides and the world's largest outdoor hot spring. There are also hula and Polynesian dance performances as well as souvenir and specialty shops. Free shuttle bus from Yumoto Station.

spots.name: Sasuichi
spots.desc: This place is famous for bowls of seafood, but strangely they also serve curry, meat and noodles.

spots.name: Asaka History Museum
spots.desc: Closed from October 2023 to March 2027 to repair damages by earthquakes..

spots.name: Morioka Castle
spots.desc: Morioka Castle was built in the 16th century by Nanbu Nobunao, the first daimyo of the area. The castle was used as a residence during its heyday until it was dismantled during the Meiji Period. The area was converted into a park in 1906 and is known today as a popular place to see cherry blossoms in the spring. It is also very pretty in winter when the snow falls on the varied landscape and old…

spots.name: Morioka History and Culture Museum
spots.desc: The museum features exhibits about the history of the city, particularly its days as a castle town, but also includes artifacts from early civilizations to modern times. There are also exhibits of the city's festivals, such as the Chagu Chagu Festival. The museum's displays were revamped in 2023 - there's little English language signage, but it offers a free audio tour covering key items. The…

spots.name: Morioka Museum of Great Predecessors
spots.desc: A museum with rotating exhibits about people who have been influential in Morioka.

spots.name: Morioka City Science Center
spots.desc: A children's museum with educational science exhibits and a planetarium.

spots.name: Oyakuen Garden
spots.desc: The garden was constructed in the early Edo Period as an herb garden and was later converted into a garden for the local lord. It became a villa in 1908 until the buildings around the garden were turned into a museum. Today the garden is a popular spot to see autumn foliage.

spots.name: Takuboku Shinkon House
spots.desc: The Takuboku Shinkon House is the former residence of Takuboku Ishikawa, a famous local poet. He lived here as a newlywed with his wife albeit only for less than 3 weeks.

spots.name: Hara-kei Memorial Museum
spots.desc: The former home of Takashi Hara which has been converted into a museum. Takashi Hara was a Morioka native who served as Prime Minister of Japan from 1918 to 1921. He is also known for being Japan's first Christian Prime Minister. The building contains documents and personal possessions.

spots.name: Fukazawa Kōko Nonoha Art Museum
spots.local: 深沢紅子野の花美術館, fukuzawa kōko nonoha no bijutsukan
spots.desc: A Morioka native, Fukazawa was a 20th-century painter of European-style art.

spots.name: Ishikawa Takuboku Memorial Museum
spots.local: 石川啄木記念館, ishikawa takuboku kinenkan
spots.desc: Closed for renewal until Dec 2024. A famous tanka poet who was born here in the Tamayama district. The museum has information and displays about him and his poetry.

spots.name: Iwate University Museum and Botanical Garden
spots.local: 岩手大学ミュージアム, iwate daigaku myūjiamu
spots.desc: A museum established by the university with a nice botanical garden outside.

spots.name: Morioka Zoo
spots.local: 盛岡市動物公園, morioka-shi dōbutsuen
spots.desc: The Morioka Zoo a great place to check out the animals in a peaceful surrounding.

spots.name: Iwate Museum of Art
spots.desc: This very modern art gallery has an impressive permanent collection (mainly made up of modern art) and hosts interesting special exhibitions, and is well worth the trip from the center of Morioka.
spots.price: ¥410 for permanent collection, more for special exhibitions

spots.name: Morioka City Multipurpose Arena
spots.local: 盛岡市総合アリーナ, morioka-shi sōgō arīna
spots.desc: Facility for indoor sports such as futsal, volleyball and table tennis. Until 2015, it was the public skating rink of the city.

spots.name: Sansa Odori
spots.desc: The much anticipated summer taiko (Japanese drum) festival. Approximately 10,000 participating taiko players, flute players, and dancers parade down the main street, making this the largest taiko festival in the world and listed in the Guinness Book of Records, Odori. After the performance is finished, viewers can join in and dance in the street with the performers as a part of "Wa Daiko". A…

spots.name: Azumaya
spots.desc: Likely the most famous wanko-soba shop in town. There are three outlets, one of which is conveniently just outside the east exit of Morioka station. Highly unusually in Japan, they even have a vegan version.
spots.price: All-you-can-eat wanko soba ¥4,500; regular sets from ¥750

spots.name: Pyonpyonsha
spots.desc: Famous for Morioka Reimen (cold noodles). There are five outlets in Morioka, one of which is at Morioka station next to Azumaya (above) just in case you didn't get your fill of noodles yet.

spots.name: Aeron Standard
spots.local: アーロンスタンダード
spots.desc: This modern izakaya has a diverse food and drinks menu which you can order from using English language touch screens. The staff are friendly, but don't speak much English.

spots.name: Rinno-ji
spots.desc: An historic temple with ponds and a large traditional garden, which is especially attractive when the azaleas are in bloom.

spots.name: SS30 Building Observation Lounge
spots.desc: This office tower has an observation deck on the 29th and 30th floors, which is open and free to the public.

spots.name: Yagiyama Zoo
spots.desc: Elephants, lions, bears, tigers! Mingle with the rabbits. Coin lockers available.

spots.name: Aoba Castle Honmaru Museum
spots.desc: A small one-room museum and theatre dedicated to the Aoba Castle & Masamune Date. A 15-minute historical documentary on the castle and Masamune Date is shown every hour. The exhibition and film are exclusively in Japanese, and the museum is of little interest to non-Japanese speakers.

spots.name: The Museum of the Forest of Depths of the Earth
spots.local: 地底の森ミュージアム
spots.desc: The museum of the stone age. In the museum, restoration exhibition of that time is carried out based on the data discovered from public presentation and there are the ruins of 20,000-year-old Saki's Old Stone Age unearthed from Tomizawa ruins (富沢遺跡).

spots.name: Sankyozawa Electric Centennial Museum (Sankyozawa 100 Year Electric Historical Center)
spots.local: Tohokudenryoku Sankyozawa Denki Hyakunenkan, 東北電力 三居沢電気百年館
spots.desc: The birthplace of hydroelectric power generation in Japan and features a functioning century-old hydroelectric plant (operating in a demonstration capacity) that remains connected to the power grid. In addition to being able to view the hydroelectric turbines in operation, a small museum and children's exploration area is on-site, albeit in Japanese-only. Immediately adjacent to the hydroelectric…

spots.name: 3M Sendai City Science Museum
spots.desc: A science museum with a focus on science and technology, natural history, and everyday life where you can experience scientific principles and laws through hands-on exhibits and stimulate your creativity.
spots.hours: Tue-Sun 09:00-16:45 (entry until 16:00) except the 4th Thu (with variations around holidays)

spots.name: Michinoku-Yosakoi Festival
spots.desc: The Sendai Michinoku Yosakoi Festival was established in 1998 as a successor to the Kochi Yosakoi Festival. Yosakoi, which is held in over 250 cities, towns and villages across the country, is a general term for festivals that follow the rules of respecting tradition and creativity and is run by the citizens, incorporating local folk songs and dancing with Naruko drums. Today, it is held in…
spots.addr: Held in various parks and public areas of Sendai City

spots.name: Benyland
spots.desc: This is a fun little amusement park. It's not exactly Disneyland, but you can have a fun few hours on the roller coasters and other rides.

spots.name: Nikka Whisky Distillery Tour
spots.desc: No English. 09:00-11:30, and 12:30-15:30. Tours are conducted every 15 to 20 minutes. Tours take one hour. Free whisky at the end of the tour.

spots.name: Sankyozawa Traffic Park
spots.local: 三居沢交通公園, Minamikoizumi Traffic Park
spots.desc: An unusual park intended for children and school groups to learn traffic rules in Japan in a simulated city environment, complete with traffic signals and pedestrian walk signs. Free bike rentals are available for children.

spots.name: Rikyu
spots.desc: A famous chain of gyūtan restaurants. Order the teishoku (set meal) - this includes meat, pickles, barley rice, leek, and a clear oxtail soup with real tail.

spots.name: Ichimuan
spots.desc: Ichimuan specializes in Kyoto Haute cuisine (kaiseki) while utilizing fine Sendai produce. The restaurant also has a teppanyaki grill counter seats where visitors can enjoy fine Sendai beef. The view from the 37th floor is pretty impressive. Lunch is buffet style. Reservations essential (to avoid disappointment).
spots.price: Lunch starts from ¥3234. Dinner courses start from ¥6930. À la carte is also available

spots.name: Oden Sankichi
spots.desc: This restaurant specializes in oden, a Japanese fish stew of sorts with ingredients slowly simmered for hours if not days in a soy broth. Goes well with beer or sake, and especially popular in winter.

spots.name: Sendai Aoba-Tei
spots.desc: A high quality gyūtan restaurant. Menu has pictures, though it may be not easy to guess what is gyūtan. Around noon, be prepared to queue.

spots.name: Mitsukoshi Food Court
spots.desc: The department store food court is an excellent place to sample Sendai's specialties.

spots.name: Kaki Toku
spots.desc: Miyagi and Hiroshima are famous for oysters, and Kaki Toku, which has been running since 1927, is one of the area's most renowned oyster restaurants.
spots.hours: Mon-Fri 11:30-14:00, 17:00-20:00; Sat 11:30-20:00; Sun 11:30-21:00. Special hours on holidays

spots.name: Kameki Sushi
spots.desc: Some locals believe it is the best sushi restaurant in Japan. Uses exclusively locally caught fish. No credit cards.

spots.name: Palinka
spots.desc: Excellent Italian restaurant near Zuihouden (the mausoleum of Date Masamune). Lunch: 11:30 - 14:30; dinner: 18:00 - 21:00. Palinka has occasional concerts on weekends.

spots.name: Namaskar
spots.desc: Authentic Indian restaurant with two locations. One in the BiVi building (opposite Yodabashi Camera) directly behind Sendai station, on the 4th floor. There they offer an extensive and reasonably priced buffet lunch on Sundays from 11:00-15:00. The other is on Minamimachi-dori. There they occasionally show Indian films and music videos on a large screen and carry a buffet lunch on Saturdays.

spots.name: Tirol
spots.desc: Great Italian on Clis Road, or just west of Izumi-chou Subway Station in the north.

spots.name: Hummingbird
spots.desc: Italian in Hotel Universe on Ichibancho-dori. Known for its fresh pasta.

spots.name: Benitora Gyoza-bo
spots.desc: Chinese dishes (spicy). Located to the north of the AER building by Sendai station. Cross the pedestrian bridge and look for the big red kanji (means 'red tiger').

spots.name: Fredrick Pantry
spots.desc: A shop and small restaurant specializing in organic and vegetarian food.

spots.name: O-hisamaya
spots.desc: Walk straight for a minute or two. The place is just after a CoCo curry shop. O-hisama restaurant has vegetables for sale out front.). Vegetarian/Organic restaurant Small place. Atmosphere is very warm and the food is awesome.

spots.name: Rock Cafe Peter Pan
spots.desc: Oldest cafe in Sendai. Great coffee. Excellent selection of rock music. Friendly and helpful service. English spoken.

spots.name: Sendai Coffee Stand
spots.desc: A cafe with a backstreet charm. Excellent coffee. Great atmosphere.

spots.name: Wadiharfu
spots.desc: A cafe with a long history. Named after the Sudanese port of Wadi Halfa, where the owner once spent time. A warm and cosy cafe, rich with character. Excellent coffee. Sushi and light meals.

spots.name: Club Shaft
spots.desc: A DJ/live band club and sports bar pub founded by Julian from England. Great atmosphere. World food and beers.

spots.name: Wadi Halfa
spots.desc: This cafe often has live performances of Indian or African music.

spots.name: E'z Bar
spots.desc: This place is a little hard to find but worth the search. It's within 5 minutes of the big Don Quixote store in Kokubuncho, so don't go too far when you're looking for it. The owner, Hatakeyama-san, speaks perfect English as he lived in New Zealand for a year. Half the fun of ordering a cocktail at this place is watching the bartender cut a block of ice down for your drink!

spots.name: Dewa Sanzan
spots.desc: the Three Mountains of Dewa, holy to the mountain ascetic cult of Shugendo

spots.name: Yamagata Castle
spots.desc: The original castle was constructed in 1357 by Kaneyori Mogami but the castle was greatly expanded by Yoshiaki Mogami nearly 200 years later. The castle contained a palace building and other structures protected by multiple walled sections with turrets surrounded by a moat. It was the largest castle in the Tohoku region, but it never had a donjon. Yoshiaki also built up the surrounding area as a…

spots.name: Mogami Yoshiaki Historical Museum
spots.desc: Mogami Yoshiaki was a daimyo of the Dewa Province. He is credited for vastly expanding Yamagata Castle and transforming the area from a modest, somewhat run-down town into a respectable modern city. He fought many battles in the region and gained territory for siding with the Tokugawa during the Battle of Sekigahara to make his domain one of the top in the nation at the time. The museum includes…

spots.name: Yamagata Prefectural Museum
spots.desc: A museum with exhibits of historic artifacts from Yamagata Prefecture. It is home to the famous "Jomon Goddess" (Jomon no Megami), a ceramic statue of a goddess forged in the Jomon Period. For Japanese history buffs, it's worth a visit just to see this object. The prefecture's famous pilgrimage shrines (the Dewa Sanzan) and temple (Yamadera) also have informative exhibits. In addition to the…

spots.name: Bunshōkan
spots.desc: A large structure constructed during the Taisho Period after British Renaissance architecture. It was used as the Yamagata Prefectural Government Building. There are a few lavishly decorated rooms that visitors can enter and look around.

spots.name: Yamagata Museum of Art
spots.desc: The museum's permanent collection contains works by Kichiro Hasegawa, Matsuo Basho, and Claude Monet. Special exhibits typically show for about a month at a time, so check the museum website to see what will be featured during your visit.

spots.name: Kyōdokan
spots.desc: Built in 1876 as a hospital, it's known for its unique architecture. It was registered as an Important Cultural Property in 1966. The exhibits show the building's history and information about medical studies during that time period.

spots.name: Seifū-sō
spots.desc: A historic building with a nice garden. It was constructed as part of a temple and served as its garden until the Meiji Restoration. The temple buildings are long gone but the garden remains. The tea house was built in 1954.
spots.price: Viewing the garden is free, but you can have tea within the building for a fee

spots.name: Museum of Yamagata University
spots.desc: Contains natural science exhibits and displays on some of the university's studies and research findings.

spots.name: Karamatsu Kannondo
spots.desc: One of the 33 temples of the Mogami pilgrimage. It's noted for its architecture, jutting out of the mountainside overlooking the surrounding area. Just below the temple stands the original Nabetaro (鍋太郎), a named nabe pot that was used during the first "Best Imoni-kai in Japan Festival" (日本一の芋煮会フェスティバル) to make imoni to serve guests. They no longer have need for this one, since they've since made…

spots.name: Yamagata City Industrial History Museum
spots.local: 山形市産業歴史資料館
spots.desc: A small museum showcasing some of the city's top quality products, particularly Yamagata imono (metal casting).

spots.name: Seikai Kunii Contemporary Calligraphy Memorial Museum
spots.desc: Seikai Kunii founded the Seishinsha, a group that studies modern calligraphy, in 1917 and this museum features his calligraphy, calligraphy he has collected, and special exhibits along with information about modern calligraphy (in Japanese).

spots.name: Tarumizu Ruins
spots.desc: Also known as Minenoura (峯の浦), it is considered the Ura-Yamadera (裏山寺), this was once a place of training for mountain worshippers, called yamabushi. It is also where Jikaku Daishi was said to have made the decision to build Yamadera. The area features different rock formations with the main highlight being a wooden torii gate in a honeycomb-shaped rock formation. It's possibly the city's best…

spots.name: Yamadera Bashō Museum
spots.desc: Across the steep valley the temple overlooks, and up a short walk to the opposite hilltop is the lovely park of Fuga-no-Kuni, where you will find this museum featuring exhibitions of Basho's poetry and scrolls. The street leading to the shrine is famous for umegaimochi, a kind of…

spots.name: Kyushu National Museum
spots.desc: It's the newest National Museum following Tokyo, Kyoto and Nara. Based on the concept "understand Japanese culture from the point of Asian view", they don't only exhibit but also preserve and investigate cultural assets, then prepare a variety of educational events to keep the museum fresh. The museum generally has interesting temporary exhibits, so check the website.

spots.name: Seifa Utaki

"Utaki" are natural places of spiritual significance in the native Okinawan religion, and Seifa Utaki was the holiest. Back when there were practitioners, only priestesses could visit the site, because it was believed that only women could speak with the gods.…

spots.name: Kuburabari

spots.desc: Jinmen-iwa is a big rock in the forest that resembles a human face. Requires 12-20 minute hike up the hill by a forest trail. No parking, nearest parking is at Tatigami-iwa.

spots.name: Gunkan-iwa
spots.desc: The "Battleship Rock", about 2 km south of Agarizaki, is a series of peculiarly-shaped reef rock formations. Supposedly, the main rock bears a close resemblance to the shape of a battleship, and that's how it got its name. It can be observed from Sanninudai.

spots.name: Tatigamiiwa
spots.local: 立神岩、タティガミイワ
spots.desc: The "Standing God Rock", at the southeast tip of the island, is also noted for the underwater ruins nearby (see Do, some with what appears to be indigenous writing. Also, it's considered a spiritual site for followers of Yonaguni's indigenous traditional religion.

spots.name: Masuda’s Historic Merchant District (Masuda’s Hidden Storehouses "Uchigura")
spots.desc: It is a district where the traditional townscape is preserved. The internal structure called “Uchi-gura,” which is not visible from the exterior of the buildings, is a distinctive feature of the area. It is designated as a nationally important architectural district.

spots.name: Fu no Yu
spots.desc: If naked planespotting sounds like your idea of a good time, check out this Japanese-style spa with views of a strip of the tarmac. Jacuzzi, jet bath, sauna and washing facilities are provided, the only lack is that there's no place to cool off (except a cold shower).
spots.price: Entrance ¥900 plus optional purchase of a towel for ¥250

spots.name: Flight of Dreams
spots.desc: Giant hangar near T2, containing the first ever Boeing 787 Dreamliner where you can visit the cockpit and stare into the maw of a 2.8m engine. There's also a kids play area (mostly free, but net climbing area ¥300), full-fledges B787 flight simulators (fees apply), and a Seattle-themed dining area.

spots.name: Aichi Prefectural Ceramic Museum
spots.desc: Temporarily closed for renovation until April 2025. This museum is home to a large collection ancient works of the Jomon era and ancient ceramic kilns. It can be reached by taking a Meitetsu bus from Owari-Seto Station to Touji Shiryoukan.

spots.name: Seto Ceramics and Glass Art Center
spots.desc: This small art center has a delightful display of glass and ceramic art made by local artists. It also sports a nice cafe.

spots.name: Setogura Museum
spots.desc: Great museum with several ceramic exhibits and a reproduction of old Seto.
spots.price: Adults ¥500, high school and college students ¥300, children free

spots.name: Kamagami Shrine
spots.desc: This shrine dedicated to the founder of Seto ceramics, Tamakichi Kato, and yields a nice view of the city. There is also a monument dedicated to those from Seto who died during the Second World War.

spots.name: Kurufuku Manekineko Festival in Seto
spots.local: 来る福招き猫まつりin瀬戸
spots.desc: This is a festival for the "manekineko" or the beckoning cat which can be seen in almost every shop, restaurant and other retail area. Hundreds of these statues are put on display and other exhibits can be seen as well.

spots.name: Setomono Festival
spots.desc: Ceramicists of the city and other regions turn out to sell their wares at a discount price. There are thousands of pieces that can be bought for almost any purpose. Great place and time to get authentic Japanese souvenirs.
spots.hours: The second Sat and Sun of Sep

spots.name: Iwayado Park
spots.desc: This park is a nice getaway from the hustle and bustle of traveling and museum hopping. There is a nice river flowing through the park which makes for a nice dip in the summertime or great atmosphere for autumn colors or cherry blossom viewing.

spots.name: Kasen Studio
spots.desc: This studio offers pottery making experience classes for both pottery making on the wheel and pottery painting. Classes are conducted in small groups, and studio owner can speak decent English.

spots.name: Seto Ginza Shopping Street
spots.desc: Named after the famed district in Tokyo this small and quaint street offers a look into pre-shopping mall Japan. It's got several restaurants and old fashioned shops. If you're interested in getting Japanese style items or green tea soft serve ice cream, this is the place to go.

spots.name: Kinchan
spots.desc: This is a great little izakaya (Japanese style bar). Arrive around 17:00, as it gets crowded quickly. Try the yakitori and the chicken hearts.

spots.name: Parti Seto
spots.desc: Numerous restaurants. If you're not sure where to go or are just tired from touring you should try this place.

spots.name: Apita
spots.desc: This large grocery store has prepared meals, and there's a food court with several restaurants inside, too.

spots.name: Mount Zao Observatory
spots.local: 蔵王山展望台, Zaou-san Tenboudai
spots.desc: With an elevation of 250 m, this observatory offers a nice 360-degree panorama of the city and Mikawa Bay. Especially nice at night.

spots.name: Koijigahama Beach
spots.desc: This sandy, arc-shaped beach near the lighthouse at the end of the peninsula is about 1 km long. Its name dubs it the "beach of romance".

spots.name: Irago Nanohana Garden
spots.local: 伊良湖菜の花ガーデン
spots.desc: A garden of yellow rape blossom flowers. The garden is only open during the blooming season, which typically runs from January to March.

spots.name: Lapin
spots.desc: A restaurant with its own original hamburg steaks with different sauces to choose from to top them off. They also have daily pasta sets.

spots.name: Mentai Park Tokoname
spots.local: めんたいパークとこなめ
spots.desc: You may want to see how pollock roe (鱈子, tarako) was made there.
spots.addr: 愛知県常滑市りんくう町1-25-4

spots.name: Okuramochi
spots.desc: A little famous store in the city that provides various Wagashi (Japanese sweets) that can be presents.

spots.name: Gekkō-ji Temple
spots.desc: During the famine from 1833 to 1844, many people starved to death. To remember these deaths, Gekkouji temple was built in 1847, and memorial services began to be held. One important part of this temple is the beautiful giant copper Buddha which is enshrined in the main hall. 500 stones on which ancestors’ names have been written are inside the body of the Buddha.

spots.name: Hoyamaji Temple
spots.desc: This temple is dedicated to Senju Kannon, a transformed Buddha that has 1000 hands. It was made by a priest named Taicho in the Nara era. Other Buddha statues are also located here. For example, you can see the Nehan Buddha, a statue of the dying Buddha, along with a picture of Buddha's crying pupils on the wall behind it. A smiling Buddha, called Obinzurusan, is standing in the front gate of the…

spots.name: Kura-no-Tsuji
spots.desc: Echizen's historic area in downtown Takefu, it is filled with old warehouses with white painted walls. This area flourished in the Edo Era as a stopping point for transporting supplies between the Kansai area and the Hokuriku district. The line of warehouses belonged to ancient traders. Now they are maintained in the district activation program, and a must-see-spot in downtown. Outdoor concerts…

spots.name: Injō-ji Temple
spots.desc: Built in 1488, Injoji was one of the main branches of the Shinsei-shū sect (真盛宗) of Tendai Buddhism. There are 9 buildings in the temple, which is one of the most famous temples in the city. It’s noted for the front gate which is completely made out of zelkova. There are great sculptures in this gate; 16 Buddhist saints, a dignified lion, a carp swimming up the rapids, and more. The huge Buddha…

spots.name: Sōja Shrine
spots.desc: This is the main Shrine in Echizen city. Gods from shrines all over Echizen are worshipped together here. The citizens call it "Osanja-san." Many believers visit this shrine during spring, summer, and fall events.

spots.name: Ryusenji Temple
spots.desc: In 1367 Ryusenji Temple was built by Tsugen-jakurei. It’s part of the Sotoshu sect of Zen Buddhism. The temple was favored by the Honda family who were wealthy landowners here at the time. The temple has protected and maintained the graves of the Honda family since its foundation.

spots.name: Takefu Town Hall Museum
spots.local: 武生公会堂記念館, takefu kōkaidō kinenkan
spots.desc: This hall was built in 1929. It was repaired to keep its former appearance, and was reopened as a museum in 1995. Now, various projects take place here, such as compiling historical materials of the area, introducing the town’s history, concerts, and cultural seminars.

spots.name: Teramachi Dōri
spots.desc: This historical street in downtown Takefu is famous for its stony paths and old-looking buildings.

spots.name: Ryūmonji Temple
spots.desc: This Temple has stood in the simple architecture of Zen temples for a long time. It opened in 1299 and afterward was changed into a fort. The fort became a local base of politics and military affairs. Oda Nobunaga, who was in control of the army, set up his camp here to prepare for the war against Asakura Yoshikage and the Buddhist revolts. Now you can see the ruins of the moat and fort inside…

spots.name: Kongō-in Temple
spots.desc: Kongoin is in the Sōtō sect of Zen Buddhism, and looks like an old temple in the mountains. It was built in 1433 and moved to its present location near Takefu Station by Tomimasa Honda in 1610. Mitama Festival is held here on July 15 every year. In the festival, the silent precinct of this temple is lit up with 6,000 candles and a group of priests walk around while reading sutras.

spots.name: The House where Chihiro Iwasaki was born
spots.local: 「ちひろの生まれた家」記念館
spots.desc: This is the house where Chihiro Iwasaki, a well-known artist, was born in 1918. The people that lived in the house restored it so that you can see and learn about the culture and lifestyle of that era. Chihiro died, but her pictures are still here for everyone to appreciate.

spots.name: Ajimano Park
spots.desc: Ajimano has a deep connection with the Manyo-shu (a Nara Era poem collaboration book). It includes 63 tragic love poems written by Nakatomino Yakamori, who was exiled to this area, and Sanono Otogamino Otome, who had to live in Nara apart from Yakamori. These poems are featured in the Manyo-shu. In this park, there is a stone monument on which 15 famous waka poems were carved.

spots.name: Man'yō-kan
spots.desc: "Manyo-shu" is a royal collection of wakas, traditional Japanese poems, from the Nara era (about 1200 years ago). Some of the "Manyo-shu" wakas are said to have been written in a part of Echizen City, in Ajimano. These poems are displayed here.

spots.name: Man'yō kikka-en
spots.desc: This is the Chrysanthemums Exhibition Hall. You can see life-size dolls covered with chrysanthemums, which are exhibited during the Kikuningyō Festival in Takefu Central Park. The flowers are displayed here and continue growing throughout the year. You can view the traditional way of growing mums. Some unique flowers are "nanahon-date" – a flower that branches off into seven directions, "kengai"…

spots.name: Reisenji Temple
spots.desc: Shiba Yoshitoshi built this temple during the Muromachi Era (1336-1573). There is a rare, 8 meter tall, black lacquered wooden statue of a standing Buddha.

spots.name: Ajimano Shrine
spots.desc: This shrine worships Emperor Keitai. Kuratani Tsugutoshi, the grandson of General Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, moved into this place in the Muromachi Era (1336-1573). Inside the shrine is a part of the small wall which used to surround Kuratani’s fort.

spots.name: Takefu Knife village
spots.local: タケフナイフヴィレッジ
spots.desc: This is a workshop where handmade cutlery is made by local artisans. You can see how to make cutlery in the traditional fashion of Echizen. You can even join a class that teaches how to make a letter opener, kitchen knife, or how to polish and sharpen knives.

spots.name: Jōfuku-ji Temple Garden
spots.desc: Jōfuku-ji Temple’s garden is designated one of the must-see spots in Japan, owing to its beautiful Japanese style garden with rocks, sand, and moss. The temple was made by Tairano Yorimori whose elder brother was Tairano Kiyomori, a samurai leader of the Kamakura Era. From here you can see the beautiful Mt. Hino. A big holly tree on a mound looks like a mountain. And the moss around it appears as…

spots.name: Kakyō Park
spots.desc: This is where we can remember Emperor Keitai’s life in Echizen. This park has a thousand cherry blossom trees. The view of them blooming is beautiful. In fall, colored leaves are extremely beautiful. You can enjoy the four seasons here.

spots.name: Usuzumi Cherry Tree
spots.desc: There are many old cherry trees on Mt. Sanri. One of them is called "Usuzumi Cherry Tree," and is about six hundred years old. A long time ago, Ohto-no-oh had to part with his girlfriend to be appointed emperor -- Emperor Keitai -- in Kyoto. There after, the tree's blossom's color became lighter, so the story goes, because of her sadness. So the cherry tree is called "Usuzumi," which means almost…

spots.name: Ōgiga Pond
spots.desc: This pond was once used as a baby’s bath for Emperor Keitai’s sons, who became Emperor Ankan and Emperor Senge. Its water is very clean, like a fountain. Now, it is shaped like a hexagon.

spots.name: Japanese Paper Plaza
spots.local: 和紙の広場, washi no hiroba
spots.desc: This plaza is about 230 meters long. Paper shops and coffee houses are lined along it. There is a music bench, a fountain with koi in it, and many kinds of trees. It’s a great place to relax or go for a walk.

spots.name: Papyrus Center
spots.desc: This building holds information and a workshop about the art of traditional Echizen paper. Visitors can make their own piece of Echizen paper in 20 minutes.

spots.name: The Cultural Museum of Paper
spots.local: 紙の文化博物館, kami no bunka hakubutsukan
spots.desc: This museum exhibits information and history about Echizen paper and other traditional Japanese papers. Exhibits include milling techniques and the origin of Echizen paper.

spots.name: The Craftsman’s Studio in Udatsu
spots.local: 卯立の工芸館, udatsu no kōgeikan
spots.desc: This building is a reconstruction of the original paper mill from the Edo period. While here you can view the traditional paper milling process. Ichibei Iwano, the current owner, is following in the footsteps of his father, a famous paper maker. He is the 9th generation of traditional paper makers in Imadate. He and his father have been given the honor of "Living National Treasure" by the…

spots.name: Kojirō Park
spots.desc: A statue of Kojiro Sasaki watches over this park. Kojiro was a famous fencer from Fukui city. Many stones stand silently here. In the garden next to Kojiro park, various flowering cherry trees are planted. This garden allows us to enjoy the cherry trees as they change during each season.

spots.name: Yanagi Falls
spots.desc: The village of Yanagi is famous for its falls, small and big. They are as wonderful as Ichijo Fall in Fukui City, where the fencer, Kojiro Sasaki, is said to have devised the invincible way of killing a flying swallow called "Tsubame-gaeshi." In particular, Nuno Fall has a beautiful flow like a thin, white cloth. Many visitors enjoy hiking around the falls.

spots.name: Echizen Washi
spots.desc: locally made paper and paper crafts - From Imadate village in eastern Echizen City.

spots.name: Katsudon
spots.desc: While most of Japan prefers to eat its katsudon (breaded pork cutlet on top of rice) topped with a sweet omelet, Fukui is famous for creating the sauce katsudon, which is instead covered by a sweet and salty sauce similar to Worcester sauce. It is ubiquitous on menus throughout the prefecture.

spots.name: Echizen Kani (crab)
spots.desc: Caught in the deep water off the Echizen coast in winter, these are some of the most prized local specialties. The male Echizen crab is huge, and it's not unusual to see a 40-cm crab (including legs). The larger crabs can go for over ¥12,000 each, while the smaller female ones cost much less.

spots.name: Ski Jam
spots.desc: By far the largest ski resort in the region, often making it crowded with people from Kyoto and Osaka, especially on weekends. Ski and snowboard rental available, but call ahead for larger sizes. Overnight bus Quick Liner provides a day trip from Osaka at Shin-Osaka station for ¥7,500-12,500 including a day pass.
spots.price: Toll road ¥1300, adult day pass ¥4500, single run ¥400

spots.name: Hataya Memorial Museum
spots.local: はたや記念館 Hataya Kinenkan
spots.desc: For a small price Hataya Memorial Museum lets you try things like using a loom, making thread, or making a cute animal out of silk worm cocoons. There is also a small cafe attached.

spots.name: Megane Museum
spots.desc: Museum for eyeglasses. You can make your own frame in the workshop.

spots.name: Kehi Shrine
spots.desc: A well-known shrine throughout its history, its gate is renowned as one of the Top 3 torii gates in the nation, and the shrine was visited in 1689 by the haiku poet Matsuo Basho on his famous trip through northern Japan.

spots.name: Matsumoto Statues
spots.local: 松本零士シンボルロード
spots.desc: About twenty bronze statues of characters and scenes from the popular anime and manga by Leiji Matsumoto are scattered across the downtown. The statues, each perhaps 1.2-1.5 m (4-5 feet) tall, were erected in 1999.

spots.name: Kehi no Matsubara
spots.desc: A recreational area along the Tsuruga Bay. It combines a large pine grove with a white sand beach, very popular with swimmers in summer season.

spots.name: Tsuruga Tunnel Hot Springs
spots.desc: The hot spring was discovered during a railway tunnel digging. An indoor and outdoor spa is located on a hill, and bathers can enjoy a beautiful view of the town and the bay.

spots.name: Charlie Chaplin Statue
spots.desc: The American silent film star visited Gifu Prefecture twice in the 1930s, where he saw cormorant fishing (鵜飼 ukai, quite literally using birds to catch fish), which he described as "Japan's highest art form", but his time was all spent in Gifu where the fishing occurs. He never visited Gero, so this is not a commemorative statue as some may assume. Instead, it was made in 2001 as the first statue…

spots.name: Gero Onsen Museum
spots.desc: Small museum with hot spring paraphanalia dating back to the Edo period, samples of water from hot springs around Japan, and some simple experiments you can perform using Gero hot spring water.

spots.name: Onsen-ji Temple
spots.desc: This temple is strongly connected to the town's history. In 1265, an earthquake destroyed the town and caused the hot springs to dry up. According to legend, a white heron led villagers to a new source of hot water. The villagers built the temple in thanks, and the heron can be seen on the town's manhole covers.

spots.name: Gero Furusato History Memorial Museum
spots.local: 下呂ふるさと歴史記念館
spots.desc: A museum showcasing the archaeological findings from throughout Gero City from the Jomon and Yayoi Periods all the way to the 20th century. Outside the building are recreated Jomon Period houses.

spots.name: Gandate Canyon
spots.desc: Centered around Mount Gandate, a sheer rock formed by the eruption of Mount Ontake over 50,000 years ago, the park is designated as one of Gifu's Natural Monuments. It's particularly popular in the fall when the leaves around the mountain change colors. The Osaka Falls (小坂の滝) are located along the river next to Gandate. There is a short walking path to visit the waterfalls.
spots.price: Gandate is free. A ¥300 donation is requested to access the Hida Osaka Falls walking path

spots.name: Zenshō-ji Temple
spots.desc: A zen temple built in the Chinese Song Dynasty-style of architecture. Along with its beautiful outer facade, it also has an attractive inner garden.

spots.name: Kato Somo Memorial Museum
spots.desc: A samurai who represented Japan on the nation's first envoy to the United States, presenting a treaty to President Buchanon. He spent 2 months in the US and an additional 7 months traveling around the world on his way back to Japan. His poems, writings, and drawings from his travels became very popular. The museum contains his actual writings on the grounds of his former home.

spots.name: Nakayama Shichiri
spots.desc: A scenic gorge with various rock formations named after things they resemble. It is a popular place for spring cherry blossoms, azaleas, and autumn leaves. The Takayama Line also runs over the gorge, making it a popular place for train photographers.

spots.name: Yokotani Gorge
spots.desc: A scenic gorge known for, and often named for its four waterfalls (横谷峡四つの滝) ranging in size from 9m to 33m tall. There is a walking path to each of the falls, so it is a popular place for nature hiking and "minus ion" (マイナスイオン) or natural negative ion therapy.

spots.name: Fountain Pond Outdoor Bath
spots.local: 噴泉池野天風呂 Fusenchi notenburo
spots.desc: This open-air hot bath can be found to the west side of the bridge, with access via the south side. Note that there are no facilities to speak of and the bathing area is mixed and clearly visible to passersby on the bridge above, but admission is also free so you get what you pay for. Swimwear required for all users.

spots.name: Yunomachi Ujo Park
spots.local: 湯のまち雨情公園 Yu-no-machi Ujō Kōen
spots.desc: Much prettier than the so-called park surrounding the Hida River, this park has a lovely 500-meter walk along a tributary landscaped into a ladder waterfall, with sculptures and memorials.

spots.name: Ideyu Morning Market
spots.desc: Small market where vendors peddle local produce (only Friday-Monday), food products, and souvenirs.

spots.name: Enzo
spots.desc: Known for its "tomato-don" using Hida beef. They also offer ramen and other dishes with Hida beef.

spots.name: Ça va pas la tête?
spots.desc: With a French name, meaning "What's wrong with your head?", it features Mediterranean-inspired dishes.

spots.name: Gujo Hachiman Castle
spots.desc: Gujo Hachiman Castle was built by Endo Morikazu in 1559 and torn down during the Meiji Restoration. The castle was rebuilt in 1933 making it the oldest wooden reconstructed castle in the nation (2nd oldest reconstruction after Sumoto Castle).

spots.name: Gujo Hachiman Museum
spots.desc: The local history museum with information about the town's famous water, the castle town, and the Gujo Odori. They perform demonstrations of the Gujo Odori at specified times throughout the day.

spots.name: Jionzenji Temple
spots.desc: The temple was built by Endo Yoshitaka, the second lord of Gujo Hachiman Castle. It is most known for its garden. The temple will give you a free calendar upon leaving.

spots.name: Sample Village Iwasaki
spots.local: サンプルビレッジ・いわさき
spots.desc: Offers the opportunity to make a wide variety of food samples, including parfaits, tarts, sushi, and spaghetti. They also have some seasonal options. Reservations required.
spots.price: Prices vary depending on what you choose to make

spots.name: Sample Kobo
spots.desc: This is one of the places where visitors can make their own food samples. They have a few different options. Reservations are required.

spots.name: Kodakara no Yu
spots.desc: Also known as the "Center of Japan Onsen" (日本まん真ん中温泉), this onsen is actually part of Minami-Kodakara Onsen Station. Gujo is one of many cities in Japan that claims to be the "true center" of Japan, so the onsen's name pays honor to that notion. The onsen itself features a handful of different indoor and outdoor baths, as well as a relaxation area outside the bath entrance.

spots.name: Gujo Odori
spots.desc: The Gujo Odori is one of the most famous obon dances (bon odori) in the country. It's one of the Top three dances and listed as an Intangible Cultural Folk Asset. It is unique in that there is dancing every night from mid-July to the first weekend in September. The height of the festival is over the obon holiday when they dance from dusk to dawn. There are a variety of dances, but none are overly…

spots.name: Ryukyo no Sato
spots.desc: A large souvenir shop that also offers food sample-making. The benefit to the sample-making here is that it does not require a reservation, but they only have a couple options.

spots.name: Harokan
spots.desc: A restaurant that specializes in the area's famous Oku-Mino Curry. They also have various pork cutlet and Hida beef dishes.

spots.name: Kazamidori
spots.desc: A popular Oku-Mino Curry restaurant with its own original Oku-Mino Twin Curry which features a mound of rice flanked by two different curry varieties.

spots.name: Funamachi Port and Sumiyoshi Lighthouse
spots.desc: More commonly known as Oku no Hosomichi Musubi no Chi (奥の細道むすびの地), which means the "endpoint of The Narrow Road to the Deep North", it was Ogaki's port along a canal that connected it to Kuwana. Matsuo Basho took a boat from the port after completing his trip through Tohoku, and a statue of him is located along the canal. The lighthouse was built in the Edo Period. The canal area is known as a…

spots.name: Moriya Tadashi Art Museum
spots.local: 大垣市守屋多々志美術館
spots.desc: Born in Ogaki, Tadashi Moriya was a well-known traditional Japanese painting (nihonga) artist. The museum features his works with permanent and special exhibits.

spots.name: Aqua Walk
spots.desc: A shopping mall just outside Ogaki Station. It contains most of the same shops as Morera (the largest mall in Gifu Prefecture) but is much easier and cheaper to access by train.

spots.name: Aeon Town
spots.desc: Aeon Town is a small mall with a variety of clothing shops, a sports shop, the large Sleeping Factory, and various entertainment and specialty shops along with some restaurants. Aeon Town consists of two buildings with Korona World between them.

spots.name: Tsuchiya
spots.desc: A local sweets shop that has been in operation since 1755. The original shop sold persimmon sweets which Mino Province (southern Gifu Prefecture) was known for and is still renowned for today. The shop continues to sell various persimmon sweets but also sells a variety of other goods. The shop is located along the historic Minoji Road which connected the Nakasendo and Tokaido Roads long ago. The…

spots.name: Eihōji Temple
spots.desc: This temple is a hidden gem. A very good place to see the fall colors and the cherry blossoms. The main attraction is the small bridge over a pond. It makes for some very picturesque views.

spots.name: Tajimi Shūdōin
spots.desc: This nice old monastery built in the early 20th century makes for a nice visit before or after Eihōji Temple and a nice break from temples. You can also buy wine and other Christian related items at the gift shop.

spots.name: Mino Ceramic Art Museum
spots.desc: See beautiful Mino style ceramics or stroll through the peaceful grounds of the museum.

spots.name: Ceramics Park Mino
spots.desc: Home to the Museum of Modern Ceramic Art, another venue dedicated to ceramics. There is also a lookout platform near the park which gives a nice view of Tajimi.

spots.name: Tenkō no Yu
spots.desc: Take a dip in a nice relaxing onsen. This hot springs has several different baths all of which helps soothe the stresses of travelling away.

spots.name: Zen Meditation
spots.desc: Experience an authentic Zen Buddhist morning service at Eihoji Temple. Available every third Sunday of each month.

spots.name: Shinanoya
spots.desc: The place where Tajimi's koro udon, a cold udon with ginger and green onions, was first created.

spots.name: Karakuri Museum
spots.local: からくりミュージアム
spots.desc: Museum displays mechanical dolls which get mounted onto the Takayama festival floats. The museum also shows over 200 lion dance masks from around Japan.

spots.name: Kusakabe Mingei-kan
spots.local: Kusakabe Heritage House, 日下部民芸館
spots.desc: The Kusakabe house is a restored old merchant's home built in 1879. The home is filled with artifacts and crafts from that time period.

spots.name: Matsuri no Mori
spots.desc: Literally "Festival Forest," Matsuri no Mori displays floats and other key items from the Takayama Festival. Similar to the Takayama Float Museum but larger. Also contains large taiko drums and hosts performances. Museum is roughly a 15-minute bus ride south of the city center.

spots.name: Sakurayama Nikkokan
spots.desc: Admission is included in the ticket to the Takayama Festival Float Museum. The hall displays one-tenth-scale replicas of 28 buildings from Nikko's Toshogu shrine, created by craftsmen in intricate detail.

spots.name: Takayama Yatai Kaikan
spots.desc: Takayama Festival Float Exhibition Hall. This is the hall where the festival floats are stored. Takayama hosts a famous yearly festival and the floats are quite ornate. The floats on display are rotated.

spots.name: Takayama Showa Museum
spots.desc: A popular culture museum with exhibits from the mid-Showa Period (1950-60s). Various streets and shops display Showa-era memorabilia. You can explore the toy shop, appliance store, restaurant, doctor's office, movie theatre, and barber shop. There are also electric collections of battledores, war relics, plastic anime and manga masks, cameras, movie posters and children's toys.

spots.name: Higashiyama Walking Course
spots.desc: A 3.5-km-long hiking trail through Takayama's temples and shrines, past some of its more rural neighborhoods, and through Shiroyama Park, the former site of Takayama Castle. The course starts and ends at the Hida Takayama Museum of History and Art.

spots.name: Miyagawa Ryokuchi Park
spots.desc: A long, simple park along the Miyagawa River which peaceful views of the water. A great spot for cherry blossom viewing in the spring as the park is lined with over 100 cherry trees.

spots.name: Hida Sashiko
spots.desc: All hand-made, beautiful stitching goods are displayed in the style of an art gallery. All of the arts and goods are for sale. Media often report Hida-Sashiko as Japanese traditional art with the beauty of goods and its skills.

spots.name: Surugaya honmachiten
spots.desc: An inexpensive supermarket, including fresh fruits and vegetables.

spots.name: Agura
spots.desc: An excellent restaurant in Takayama built out of an old warehouse, Agura serves Western-style pizza and a variety of other Japanese and vegetarian friendly fare. A good place to go if you need "something for everyone". Hours are a little odd, dinner only. Prices are moderate, ranging from ¥800-1,500. They do accept credit cards.

spots.name: Beef Bun and Cafe Kihachiro Kamisannomachi
spots.local: 牛まんカフェ喜八郎 上三之町店
spots.desc: A great stop for lunch or a quick snack, this small shop in the middle of Sannomachi is most well known for its beef buns. They also serve small lunch type food, such as sakura pudding, tea, and beer.

spots.name: Chitose
spots.desc: A casual restaurant specializing in yakisoba, a dish made from fried soba noodles. English menu available.

spots.name: Crepe and Wine Hanchikutei
spots.local: クレープとワイン はんちくてい
spots.desc: One of the best dessert shops in town, this tiny crepe and wine store has amazing treats and the owners are super friendly! It's still open later in the evening when many of the surrounding shops are closed.

spots.name: Hatoya
spots.desc: Traditional Japanese restaurant specializing in Hida beef. They are especially known for their sukiyaki, which is hot pot cooked beef dipped into raw egg and eaten. A pricey splurge but totally worth it! Group plans available.

spots.name: Maruaki
spots.desc: Traditional Japanese restaurant with reasonably priced Hida beef. English menu available, friendly staff, grill and hot pot options.

spots.name: Sakaguchiya
spots.desc: Traditional Japanese restaurant located on the main sannomachi street. The menu has local soba and miso dishes. They have excellent hōba miso steak. You get a large piece of beef which is of high quality. Good value for money. This place is popular among Japanese tourists.

spots.name: Desolation Row
spots.desc: Cozy cellar whiskey bar with plenty of vinyl records from the 1960s through the 1990s. Owner knows a lot about music.

spots.name: "Doya"
spots.desc: No phone number. No menu. No actual name. Locals simply know it as "Doya". No sign out front, just a blue and white curtain with two big circles on it. Cool urban jazz and a very earthy, hip atmosphere. The proprietor speaks decent English. Despite the lack of menu, drinks are varied and priced reasonably up to ¥700. Light food is also available. Room for only about 12 at the bar only, but worth…

spots.name: Japanese Pub Yu
spots.desc: Yuichi Sano, the owner, is very friendly and welcoming. Great cocktails, even better conversation!.

spots.name: Red Hill Pub
spots.desc: Stocks imported beer and serves the usual cocktails and liqueurs. Light food such as pasta, salads, snacks, etc available. The proprietress, Hisayo, speaks fairly good English. Expect to pay ¥600-800 for drinks. Popular with local foreigners.

spots.name: Rum Dance Hall
spots.desc: A lot of different shochu and rum. Owner speaks English; good place to finish after "Doya." Best to ask your way from Doya; the Rum dance hall is very close.

spots.name: Kitamaebune Ship Museum
spots.local: Kitamaebune-no-sato, 北前船の里資料館
spots.desc: Kitamaebune ships followed a shipping route mainly through the Sea of Japan from late Edo Period to the Meiji Period. Built by Chohei Sakatani, a former owner of a Kitamaebune Ship, in 1878 (Meiji 11), this museum is beautifully built and registered as a national tangible cultural assets.
spots.price: Adult ¥310; 75 or above ¥150; Free entry for the handicapped and those under 18 years of age

spots.name: Kutaniyaki Kiln Museum
spots.desc: Constructed in 1826, the "Kama-ato" (pottery oven) used by the Yoshida Family is displayed here. As well, the history and process of making Kutaniyaki Porcelain are explained in detail and examples of the products and tools used in the process are displayed. Hands-on activities such as painting and pottery making are available.
spots.price: Adult ¥310, free entry for those who are 18 or under, 75 or above ¥150

spots.name: Gogan Shinji Festival
spots.desc: Large crowds gather to watch local young people smash and burn over 200 bamboo poles. The ritual is believed to drive away disease and encourage a bountiful harvest.

spots.name: Sakura Festival
spots.desc: A small-town celebration to welcome spring and enjoy the beauty of the new blossomed cherry trees. Festivities include lion dances and a procession of a portable shrine.
spots.addr: Daishoji on the banks of Kumasaka River

spots.name: Shobu-yu Matsuri
spots.desc: This festival is the largest in Yamashiro. More than 200 young people carry a portable shrine stuffed with irises through the streets of Yamashiro. In the past, the scent of the irises were believed to ward off evil.

spots.name: Fireworks festival
spots.desc: A fireworks display is given every night at Lake Shibayamagata. The fireworks are easily visible from the surrounding areas.

spots.name: Guzuyaki Festival
spots.desc: In this lively festival, the people of Iburihashi shoulder two large (5-6 m long) fish-shaped floats made of bamboo frames topped with plaited straw mats and bamboo and make their way through town. Upon reaching the station, the fish "fight" to the cheers of the crowd. The losing float is burned in front of the local shrine to ward off evil spirits. Children are believed to gain luck by standing…

spots.name: Jumangoku Festival
spots.desc: A smaller scale celebration similar to nearby Kanazawa's Hakumangoku Matsuri, this festival celebrates the traditions and history of the former Daishoji ruling family. The name Jumangoku refers to rice production. Juman means "100,000", and the koku is a measurement of rice production. During this festival an extremely large piece of Kutani pottery is paraded through town.

spots.name: Kutani porcelain (Kutani yaki)
spots.desc: Porcelain dishes & artwork with bright colored glazes not unlike Chinese porcelain.

spots.name: Yamanaka Lacquerware
spots.desc: A stunning example of craftsmanship, yamanaka lacquerware comes in a range of tableware and displays an artistry which blends modern concepts and time-honored traditions.

spots.name: Cafe Jiri
spots.desc: A pleasant little bakery and coffee shop with delectable cakes, tortes & cookies as well as a selection of coffee, tea & juices.

spots.name: Guranpa
spots.desc: A family restaurant with excellent katsudon and other tasty Japanese dishes.

spots.name: Kihachi Raku Hachi
spots.desc: A Japanese izakaya with an up-scale atmosphere and a wide selection of well-made food at reasonable prices.

spots.name: Portico Tea House
spots.desc: English tea shop with a great selection of teas, amazing homemade cakes and sandwiches in an elegant setting. Seasonal concerts are also held here.

spots.name: Shirokawa
spots.desc: A mom & pop restaurant which serves up local favorites. English menu available.

spots.name: Spice
spots.desc: Spice is a tasty, SE Asian fusion restaurant with a classy, but comfortable atmosphere. The staff are extremely friendly & willing to accommodate dietary restrictions. An English menu is available and the staff (especially the cook) speak a bit of English. Serving sizes are small, but delicious so prepare to order an appetizer/salad as well as an entree. Course menus are also available.…

spots.name: Taihei Sushi
spots.desc: Reasonably priced & extremely fresh selection of sushi served on conveyor belts.
spots.hours: 11:00-22:00 (21:30 last order); closed the second Wed of every month

spots.name: Komatsu no Mori
spots.desc: Komatsu Ltd. created this park at the former Komatsu Plant site nearby JR Komatsu Station. The Waku-waku Komatsu Kan (Kids Pavilion), built to recreate the original head office of Komatsu Ltd., the Genki-Satoyama, a domestic woodland to recreate igneous environs of the local Kaga region, and an exhibition space for a 930E model of the world's largest class dump truck, which was actually used in a…

spots.name: Steak Ogawa
spots.local: ステーキハウス小がわ
spots.desc: A great place to eat a steak lunch or dinner. They cook the steak in front of your eyes and serve many delicious side items with the steak. Side items include vegetables, salad, rice, and miso soup. You'll also get ice cream for dessert with your choice of tea or coffee.

spots.name: Aperitif Wine Bar
spots.desc: This cozy wine bar offers one of the best happy hours in Ishikawa — half off any drink between 18:00 and 20:00. The bar master is friendly and enjoys practicing his English with customers. Wine selections come from Chile, Spain, France, and California, and are all solid. You can also custom-order cocktails and try umeshuu (plum liquor) or Nihon-shuu (Japanese liquor made from wheat, sweet…

spots.name: Le Musée de H Confectionary Museum
spots.local: ル ミュゼ ドゥ アッシュ
spots.desc: The museum consists of a single room displaying a collection of sculptures made of sweets. The artist, Hironobu Tsujiguchi, was born in Nanao and is a world renowned confectionery chef. Adjacent is a patisserie with a variety of delicious if not somewhat expensive coffees and cakes.

spots.name: Seihakusai Dekayama Festival
spots.desc: If there's one event you must see in Nanao, it's this one! Taking place during Golden Week on May 3, 4, and 5th, this festival is designated as Japan's Important Intangible Cultural Property and consists of pulling massive structures called Dekayama ("Huge Mountain") through the streets of Nanao. These Dekayama are as high as 12 meters and weigh almost 20 tons, and the diameter of their wheels is…

spots.name: Notojima Aquarium
spots.desc: This aquarium has species from all over Japan including some that inhabit the Noto Peninsula's coast. Visitors can enjoy various attractions such as the Dolphin Show, the Sea Bream Light and Sound Show and the Sea Otter Feeding Show. It also has a tunnel tank that makes one feel as if they're underwater with the dolphins!
spots.price: ¥1,850, ¥510 for students in junior high school and younger

spots.name: Komaruyama Park Cherry Blossom Viewing
spots.local: 小丸山公園さくらまつり
spots.desc: By far the best view of cherry blossoms to be had in Nanao city, Komaruyama comes alive when sakura bloom in early April. Bring along some friends and enjoy a drink together while taking in the beauty of the park.

spots.name: Monterey Jazz Festival in Noto
spots.local: モントレージャズフェスティバル イン能登
spots.desc: Nanao has enjoyed this international jazz festival every year since its inception in 1989. So named for its sister city relationship with Monterey, California, musicians from all over the world come to play and enjoy this one-day-only event at Fisherman's Wharf - rain or shine. The event takes place on the last Saturday of July.
spots.price: Tickets are ¥5000 each pre-ordered or ¥6000 the day of the event

spots.name: Noto Marathon and Oyster Festival
spots.local: 能登和倉万葉の里マラソン
spots.desc: This event is as much a race as it is a sight-seeing tour of the beautiful areas surrounding Nanao Bay and Notojima. Taking place in March, the weather is perfect for a run. Courses range from 5km to the full marathon, and non-participants are welcome to enjoy the DIY grilled oysters and other food booths. Note: be sure to sign up early (in October) for this event.
spots.price: ¥2000-5000, depending on event entered, including refreshments, sports towel, time sheet, etc

spots.name: Kouda Fire Festival
spots.desc: This event takes place on the last Saturday of July every year, and is one of three special summer fire festivals in Japan. Many people gather to pull floats from local shrines to a central location, where small torches are thrown into an open space, creating one huge (30 m high) column of fire. People tell fortunes of the year's catch of fish and harvest by the direction of the torch when it…

spots.name: Issaki Houtou Festival
spots.desc: This is a fun event that really gives you a taste of what local festivals are all about. Taking place on the first Friday and Saturday in August, six big floats 15 m high, 9 m long, and weighing in at 2 tons are carried by 100 men and marched in procession around the alleyways of the small fishing village to the tune of tradtitional flutes and drums. Everyone is there to have a good time and…

spots.name: Hyokkori Onsen
spots.local: ひょっこり温泉島の湯
spots.desc: This public onsen is at a nice, quiet location with a beach out front and a view of central Nanao.

spots.name: Fisherman's Wharf
spots.local: 能登食祭市場 Noto Shokusai Ichiba
spots.desc: The first floor of Fisherman's Wharf is full of small shops specializing in souvenirs from the Noto. While a lot of it is the kind of over-priced junk one would find in any souvenir shop, there are some legitimately unique and interesting items including: books on the Noto Peninsula, pictures and postcards of the Noto, food/snacks unique to the Noto, and Noto wine. This is the best place to shop…

spots.name: Ipponsugi street
spots.desc: It is one of Nanao's main traditional shopping streets, located about halfway between Nanao station and Fisherman's Wharf. While home to a few heritage buildings and craft shops, most of it is distinctly ordinary. It does make for a nice stroll, especially at night when traditional lanterns are lit.

spots.name: Takazawa Candle Shop
spots.desc: Nanao began making candles around 1650 due to the influence of the Kitamaebune. Wax is made from a special type of Japanese tree, and the wick is made from a rush, or Japanese-style paper (washi). These traditional candles are completely made of natural ingredients. It is said that these types of candles are brighter and last longer than Western-style candles.

spots.name: Shirai
