spots.name: Denchu Art Museum
spots.desc: A museum featuring the works of Hirakushi Denchu, a renowned wood sculptor who was born here in Ibara.
spots.price: Regular admission ¥400, more for special exhibitions

spots.name: Narutaki Gorge
spots.desc: A popular walking/hiking area with ten small but attractive waterfalls along the course.

spots.name: Bisei Astronomical Observatory
spots.desc: The Bisei area has been known as a great place for stargazing since it was founded, so it's fitting that they chose to build an observatory here. The observatory has exhibits and a museum inside, but the highlight is the 101-cm telescope. While the nighttime hours are the obvious recommended time to come to see the stars, visitors can also locate daytime stars when visiting during the daytime…

spots.name: Chusei Yumegahara
spots.desc: Remains of ancient civilizations have been found around Ibara, so this is a reconstructed village from the Middle Ages (chusei). Visitors can stroll about the town to feel what it was like in the past. The village features old houses, farmhouses, and samurai residences among other buildings. There are activities that visitors can participate in, as well as events throughout the year. The area has…

spots.name: Indian Dining Sukoon
spots.local: インドダイニングスクーン井原店
spots.desc: A local Okayama chain restaurant serving curry and naan and other Indian dishes.

spots.name: Kabutogani Museum
spots.desc: The most well-known attraction in the city, the Kabutogani Museum features exhibits about horseshoe crabs (kabutogani) the so-called "living fossils". The surrounding Dinosaur Park features life-size dinosaurs, such as a T-Rex, which once shared the earth with horseshoe crabs.

spots.name: Ono Chikkyo Art Museum
spots.desc: Ono Chikkyo was a modern nihonga artist born here in Kasaoka. His artwork focuses on ordinary scenes of nature, many of which depict indistinguishable places in northern Okayama.

spots.name: Ikasa Railway Memorial Museum
spots.desc: A museum with artifacts, images, and information about the former Ikasa Railway, which served Kasaoka, Yakage, Ibara, and northern Fukuyama.

spots.name: Konoshima 88 Temple Pilgrimage
spots.desc: The Konoshima area has its own 88 Pilgrimage walking route for those who cannot complete the Shikoku Pilgrimage. This pilgrimage is 29 km long and can be completed in two days.

spots.name: Himawari Festival
spots.desc: This festival celebrates the blooming of more than 1 million sunflowers around the Michi no Eki. Food stalls are set up, and there is a viewing platform from which you can see the entire field of sunflowers. If you prefer a closer view, you can alternatively walk in the fields.

spots.name: Konoshima Tenjin Matsuri
spots.desc: Boats from the seven areas of Konoshima gather with loud chanting.

spots.name: Ajitokoro Eiseimaru
spots.desc: A popular Kasaoka Ramen restaurant that prides itself in using ingredients from within Okayama Prefecture.

spots.name: Kanba Falls
spots.desc: Designated as one of Japan's Top 100 Waterfalls, at 100 m tall and 20 m wide, it's the largest waterfall in Western Japan. Below the falls is the Tamatare Falls (玉垂の滝), which is a small 2-meter drop of numerous neverending drips that fall like thin threads from moss on the rocks. Wild monkeys live around the falls, so lucky visitors may see them. If you do see monkeys, do not approach them.…

spots.name: GREENable HIRUZEN
spots.local: グリーナブルヒルゼン
spots.desc: A monument to sustainability, the Kaze no Ha (Wind Leaves), is a large structure designed by architect Kengo Kuma featuring wood panels attached to steel that look like leaves blowing upward in the wind.

spots.name: Japanese Giant Salamander Center
spots.desc: A museum about the endangered and protected giant salamanders that inhabit the rivers that run through Yubara.

spots.name: Daigo-zakura
spots.desc: Named after Emperor Go-Daigo who is said to have stopped to admire the tree on his road to exile, the tree is over 1000 years old. It is one of the most famous single cherry trees in the country.

spots.name: Bitchu Kanachi Cave
spots.desc: A limestone cave featuring an attractive red bridge leading to the Cave Mount Fuji, a massive 3 meter tall, 5 meter wide stalagmite and a 22-layer stalactite that is said to be the largest of its kind in Japan. The cave was chronicled in 901, making it the oldest documented cave in Japan.

spots.name: Former Senkyo Jinjo Elementary School
spots.desc: An elementary school that operated for 84 years from its opening in 1907 to its closing in 1990. It was constructed of wood and was designated a National Important Cultural Property as an authentic Meiji Period school building in the Renaissance architectural style that was common among schools in the Chugoku Region at the time. School uniform rentals are available.
spots.hours: School 09:00-18:00, Shop 10:00-17:00, Closed We and New Years

spots.name: Katsuyama Samurai Residence
spots.desc: Home of Watanabe Tobei, a vassal of Akitsugu Miura, dating back to 1764. The house is well-preserved and filled with artifacts and weapons.

spots.name: Katsuyama Folk Museum
spots.desc: Features exhibits about the local history, such as information and artifacts related to the former castle town and the Miura family that ruled the area and objects used in daily life by ordinary citizens of the time.

spots.name: Kazan-tei
spots.desc: A resthouse in one of the buildings in the historic district. It has its own noren and is sometimes used during special events to sell unique and festive treats, such as Toshikoshi Soba (New Years Eve soba) during New Years and sweet buns during the Hina Doll Festival.

spots.name: Yubara Onsen Sunayu
spots.desc: The Sunayu is a mixed gender, open-air onsen below Yubara Dam. There are small changing areas for men and women. People used to be permitted to enter fully nude, however since 2020, they ask visitors to cover their lower half.

spots.name: Tsuji Honten Sake Brewery Tours
spots.desc: A sake brewery that began in 1804. Their sake is called "Gozen-shu" (御前酒). "Gozen", a respectful way to refer to rulers, is used because the sake was produced for the Miura family who ruled over Mimasaka Province in the feudal era ("shu" is another reading of the character that means sake). The brewery offers three different tour options: The 40 minute "Good Plan" focuses on sampling "Soyashi…
spots.price: Good Plan: ¥1500, Surprising Plan: ¥5000, Amazing Plan (prices yet to be finalized)

spots.name: Maeda Kashiten
spots.desc: A local sweets shop famous for its sake manju, a unique manju made with actual sake from the nearby Tsuji Honten. They are sold individually, so most visitors buy and eat them as a they stroll around the historic district.

spots.name: Hinoki Weaving and Dyeing Atelier
spots.desc: Also called Studio Hinoki, it is the shop of Yoko Kano, the local creator of the town's famous noren. As the shop name suggests, she is skilled in both dyeing and weaving. If you enjoy the noren you see in the town, you can purchase your own here.

spots.name: Sugi Hakimono Souvenir Shop
spots.desc: A local souvenir shop featuring local goods, such as Katsuyama's dango and other snacks, as well as chirimen products and geta, traditional Japanese shoes. The shop's noren features the geta straps.

spots.name: Yamana Shokudo
spots.desc: One of the city's Hiruzen Yakisoba destinations, they have three dishes that are a play on words. 'Hiru' can refer to "Noon", so in addition to Hiruzen Yakisoba, they also offer Asa-zen Yakisoba ("Asa" meaning "morning"), which has an egg on top and Yu-zen Yakisoba ("Yu" meaning "Evening/Night") which has ginger in it.

spots.name: Kougen-tei
spots.desc: A Hirzuzen Yakisoba restaurant with the morning and evening varieties, along with their own original "Horumon Yakisoba", which uses horumon, giblets famous in Tsuyama, instead of the traditional chicken.

spots.name: Oni no Sumika
spots.desc: A simple restaurant mainly open during lunch hours that serves curry and naan, along with desserts. It is one of the noren buildings in Katsuyama's historic district, and because "oni" (demon/ogre) is in the name, its noren features a Japanese ogre.

spots.name: Raikyū-ji
spots.desc: A zen temple of the Rinzai sect that dates back to 1504. The beautifully constructed garden within the temple grounds was designed by Kobori Enshu, who is one of the founders of the Japanese tea ceremony. It's about 15 minutes from JR Bitchu Takahashi Station.

spots.name: Takahashi Museum of History
spots.local: 高梁市歴史美術館 Takahashi rekishi bijutsukan
spots.desc: A museum dedicated to the city's long history from its days as part of the ancient Kibi Kingdom to the feudal era when the wider Bitchu Province was ruled from Bitchu Matsuyama Castle to the present day.

spots.name: Shōren-ji
spots.desc: This temple, built atop a large stone wall, looks more like a fortress than a temple.

spots.name: Yakushi-in
spots.desc: Yakushi-in gained its fame as the setting of the movie "Otoko wa Tsurai yo" (男はつらいよ).

spots.name: Takahashi Church
spots.local: 高梁基督教会堂 Takahashi kirisuto kyōkaidō
spots.desc: Constructed in 1889 (Meiji 22) by a Western architect, it's the oldest church in Okayama. Worship services are still held on Sunday mornings.

spots.name: Orii House
spots.desc: A former samurai residence. Visitors are free to walk in and around the house. Don't forget to go around the back to the small museum featuring samurai armor and other objects owned by the Orii family.

spots.name: Hayama Gorge
spots.desc: A scenic gorge with picturesque rock formations. It is also popular among rock climbers.

spots.name: Nariwa Museum
spots.desc: A remote art museum along the Nariwa River. It was founded as a way to showcase the art of Torajiro Kojima who was born here. The museum also features special exhibits throughout the year. The building was designed by the famous architecture, Tadao Ando.
spots.hours: Tue-Sun 09:30-17:00, periodic closures when changing exhibits

spots.name: Fukiya Bengara Village
spots.desc: One of Japan's many remaining Edo-period villages, Fukiya is well known for the unique burnt orange color of the buildings. The color comes from a mix of iron-oxide and vermillion known as bengara, a bastardized pronunciation of Bengal, where the pigment was originally produced. Some of the buildings are locally-owned shops, while others, such as the post office, can only be viewed from the…

spots.name: Fukiya Elementary School
spots.desc: Built in 1909 when the area was still wealthy from the copper mines, the school, like the rest of the Fukiya area, saw its population dwindle as the mines closed. In 2009 only 6 students remained in the entire school. It was known as the oldest wooden school still in use in Japan until it finally closed in 2012. The school has been preserved as an important local landmark and popular attraction…

spots.name: Bengara Factory Museum
spots.desc: A collection of buildings that walk visitors through the steps of gathering and creating the bengara dyes, as well as the dyeing process.

spots.name: Nishie Residence
spots.desc: The house was built by the Nishie family who prospered from both the copper mines and the bengara dyes and fabrics. The house remains the property of the Nishie family.

spots.name: Hirokane Residence
spots.desc: The house, built in 1810, belonged to the Hirokane family, a merchant family who made money off the copper mines.

spots.name: Bengara Dyeing
spots.desc: The Fukiya area is famous for its rusty-red bengara dyes which it has been producing since the Edo Period. Those who like the color can of course purchase various articles of dyed clothing at various shops in the town however, there is another option for those interested in bengara dyes: learn to dye your own scarves. Those interested in the dyeing experience need a reservation at least 2 days in…
spots.price: Dye a small scarf ¥1,500, dye a long stole scarf ¥3,000

spots.name: Castle Viewpoint
spots.desc: The view of Bitchu Matsuyama Castle shrouded in a sea of clouds (雲海 unkai) has gained a lot of attention. Castle fans and professional and amateur photographers alike have become interested in how to get the shot of the "Castle in the Sky" (天空の城) themselves. There is a viewpoint about 8.5 km from Bitchu-Takahashi Station. An early morning bus is available during peak season to take visitors to…
spots.hours: 24h, but Nov-Mar early morning to 08:00 offers the highest chances of seeing the sea of clouds

spots.name: Nariwa Atago Firework Festival
spots.desc: A firework festival with roots dating back to the Edo Period.

spots.name: Matsuyama Odori
spots.desc: A dancing festival that began in the 17th century. It features a dancing parade, a samurai dance performance (仕組踊り), and the yatosa (ヤトサ) in which observers are welcome to join the dance.

spots.name: Fukiya Bengara Lantern Festival
spots.desc: Lanterns line Fukiya's historic street and traditional dances are performed.

spots.name: Asada Hyakka-ten
spots.desc: A shop selling bengara products, such as scarves, clothing, and paper, as well as bengara powder and other local goods.

spots.name: Koyagawa Tourism Center
spots.local: 高梁市観光物産館紺屋川
spots.desc: A great place to purchase Takahashi's local products and handicrafts.

spots.name: Cafe Rest Chateau
spots.local: カフェ・レスト・シャトー
spots.desc: Sells set lunches & dinners for about ¥800. Also sells pasta, omurice, and curry. Famous for having amazing parfaits, as well as for 'bucket parfaits' - parfaits served in a pail, or if you reserve in advance and have enough people, you can order the giant parfait served in a tub (14-16 people recommended).

spots.name: Kawakamiya
spots.desc: A convenient katsu-don (pork cutlet) restaurant with other similar foods.

spots.name: Kappo Uno
spots.desc: Serves yuzu miso katsudon (pork cutlet with yuzu miso sauce over rice), a local specialty.

spots.name: Organic Shokudo Kaneya
spots.local: オーガニック食堂 金子や
spots.desc: An organic restaurant. Its Bengara vegetable curry and Bengara vegetable katsu curry are fairly popular. The black curry is both interesting to look at and delicious.

spots.name: Shibukawa Beach
spots.desc: A calm white sand beach with pine trees, about 1 kilometer long. Excellent for windsurfing or sailing year-round. Free parking. Showers, lockers, changing rooms are only available during the official season, though you might be able to enter the beach in the off-season.
spots.hours: Last Sun of Jun to last Sun of Aug

spots.name: Shibukawa Marine Aquarium
spots.desc: Includes 180 species, most of which are native to the nearby Seto Inland Sea.

spots.name: Gallery Minato
spots.desc: A gallery/rental atelier for local artists. Open atelier held every first Sunday of the month.

spots.name: Gallery sans quois
spots.local: アートギャラリー サンコア
spots.desc: A fine art gallery featuring local and international artists.
spots.hours: 10:00-17:00, closed on all dates including the numbers 4 and 8

spots.name: Chinu - the Black Sea Bream of Uno
spots.desc: Sculpture by Yodogawa-Technique. A colorful sculpture created from recycled cans, bottles, and household items. Artwork No. 182 of the Setouchi Triennale Art Festival.

spots.name: JR Uno Port Line Art Project
spots.desc: Project by Esther Stocker. Four stations from the Uno Line are transformed into artwork by simple compositions of geometric lines done in black and white. Artwork No. 187 of the Setouchi Triennale Art Festival.
spots.addr: JR Uno, Bizentai, Hachihama, and Tsuneyama Stations

spots.name: Memory of Ship's Hull
spots.desc: Sculpture by Atsushi Ozawa. A large metal sculpture incorporating an anchor from a former Japanese Imperial Navy vessel and the propeller of a Norwegian ship. Artwork No. 184 of the Setouchi Triennale Art Festival.

spots.name: The Sea's Memory
spots.desc: Sculpture by Haruyuki Uchida. Sea water is enclosed within a mirror-like titanium sculpture in the form of a boat. Artwork No. 186 of the Setouchi Triennale Art Festival.

spots.name: Miyama Park
spots.desc: A 200-hectare park with over 300 species of trees, including cherry blossom, Japanese plum, camellia, azalea, and maple trees. Includes and English garden.

spots.name: Ojigatake Hill
spots.desc: A scenic mountain trail within the Setonaikai National Park with unique-shaped rocks overlooking the ocean. Spectacular view of the Great Seto Bridge and scattered islands of the Seto inland sea. Hiking trail from the beach to the summit, and around the observatory. Other activities such as rock climbing and paragliding available.

spots.name: Setouchi Onsen Tamanoyu
spots.local: 瀬戸内温泉 たまの湯
spots.desc: A natural hot spring spa with the widest variety of open-air baths in Okayama prefecture overlooking the Seto Inland Sea. Traditional Japanese building with baths, spas, lounges, and an authentic Japanese restaurant (vegetarian meals available). Free Wi-Fi, English speaking staff, accepts major credit cards. The onsen reserves the right to refuse entry to anyone heavily intoxicated or with…
spots.hours: 10:00-23:00 daily (closed for maintenance every third Tue of the month)

spots.name: Cafe Restaurant Sonaru
spots.local: カフェ・レストラン ソナール
spots.desc: Serves beef stew, curry, pancakes, etc. It's also one of the restaurants where you can get the local specialty Ontama meshi.

spots.name: Jidaiya
spots.desc: Serves curry and steak with their own special sauce. It's also a popular ontama meshi restaurant.

spots.name: Mt. Hoshitaka
spots.desc: A mountain close to Gotsu station, with legend of a meteor strike in ancient times. The giant star symbol near the top is used for illumination in summer. It's a good half day hike or a quick drive and the top is a great place for a picnic.

spots.name: Ogawa Residence
spots.desc: The Ogawa family were a wealthy family descended from Wake Kiyomori and employees of the imperial court. When the family moved here, they developed the area to establish a town. During the Muromachi Period, the famous painter-poet Sesshu stayed at the Ogawa house and during that time, he designed and built their garden. Today visitors can enter the house and enjoy the garden.

spots.name: Gotsu Honmachi Iraka Kaido
spots.desc: A scenic district of historic houses that have been preserved from area's heyday as a port town.

spots.name: Aquas Aquarium
spots.local: 島根県立しまね海洋館アクアス
spots.desc: A small but interesting aquarium with 10,000 fish and mammals across 400 species. The main tank has a tunnel you can walk through as sharks swim above.

spots.name: Hamada Castle
spots.desc: It was built in 1620 and destroyed in the final days of the Tokugawa shogunate. The foundations are surrounded by a pleasant park, on a hill overlooking the harbor. A prefectural cultural asset.

spots.name: Iwami Kokubunji Temple
spots.desc: Believed to have been built in the late 8th century, although today only the great foundation stones of its tower remain. A prefectural cultural asset.

spots.name: Tadaji
spots.desc: Thought to date from somewhere between the mid-10th and late 11th centuries, the temple houses 59 wooden Buddha statues (木造天部像群) in its main hall. A prefectural cultural asset.

spots.name: Iwami Tatami ga Ura
spots.desc: A rock configuration created by an earthquake in 1872, which rose the seabed 1.5 meters, leaving circular rocks protruding above the seashore. A national natural monument.

spots.name: Kokufu Beach
spots.desc: An amazing surf spot in Shimane. Locals are friendly. The surf is variable, better in winter, but extremely cold. In summer the water is warm, but the sea may be flat. A good place to be during typhoon season in late summer/autumn.

spots.name: Iwami Seaside Park
spots.desc: Nice beaches for swimming, snorkeling, and surfing. There are cabins and campsites for rent. Beware of strong currents on rough days, though. You can also watch kite surfers at the weekend.

spots.name: Grand Toit
spots.desc: Art Museum and concert hall. To visit the art museum one time costs about ¥1000. If you think you will go to the museum three or more times in one year, you may want to consider getting the "passport" option that allows you unlimited entry for ¥3000.

spots.name: Ikoji
spots.desc: Built in 1363, this temple is known for having hosted the famous Zen Buddhist monk and artist Sesshu (1420-1506) as its fifth chief priest from 1460 to 1485. Sesshu designed a garden here, now designated an important cultural property. The main gate was relocated from Nanao Castle.

spots.name: Manpukuji
spots.desc: Built by the Masuda family, this temple's garden was also designed by Sesshu, and its Kamakura-style main hall was designated a nationally important cultural property.

spots.name: Sesshu Memorial Museum
spots.desc: The museum has a small collection of Sesshu's art and information about him.

spots.name: Taikian
spots.desc: Built where Toko Temple (where Sesshu spent his last years) once stood. It is said that Sesshu visited Masuda again in the Meiou period (1492–1506), entered Toko Temple (Taikian) and stayed there until he died at the age of 87 in 1506. His grave was built on the hillside behind Taikian.

spots.name: Hikimi Gorge
spots.desc: It's in Hikimi, a village that merged with Masuda a few years ago. It is considered one of the most beautiful areas in Shimane.

spots.name: Dangyo Falls
spots.desc: Listed as one of Japan's top 100 waterfalls, Dangyo Falls drops 40 feet from above Dangyo Shrine.

spots.name: Adachi Museum of Art
spots.desc: Although it is an art museum, Adachi is most famous for its gorgeous 43,000 m² garden, deemed Japan's best garden by the American Journal of Japanese Gardening for 10 years straight. The gardens are ranked according to how well they utilize sukiya living and there is a bias towards gardens that are less-frequented and less-famous but still well-kept. However, visitors can only view it through…
spots.price: \2300 (foreigners get a discount to \2000 by showing passport); recorded English tours \600

spots.name: Yasugibushi Theater
spots.desc: Will reopen 26th May 2024. Yasugibushi is one of the most popular folk songs and dances in Japan, featuring the humorous loach-scooping dance dojousukui. (The loach is a kind of fish.) Regular performances on weekends and holidays only; 11:20-12:00 and 13:20-14:00. On weekdays, group of 20 or more can reserve a performance.

spots.name: Hirose Kasuri Center
spots.desc: Hirose Kasuri is a traditional method of weaving cloth, and this technique has been designated as an intangible cultural asset by Shimane Prefecture. Cotton thread is dyed in wool with indigo to show patterns on the cloth. You can see weavings on the loom and buy handmade Kasuri and indigo-dye articles here. This living textile heritage has been a part of the local scene for 170 years. For ¥800…

spots.name: Wako Museum
spots.desc: Wako means Japanese steelmaking. This museum stands next to the Port of Yasugi, which prospered at the end of the Edo era as a steel port. Many fine samurai swords, for example, were made of steel from Yasugi. Using HDTV and robots, Wako Museum describes the tatara method of steel-making employed here along with much else about steel-making in Japan.

spots.name: Kano Museum of Art
spots.desc: This museum has a very rare collection of Japanese old style pottery Bizen-yaki (including kobizen which are made before the Momoyama Period). Closed Last Tuesdays of February, May, August, and 25 Dec to 10 Jan.

spots.name: Kiyomizu Temple
spots.desc: Surrounded by wooded hillsides, this temple boasts an especially beautiful main hall and three-level pagoda. Founded in 587, in the 9th century Kiyomizu Temple prospered as the foremost center of the Tendai sect, a Buddhist sect that favored mountain recluses. You can enjoy traditional vegetarian cuisine at two inns and a restaurant within the temple grounds (bookings recommended).

spots.name: Gassan Toda Castle Remains
spots.desc: These are the ruins of the castle of the Amako clan, who ruled this area during Japan's period of warring states (1467-1568). The castle was famed as an impregnable redoubt, spreading over the entire summit of Mt. Gassan, 184 m above sea level. At the ruins only stone walls and old stone pavement remain as traces of the past. The castle in Matsue was built to replace this castle.

spots.name: Saginoyu Onsen
spots.desc: Its name means "the heron's hot spring"; according to local legend, it was discovered 1300 years ago, when a white heron alighted on a rock just as hot water welled up, healing its leg.

spots.name: Yasugi Tsukinowa Festival
spots.desc: This festival reenacts the story of the Inomaro-densho, recorded in the Izumo-Fudoki. In this tale, the spirit of the daughter of Katari-no-Omiimaro sets off for the underworld. The purpose of the festival is to comfort the daughter's restless spirit. Four festival floats, called dashi, parade through the streets accompanied by flutes and drums.

spots.name: Hakuta Tulip Festival
spots.desc: A Tulip Festival with thousands of tulips of numerous types and colors. At the festival you can purchase Tulips for ¥50 each. Built to provide a nice background for the tulips, Hakuta has a sort of Dutch-looking windmill.

spots.name: Cafe Rosso
spots.desc: One of the most famous cafes in Japan. The owner, Hiroyuki Kadowaki, won the Japan barista championship and placed 2nd in the 2005 World Barista Competition in Seattle. It's on Route 9 near the border with Yonago.

spots.name: Shirai Omachi Wisteria Park
spots.desc: Open only during the wisteria season, typically the weeks around Golden Week (late April-early May), the park features a variety of wisteria trellises surrounding a central fountain. It bills itself as the "Best Wisteria in the San-in Region". Carp streamers are hung over the hill above the trellises to celebrate Children's Day.

spots.name: Mikobata Ore Processing Site
spots.desc: The site was built to process what was mined from Ikuno Silver Mines. At its peak, it was the largest processing site in Asia. Like the mines, it is no longer in use, but the site has been preserved as a historic park.

spots.name: Ikuno Silver Mines
spots.desc: The mines were originally operated by Tajima Province and it is said that Takeda Castle was built in part to maintain and protect ownership of the mines, and battles were fought from the castle over control of the mines. As the nation was being unified, Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi took great interest in the mines and sent their own government magistrates to oversee the mines. During this…

spots.name: Ikuno Silver Mine Culture Museum
spots.local: 生野鉱物館・生野銀山文化ミュージアム
spots.desc: Has information about the history of Ikuno Silver Mine and a large variety of rocks and minerals mined here.

spots.name: Tatsuno Castle
spots.desc: The castle was built here during the Edo Period as a split-castle with the mountaintop castle being its other half. It was a palace castle, so it never had a donjon. Although there were no blueprints, historical documents were used as the basis to reconstruct the walls, gate, turret, and palace building. Visitors can enter the palace. The paintings inside were made by a famous local artist. It's…

spots.name: Sekai no Ume Park
spots.desc: The name means "World Plum Park" and was given to highlight the fact that the plum blossoms here come from China, Taiwan, and Korea along with Japanese varieties. The park contains over 1200 trees that blossom from mid-February to early March. The building in the center was built by builders from China. There are also hydrangeas that bloom around mid-June.

spots.name: Tatsuno City History and Culture Museum
spots.local: たつの市立龍野歴史文化資料館
spots.desc: Showcases the history of the city with exhibits about the Kofun Period, Tatsuno Castle and life in the castle town, and the old Sanyo Road.

spots.name: Togetsukyō Bridge
spots.desc: This picturesque bridge spans the Hozu River, which usually has a healthy and fast current of water in it. Please note that the sidewalks are one-way.

spots.name: Tenryū-ji
spots.desc: One of the city's UNESCO World Heritage Sites and the main temple of the Rinzai sect of Buddhism in Kyoto; it's also considered one of Kyoto's Five Great Zen Temples. Tenryu-ji was founded in 1334, but the current buildings all date from the last century: pleasant, but unremarkable. However, there is a lovely garden and pond, designed by the Zen master Musō Soseki, that is worth a look - and well…

spots.name: Ōkōchi Sansō
spots.desc: A splendid mountain retreat, previously occupied by Japanese silent screen legend Ōkōchi Denjirō. The grounds have something beautiful to offer each season but are probably at their best during autumn, when the trees explode into fiery shades of red and gold. Take a long, leisurely walk through the villa's beautiful gardens and savour the fine views of the city below. There is a small museum on…
spots.price: Entrance is ¥ 1000; the price includes a cup of matcha (green tea) and a small dessert in the villa's teahouse

spots.name: Nonomiya Shrine
spots.desc: A small shrine located amidst Arashiyama's famous bamboo forest. It was here that women were once trained prior to becoming shrine maidens at Ise Shrine, the holiest Shinto Shrine in Japan.

spots.name: 19th Century Hall
spots.desc: A museum covering the unlikely combination of steam locomotives and pianos. Probably best to look at it from the outside, and listen to the amusing tinny music it blasts out.

spots.name: Otagi Nenbutsu-ji Temple
spots.desc: Despite being omitted from virtually all guidebooks, it's one of the true unknown gems of Kyoto. It was founded in the eighth century, and went through an unlucky patch for a millennium or so; by turns it was destroyed by flood, fire and typhoon, and had to move location a few times. Today, it sits a short distance from the end of Saga Toriimoto, one of Kyoto's three historic preservation…

spots.name: Daikakuji Temple
spots.desc: While it is a temple today, originally, it was the villa of Emperor Saga. It is well-known by those who practice Ikebana, the Japanese art of flower arranging, as it is the birthplace of Saga Goryu, a school of Ikebana. Often, there are examples of Saga Goryu near the entrance to the temple. The temple itself is reasonably large, with some artwork inside. The view of the Osawanoike Pond is quite…

spots.name: Adashino Nenbutsu-ji
spots.desc: The famous Priest Kūkai established this temple for the purpose of saying prayers for Arashiyama's dead. The temple grounds are filled with approximately 8000 Buddhist statues, each representing an unknown or forgotten person. Although it is famous for its statues, just like Otagi Nenbutsu-ji, Adashino Nenbutsu-ji is a spiritual place and a graveyard, so it has greater historical and spiritual…

spots.name: Giōji Temple
spots.desc: Mentioned in the Tales of Heike, this is the site where sisters Gio and Ginyo come to devote their lives to Buddhism. Although the temple itself is rather small, the visit is made worthwhile by its vivid bright green moss garden.

spots.name: Takiguchi-dera Temple
spots.desc: A quiet, peaceful temple of less interest than nearby Gioji Temple.

spots.name: Jōjakkōji Temple
spots.desc: This temple is quite beautiful in the autumn when the leaves are changing, and the view of the city from just above the pagoda is a truly spectacular.

spots.name: Nison-in Temple
spots.desc: A large temple complex that houses two ancient sculptures of Buddha; one of Shakamuni Buddha and the other of Amida Buddha. It also houses the graves of some famous Japanese people. Unless you have interest in visiting one of the graves, the complex seems expensive compared to other temples of the same price with much more interesting sites and history.

spots.name: Hōkyō-in
spots.desc: Home to the graves of the court's former enemies, as well as a beautiful moss garden.

spots.name: Seiryō-ji
spots.local: 清凉寺; 峨釈迦堂, sagashaka-dō
spots.desc: This is the former home of Minamoto no Tōru who is believed to be the man that the famous Tale of Genji's protagonist Genji was inspired by.

spots.name: Senkō-ji
spots.desc: This temple was built as a memorial temple for those who died while working on dams and other projects under Suminokura Ryōi. There are a variety of monuments and statues on the temple grounds, and a haiku from the famous poet Matsuo Bashō was written about the cherry blossoms on the temple grounds. The walk along the Hozu River leading to the temple is arguably more enjoyable than the temple…

spots.name: Kōryū-ji Temple
spots.desc: Of all the temples in Kyōto, Kōryū-ji is the oldest, dating back to the 12th century. It also houses the Miroku Bosatsu, the first item in the nation to be designated a National Treasure.

spots.name: Toei Kyoto Studio Park
spots.local: 東映太秦映画村, tōei uzumasa eiga mura
spots.desc: An active film studio built by the Toei Company, one of Japan's largest entertainment companies. The highlight is the backlot with recreated Edo-period streets, where many period dramas (時代劇 jidaigeki) were filmed, and continues to be in active use so you may catch a filming session going on if you're lucky. Also has many shows and exhibits about filming techniques, as well as plenty of…

spots.name: Matsunoo Taisha
spots.local: 松尾大社, matsunoo-taisha; nickname: matsuo-taisha
spots.desc: A shrine that's rarely visited by foreigners, Matsuo Taisha (as it's more commonly known) is a popular place for sake brewers to pray. The shrine existed prior to the establishment of Kyoto as Japan's capital and later received offerings from the Heian court. The shrine is famous for its water, said to be pure, as well as its interesting gardens and landscape.
spots.price: Shrine is free, ¥500 to see shrine treasures and garden area

spots.name: Katsura Imperial Villa
spots.desc: A real cultural treasure, renowned for its magnificent gardens and fine classical architecture. You can obtain permission to join a tour of the property either through the Imperial Household Agency's official website (which also contains a detailed list of instructions ) or by applying in person at the agency's Kyoto office (near the Imperial Palace). Be sure to apply well in advance of your…

spots.name: Umenomiya Shrine
spots.desc: This shrine is oddly dedicated to gods of both easy delivery and sake, because it is believed that the goddess Saketokekono was so delighted at the birth of her son that she made and drank sake. In addition, the stone to the right (upon entering) is believed to ensure pregnancy to any woman who steps over it, as a former Empress originally who was originally thought to be barren got pregnant…
spots.price: The shrine grounds are free, but to enter the shrine costs ¥500

spots.name: Suzumushi-dera
spots.desc: "Suzumushi-dera" means "cricket temple", and as you might guess, there is a large case of crickets all along the wall inside the temple. Ever since the temple was featured on the NHK, Japan's national television station, it has received quite large crowds of people waiting to enter, but don't let the crowds scare you away. The purpose is to enjoy the crickets chirping, so upon entering, visitors…

spots.name: Kokedera
spots.local: 苔寺; officially 西芳寺, Saihō-ji
spots.desc: Kokedera, also known as Saiho-ji, is one of Kyoto's World Heritage Sites famous for is beautiful moss garden. In the past, visitors could come and go freely, like most temples however, due to tourists stepping on and killing the moss, the temple had to limit the number of visitors and now requires a reservation in order to visit. The only accepted method is by mail. You need to send a letter…
spots.hours: The temple will tell you when your reservation is scheduled for in their response letter if you have been accepted
spots.price: Admission is ¥3000 (the most expensive temple in Kyoto)

spots.name: Hozu River Cruise
spots.desc: To experience Arashiyama to the fullest, the river cruise is your best bet! A variety of boats, small or large, both rowed and motored, are waiting on either side of the river. Be sure to confirm how far and for how long the trip goes, though. Some are as long as two hours, and others will do a quick turnaround in less than twenty minutes. Be prepared to get splashed and take appropriate…
spots.hours: Departures run from mid March to the end of November roughly on the hour starting at 09:00. Last boat leaves at 15:30.…

spots.name: Ride in a Rickshaw
spots.desc: For those looking to experience Kyoto from a different perspective, travelling in a rickshaw allows you to do just that. You can arrange where they will take you (and check the fees, of course) and then they will take a picture of you inside the rickshaw. Depending on where you are, you may even be able to get the Togetsukyo Bridge in the background. While you travel, the rickshaw puller will…
spots.price: Prices range from about ¥5000-7000, depending on where you go

spots.name: Sagano Romantic Train
spots.desc: A scenic train clinging to the sides of the Hozu river gorge that runs from Arashiyama to Kameoka. Many people enjoy riding the train to Kameoka and then taking the Hozu River Cruise back to Arashiyama.
spots.hours: Trains depart from Torokko Saga Station every hour from 08:50 to 16:50 and from Torokko Arashiyama Station every hour…

spots.name: JJ Sagano
spots.desc: A nice souvenir shop with a variety of Hello Kitty goods, as well as many local souvenirs.

spots.name: Shinpachi Tea House
spots.desc: Despite being called a teahouse, Shinpachi is popular for its gelatto ice cream. They also have ice cream cones and parfaits. It is also a souvenir shop, so visitors often enjoy eating their gelatto while browsing the shop.

spots.name: Shintogetsu
spots.desc: Serves a variety of meal set, with soba and the famous Yodofu (tofu) being among the most popular.

spots.name: Hirokawa
spots.desc: A great restaurant for those who enjoy eating eel. Reservations may be made one month in advance.

spots.name: Chishaku-in Temple
spots.desc: Buddhist temple affiliated with Shingon-shū Chizan-ha Buddhism. The temple has a historic garden that was said to be a favourite of Sen no Rikyū.

spots.name: Higashi Ōtani Mausoleum
spots.local: 東大谷; 大谷祖廟 Ōtani Sobyō
spots.desc: Located in a cemetery, tourists typically visit this site accidentally however, because some of the ashes of Shinran, the founder of Jōdo-Shin Buddhism, are contained inside the mausoleum, it is a popular place for Buddhists to come to pay their respects.
spots.price: Entrance to the grounds is free

spots.name: Ryozen Gokoku Shrine
spots.desc: This shrine was built to house the souls of all those who died in the Pacific War, from the Meiji Restoration uprisings and the Russo-Japanese War to the end of World War II. It is the first shrine in the nation to be officially recognized as a shrine for war dead.

spots.name: Anraku-ji
spots.desc: A temple built to console the souls of Anraku and some concubines who were killed by order of the Imperial Court who did not approve of their Buddhist sect.

spots.name: Kōun-ji
spots.desc: A temple designed around the borrowed scenery of the surrounding mountains, it was once owned by Empress Go-mizunoo.

spots.name: Nyakuoji Shrine
spots.local: 若王子神社 Nyakuōji-jinja; 熊野若王子神社 Kumano Nyakuōji-jinja
spots.desc: Established in 1160, a nice shrine to visit in the autumn when the leaves are changing. It's a worthwhile stop for those travelling along the Philosopher's Path, but probably not worth making the trip just to see this shrine.

spots.name: Eikandō Temple
spots.desc: A large temple said to have been constructed by Priest Kūkai. The temple features a unique statue of Amida Buddha, Mikaeri Amida, that looks to the right rather than facing forward; there's a charming legend attached to it. The temple grounds also feature a Tahōtō pagoda and a lake. The temple is particularly pleasant in the autumn when the leaves are changing (and the admission fee jumps to…

spots.name: Walk the Philosopher's Path
spots.desc: The 2-km-long path through north-eastern Kyoto, along which a philosophy professor, Kitarō Nishida, used to frequently walk. It is a surprisingly pleasant and relaxing walk even today, though you will undoubtedly share it with more tourists than Kitaro did. The walk runs south from Ginkakuji beside an aqueduct to Nyakuōji Shrine, many guidebooks suggest that the walk continues further south from…

spots.name: Ride in a Rickshaw
spots.desc: Unlike the days of old when rickshaw pullers were looked down upon, the men pulling them today are quite highly regarded (and highly attractive). Some of the most popular pullers may even have their own patrons. These men do not simply transport you; they also act as guides, sharing information about the area and attractions. For those who can understand Japanese, it can be as informative as it…
spots.price: Prices vary depending on what route you choose, but they typically range from ¥5000–7000

spots.name: Tea Ceremony at Shoren-in
spots.desc: The ceremony is held in the former study of retired Emperor Gosakuramachi known as the Kōbun-tei, typically not open to visitors. The room was rebuilt in the 1990s after a fire burned down the original, but it is still an interesting place nonetheless, and the tea ceremony is an interesting experience.
spots.hours: Open from 10:00-15:30 on the vernal equinox, May 5, and throughout November
spots.price: The ceremony costs ¥1000 in addition to the temple entrance fee, costing ¥1500 total

spots.name: Camellia, Tea Ceremony
spots.desc: You can enjoy an authentic tea ceremony in a beautiful 100-year-old traditional Geisha house just five minutes from Kiyomizu Temple. Instruction, demonstration, a bowl of tea and a sweet are included. Each session starts every hour on the hour, between 10:00 and 17:00. Cash and credit card accepted.

spots.name: Geisha Walking Lecture
spots.desc: If you're interested in the world of the geisha, you shouldn't miss the walking lecture by well-renowned cultural expert Peter MacIntosh. The walk will have you tour the geisha district of Gion, where Peter will give you an insider's view into the past, present and future of this unique and exotic world. If you're lucky, you might see a geisha walking by to one of her appointments. Reservation is…

spots.name: Photo session as Maiko/Geiko
spots.desc: If you are interested in having a photo session dressed up as a maiko or geisha - or, for men, as a samurai - several studios in Kyoto provide this service at affordable price, a practice known as henshin. The session includes full make up and dress in a kimono and normally lasts for 1½–2 hours. Options include indoor or outdoor shots (strolling in Gion dressed up as a geisha!) - plus, at…
spots.addr: 4F Ouka Bldg., 576 Gion-cho Minamigawa Shijo-tori Hanamikoji Nishi-iru Higashiyama-ku

spots.name: Rakushisha Paper Crafts
spots.desc: A great souvenir shop with some more original and less tacky souvenirs. In particular, for those looking to purchase nice paintings or copies of famous Japanese paintings, this shop offers a variety of paintings on paper that are attractive and more sophistocated-looking than those that you will find along Shijo, near Kiyomizu-dera, and other high-traffic tourist areas. There are also authentic…

spots.name: Honke Nishio Yatsuhashi
spots.desc: The best store to buy raw yatsuhashi, it offers the largest variety of flavors, including seasonal varieties.

spots.name: Torikizoku
spots.desc: Torikizoku is the most popular yakitori chain in Kansai. There are several locations in Kyoto - most convenient for travellers is in Kawaramachi/Shijo, just before the bridge, or between sanjo and shijo, on kiyachou-dori. The yakitori is delicious, comes in generous serves and is very cheap. It's very popular with both locals and expats, and is always busy. Try to come before 19:30 to secure…

spots.name: Toryanse
spots.desc: A restaurant with vegan options. The interior features photos of cat that roam around the Philosopher’s Path. Cash only.

spots.name: Il Pappalardo
spots.desc: One of Kyoto's best Italian restaurants. Dishes tend to be pricey, but the food tastes delicious. Pizzas are sold at more affordable prices.

spots.name: Saryou Tsuriji
spots.desc: Famous for its matcha (grean tea) parfait, this restaurant is quite popular among Japanese tourists. It is not uncommon to wait 30 minutes just to get inside. Mainly ice cream is served, and most of it is grean tea flavored, as it is a Kyoto specialty. It's a nice experience for those who like to make eating part of their travel experience, but for those on a budget, there are plenty of vendors…

spots.name: Sweets Paradise
spots.desc: Sweets Paradise is the famed all-you-can-eat cake and dessert restaurant. While they do offer some main dishes, no one comes here for anything but the sweets! After you pay, you can eat as much as you want for 90 minutes.
spots.addr: 392 Komeya-cho, Nakagyo-ku (Koto Cross Hankyu Kawaramachi, 6th Floor)

spots.name: Gion TAC
spots.desc: Not the cheapest, but really great Italian food in a very hospitable environment, with friendly staff, nice music and great dessert.

spots.name: Kikunoi (main restaurant)
spots.desc: One of Japan's most famous ryotei, serving kaiseki using the finest regional seasonal ingredients. Very expensive for dinner, but lunches are much more reasonable. Bookings essential well in advance. Staff don't speak much English, but the restaurant does publish English books with descriptions of some of their dishes.

spots.name: Utamikumari Shrine
spots.desc: The shrine's main hall, built in the Kamakura Period, is a designated National Treasure.

spots.name: Uda Matsuyama Castle
spots.desc: It was built by the local lord, Akiyama, and was called Akiyama Castle.The castle was demolished in 1615 as part of the "One Castle per Province" policy. The castle was added to the "Continued Top 100 Castles" list in 2017.

spots.name: Muro Art Forest
spots.local: 室生山上公園芸術の森
spots.desc: An open-air art museum of sculptures surrounded by mountain forests.

spots.name: Tempozan Harbor Village
spots.local: 天保山ハーバービレッジ
spots.desc: Plaza and shopping centre, which houses an aquarium, Ferris wheel, an art gallery, Legoland and a cruise terminal. On the weekend, musicians and street performers offer additional entertainment to people outside the aquarium.

spots.name: Naniwa Kuishinbo Yokocho
spots.local: なにわ食いしんぼ横丁
spots.desc: Food theme park (or food court, depending on who you ask), with an aesthetic and theme of nostalgia for the 1960s streets of Osaka. Various Osaka delicacies are available here, including Takoyaki, Okonomiyaki, Kushikatsu, and Ikayaki.

spots.name: Maishima Sludge Center and Maishima Incineration Plant
spots.desc: Without a doubt, the best sludge center you've ever seen. The incineration plant makes other waste facilities look like dumps. These two buildings were designed by eccentric Austrian architect Friedensreich Hundertwasser. They are fantastical works that have to be seen to be believed. There are display panels in the lobby of the sludge centre. Tours are available if you contact the facilities in…

spots.name: Maishima Pottery Village
spots.desc: Maishima Pottery Village opened in Osaka’s manmade island in 1998 for the education and promotion of naniwazuyaki, made from the vast amounts of unwanted marine clay which resulted from the construction of Kansai International Airport. The main building has studios with electric and momentum potter’s wheels, rooms for preparing clay and glazes, a gallery, a noborigama climbing kiln and an anagama…
spots.price: 1-day workshop for hand forming ¥500–3500. Additional charge for shipping your work. Booking required.

spots.name: Boat Race Suminoe
spots.desc: There's no "bettor" place to see one of Japan's unique gambling sports, hydroplane boat racing, than the race course that typically helps crown the sport's champion every December. If you're interested in placing a bet, you might want to do some research at the official multilingual site of the sport, as there is practically no English guidance available once you arrive.
spots.price: General admission ¥100, reserved seating for additional charge

spots.name: Takopa (Takoyaki Park)
spots.desc: Visitors can sample fare from six leading takoyaki shops that Osakans, famously particular about their takoyaki, unreservedly recommend.
spots.price: Admission free, Octopus dumpling ball available for sale at 6 stores

spots.name: Samegai-juku Museum
spots.desc: The Samegai-juku is one of the posts of the former Nakasendo Route that connected Kyoto to Edo. The Museum has a few exhibits and also serves as a small rest area at the center of the historic street. The stream in front of the museum is known for the Japanese Batrachium flowers (梅花藻 baikamo) that bloom in stream in July and August.

spots.name: Seiganji Temple
spots.desc: Seiganji is one of the Seven Lucky Gods of Omi Province temples, with Fukurokuju as its representative god. It's most known for its garden, constructed by the same man who designed Rakurakuen Garden in Hikone. It's a zen garden that uses rocks to represent mountains, islands, and bridges, with the river area being covered in vibrant green moss.

spots.name: Garden Museum
spots.local: ガーデンミュージアム比叡
spots.desc: The Garden Museum features spectacular views of Lake Biwa, garden flowers, art galleries, a cafe, large outdoor reproductions of famous works of French Impressionism, and a lily pond with arched bridge that aims to replicate the Japanese garden designed by Claude Monet in Giverny, France and featured in many of his late paintings. It also houses the grave of Saichō (Dengyō Daishi) the founder of…

spots.name: Enryaku-ji
spots.desc: The temples on Mt. Hiei are collectively known as Enryaku-ji, literally "Long Calendar Temple". The large complex is generally divided into three sections known as the Eastern Pagoda (東塔 Tōdō), the Western Pagoda (西塔 Saitō) and Yokawa (横川); neither of the pagodas actually exist any more, but the names live on. Most of the better-known temples are concentrated in the Eastern Pagoda area.

spots.name: Konpon Chudō
spots.desc: The central hall of the temple. It contains the Inextinguishable Dharma Light (不減の法灯), a fire that has been burning for 1200 years. There is always a monk assigned to tend the fire and chant sutras here.

spots.name: Bruno Petzold Monument
spots.desc: There is a station near the top of the Sakamoto Cable run called Motateyama. Walking a few hundred meters from this stop will bring you to a monument which has been erected to the memory of Bruno Petzold, a German Tendai Bishop and scholar who lived in Japan until his death in 1949.

spots.name: Kokuhoden Museum
spots.desc: As the head temple of Tendai Buddhism, a wide variety of artwork has been produced and acquired by Enryaku-ji Temple. This museum was built to showcase some of the many artifacts owned by the temple. The Buddhist statues are particularly interesting.

spots.name: Danjō-garan
spots.desc: It is a temple complex designed by Kukai on the western side of town. One notable temple in the complex is Miedo which holds Kobo Daishi's statues, it is considered Mount Koya's most elegant building due to it gentle sloping roof. In the complex's center is the Konpon Daitō (根本大塔) pagoda, which according to Shingon doctrine represents the central point of a mandala covering Mt. Koya and all of…
spots.price: Free for access to the temple ground, ¥500 for the Konpon Daito Pagoda or the Kondo Hall (¥1,000 for both)

spots.name: Reihokan Museum
spots.desc: Museum that houses many of Mount Koya's treasures. The museum is style after Byodoin in Uji.
spots.price: ¥1300, ¥1100 if you hold the Koyasan World Heritage Ticket or Kansai Thru Pass

spots.name: Daishi Kyokai
spots.desc: The administrative center of Shingon Buddhism. Various Buddhist activities are offered at the hall such as copy scriptures and meditation.

spots.name: Daimon
spots.desc: Large gate considered the main entrance to Mount Koya. Two statues in the gate guard the town.

spots.name: Nyonindo
spots.desc: Until 1872 women were forbidden from entering Mount Koya's main town. During that time a collection of temples outside the town center was the only place where women could worship. Only one of these temples remains; it is visited by many women.

spots.name: Tokugawa Mausoleum
spots.desc: Built by Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1643, this is one of numerous mausoleums in Japan dedicated to the Tokugawa Family. It took 20 years to complete and enshrines Tokugawa Iemitsu, the third Tokugawa Shogun.

spots.name: Gokusho Worship Hall
spots.desc: Worship hall where visitors can make offerings to various deities. Visitors are also encouraged to throw water at the statues, while praying to departed family members.

spots.name: Tōrōdō
spots.desc: Okunoin's main worship hall where over 10,000 lanterns are kept eternally lit. The hall also features 50,000 statues kept in the hall's basement.

spots.name: Kobo Daishi's Mausoleum
spots.desc: Mausoleum where Kobo Daishi, the founder of Shingon Buddhism was buried. Pilgrims come from all over Japan and many who finish the 88 Temple Pilgrimage visit the mausoleum after their pilgrimage to thank Kobo Daishi. Visitors may not enter the mausoleum but many visitors burn incense and chant sutras in front of the Mausoleum's entrance. When crossing Gobyo-bashi bridge, the final bridge before…

spots.name: Ochadokoro (Shotokuden)
spots.desc: On your way out, stop at this little pavilion for a cup of tea, which you can ladle out yourself from the large bronze cauldrons kept simmering in the back. The tea is free, but there is a conveniently placed donation box nearby.

spots.name: Bon-on-sha
spots.desc: On the left hand side of the main road as you walks from the centre of town to Okunoin cemetery, 150 m from the main traffic lights. This cafe and art gallery specialises in organic vegetarian lunches (price varies depending on contents of set. ¥800-1200). The menu changes daily, and a number of homemade cakes are available, as are coffees and teas (¥300). The couple who run the cafe are…

spots.name: Hanabishi
spots.desc: This classy restaurant has been serving customers for over 120 years and is a good option for sampling Buddhist vegetarian fare if you're not staying overnight. A shōjin ryōri lunch set runs ¥2100, while a full-on multi-course vegetarian kaiseki experience runs ¥5000-10,500 (cheaper at lunch). Some of the Bento sets are not vegetarian, so stick with shōjin ryōri for the "real thing".

spots.name: Hachiyo
spots.desc: The primary selling point of this all-round Japanese eatery is its perfect location right next to the Okunoin-mae bus stop and the start of the Okunoin trail, but the food is a cut above the average shokudo. Try the sansai soba noodles with mountain vegetables, made from fresh vegetables instead of the usual prepacked mix.

spots.name: Inoue
spots.desc: Near the Okunoin-mae bus stop. Boasts the largest Omu-Rice (omelette filled with rice and some meat) in Japan, ¥550. English menu available.

spots.name: Miyasan
spots.desc: Centrally located in the middle of Koyasan, just south of the main traffic lights, it has a menu of about 50 items ranging from ¥200-1000. The inn's banner states that its specialty is fried chicken, although all the items are of high quality. The Ramen is particularly filling. English Menu available.

spots.name: Historical Street
spots.desc: An area along Onogawa River in Sawara with merchant houses and tradesmen's houses from Edo and Meiji eras. It has been selected by the National Government as an important traditional building group preservation district and has been used as a backdrop for several TV shows.

spots.name: Western River Railroad
spots.desc: Tokyo Disneyland's railroad makes a sightseeing trip around Adventureland, Westernland, and Critter Country. It cannot be used to travel from one area of the park to another.

spots.name: The Castle
spots.desc: Cinderella Castle at the center of Disneyland is icon and dominating feature of the resort. This is a 51-meter-tall fairy tale castle. While the cynic will notice the stark plastic construction, the castle's fascination cannot be denied by anybody who grew up with Disney style comics.

spots.name: Gunma Museum of Art, Tatebayashi
spots.desc: The second prefectural museum of art in Gunma, collecting modern art of sculpture. The annex exhibits the studio of a French sculpture, François Pompon.Beautiful garden and a nice view of the building amuse visitors. There is a sculpture pathway (彫刻の小径) in the pine woods near the museum where about 40 sculptures are settled along the pathway.

spots.name: Tatebayashi Castle
spots.desc: located at Shiromachi 2 chome, Tatebayashi, founded in the 15th century by Akai clan. It's also called 'Obiki Castle' that means dragging tail castle which derives from the legend that a fox once saved by Akai Terumitsu, the founder of the castle, showed him where to build a castle by dragging its tail. After Tokugawa Ieyasu overthrew Hojo clan in the Kanto region, in 1590, Sakakibara Yasumasa…

spots.name: Morinji Temple
spots.desc: Morinji Templeis a temple of Soto sect, famous for the tale 'Bunbuku Chagama'. Visitors will be welcomed by many pottery statues of raccoon dogs. The Bunbuku Chagama is treasured at the temple.

spots.name: Tomioka Silk Mill
spots.desc: Japan's oldest modern silk mill, which was in operation between 1872 and 1987. It was designated a Historic Site in 2005, an Important Cultural Property in 2006, and both a National Treasure and a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014.

spots.name: Nukisaki Shrine
spots.desc: The Ichinomiya for Kōzuke Province (most of Gunma Prefecture). Much of the shrine is an Important Cultural Property.

spots.name: Gunma Safari Park
spots.desc: This is the type of zoo where you either drive through in your own car (in which case you must pay ¥500 for a guide radio, which is available in Japanese or English) or are driven around (¥500 for the safari bus, or ¥1300 for either the feed-the-animals bus or the off-road ranger tour in a four wheel drive). The most interesting animals are the white tigers and Japan's only Sumatran elephants…
spots.hours: 9:30-16:30 (last admission 15:30) November-February, 9:30-17:00 (last admission 16:00) March-October, closed Wednesdays

spots.name: Ushiku Daibutsu
spots.desc: At 120m tall, it is the tallest Buddha statue in the world. There is a viewpoint at 85 meters that looks out through the statue's chest - don't worry, this modern structure completed in 1993 has an elevator inside. There is a pond and a garden around the base of the statue.
spots.price: \800 to enter inside;\500 for the garden only

spots.name: Backside of Enoshima
spots.desc: The points located on the backside of Enoshima near the cave are a sight worth seeing. Tidal pools brim with crabs and trapped fish. The backside of Enoshima is the local fishing secret.

spots.name: Iwaya Caves
spots.desc: A system of two sea-eroded caves (152 m and 56 m deep) at the back of the island, considered a spiritual site and the birthplace of Enoshima Shrine. For centuries, they were a destination for religious pilgrimages. Inside, you can find stone statues and exhibits on local history and folklore. You get a candle to explore the darker sections. The second cave features a statue of a dragon god.

spots.name: Lovers Bell
spots.desc: Couples pledge their eternal love by ringing this bell and attaching a padlock. Offers a scenic view of Sagami Bay.

spots.name: Tobiccho
spots.desc: The main (本店 honten) of the 3 Tobiccho shopts, and one of the most popular seafood restaurants in the island. The meals are all fresh and good. It has a pretty view of the harbor.

spots.name: Shōnan Cafe
spots.desc: Has good food. You can eat a bowl of rice with avocado salad, fresh juice, Loko Moko, hot dog and so on. 'Enoshima Loko Moko' is a recommended dish of avocado, chicken & rice.

spots.name: Ōgiya
spots.desc: It is a Japanese style confectionery. This store is well-known for its confections made in the shape of the famous Enoden train in the area. Recommended are ohagi and monaka. Ohagi is a cake made of rice flour with lots of taste. Other items are made from soy bean flour, sweet bean paste, sesame etc. Monaka is a wafer cake filled with red or white bean jam that costs about ¥100.

spots.name: Tenzan Tōjigō
spots.desc: (天山湯治郷), Hakone-Yumoto, Chaya 208. Large, popular hot spring operation with indoor and outdoor baths, sauna, etc. Free shuttle bus from outside the bus station. Open 11:00-20:00 daily. ¥1000/630 adult/child.

spots.name: Hiking
spots.desc: The area has some nice hiking trails. The visitors' center in Togendai has a model of the area including many of the hikes around the Lake Ashi. For example there is a hike from Togendai to Owakudani and from there to Mt. Komagatake passing the peaks of Mt. Kanmurigatake and Mt. Kami. From Mt. Komagatake take the cable car down and the bus back to Togendai (beware: last cable car leaves Mt.…

spots.name: Black eggs
spots.desc: Boiled on site, their shells are a mottled black due to a chemical reaction with the sulphurous water, but the inside is quite tasty. According to Japanese legend, every one you eat will add seven years to your life. 5 eggs (and hence 35 years) will set you back just ¥500.

spots.name: Sagamiya
spots.desc: If you miss the taste of a warm brownie, try the mountain brownies at this shop. You can't miss the smell, as they are made on site! Also has a branch in Ginza, Tokyo.

spots.name: Nukafuku
spots.desc: Vegan and gluten-free bakery inside the souvenir shop, selling rice bran sweets, including doughnuts.

spots.name: Tamura Ginkatsu-Tei
spots.desc: Restaurant specialising in tofu katsuni, a dish containing tofu and pork, however they are able to make a vegetarian version on request. The restaurant is very popular and operates a ticket system, so it is recommended to arrive early.

spots.name: PUBSTOP Pizza & Bar
spots.desc: Small bar serving draught beers from the Gora Brewery, and pizzas including vegetarian and vegan options. Accepts card payments.

spots.name: Yashio Ekimae Park
spots.desc: A spacious park with a children's playground. A popular spot for picnics, dog walks and a place for young people to hang out.

spots.name: Nakagawa Yashio Flower Park
spots.desc: This park has over a hundred peach trees which bloom turn a vivid pink during springtime.

spots.name: Frespo Yashio
spots.desc: A 3-storey suburban shopping mall. Lacks the overwhelming crowds that you would find in the similar kinds of malls in downtown Tokyo.

spots.name: Uramigataki hot spring and waterfall
spots.desc: This is a free open air hot spring (onsen). The hot spring is mixed and you enter with swimming suit. After enjoying the hot water, take a short walk through lush forest to the nearby waterfall. If you feel a little adventurous, on the way to the waterfall, rock scramble the steep short path that will lead you to a small Shinto shrine.

spots.name: Sea Dive
spots.desc: Is a good outfit, with a friendly staff, recommended by the guys at the Anchor pub. Little English is spoken, but they seem pretty acquainted dealing with foreign tourists.

spots.name: Sokodo beach
spots.desc: A very popular beach for snorkeling with the local sea turtles. The beach is sheltered and has shallow reefs of beautiful hard coral and colourful subtropical fish.

spots.name: Nazumado
spots.desc: This is the most popular dive spot. Entry is a little slippery and ropes are provided to help. The site features rich marine life and a scenic swim through.

spots.name: Habuminato
spots.desc: A harbor that was carved out in the 1700s by a great tsunami. Inside is a traditional Japanese fishing village that never quite managed to catch up to modern times. You can watch fishermen dragging in their latest catch here. You can also sample some of the finest sushi in the world at the sushi restaurant Nishikawa. There are several overlooks that provide stunning panoramic views of the harbor…

spots.name: Mt. Mihara
spots.desc: An active volcano that last erupted in 1986. Surrounded by a vast desert of lava, one can travel up to the rim and peer down into the brightly colored several-hundred meter drop. It is best to go on a clear day, as clouds can obscure your vision tremendously and make getting lost quite easy.

spots.name: Izu-Ōshima Museum of Volcanoes
spots.desc: Established in 1990, after the 1986 eruption of Mt. Mihara. The first floor of this large museum features the complete history of the last eruption and provides just enough English explanation to be able to follow the main thread. The second floor is reserved for more general information about volcanoes with less English explanation, but many photographs from volcanoes worldwide.
spots.price: Entrance ¥500, half hour film about the last eruption ¥200

spots.name: 大島一周道
spots.desc: Exposed stratum layers are visible along the inner side of the loop road between the villages of Nomashi and Mabushi on the west side of the island. Discovered by road construction crews in the 1950s, over 90 layers of stratum are visible. The island's geological history is made obvious when one looks upon the layers of ash, interspersed by fault lines.

spots.name: Oshima Park
spots.desc: Famous for its world-record holding collection of camellia trees. The park has over one hundred different varieties, and is an excellent place to take a stroll or jog, especially from early February to late March when the camellia flowers are blooming.

spots.name: Oshima Zoo
spots.desc: Part of Oshima Park. Be sure to bring some ashitaba (a flowering plant) to feed to the animals! The zoo is under construction, but approximately one-third of the exhibits are open.

spots.name: Kaminarimon
spots.desc: Up first, it features a much-photographed giant lantern and statues of guardian gods Raijin (god of thunder) and Fūjin (god of wind). First built in 942, the gate has been destroyed numerous times and the current incarnation dates to 1960. The Nakamise shopping arcade leading up to the temple starts after the gate (see Buy).

spots.name: Hōzōmon
spots.desc: At the end of the arcade, it is the main gate, notable for a giant straw sandal (waraji) hung up on one side. This gate too is guarded by ferocious guardian gods. Rebuilt 1964.

spots.name: Kannondō
spots.desc: Behind the gate, the main hall of the temple is perennially busy with a steady stream of worshippers wafting incense over themselves and trooping up the steps to pray and donate. According to legend, the hall was first built in 628 to house a statue of Kannon, the Goddess of Mercy, fished out of the Sumida River by two brothers. Rebuilt 1951–58.

spots.name: Gojūnotō
spots.desc: It reputedly contains some of the ashes of the Buddha. Rebuilt 1973.

spots.name: Asakusa Jinja
spots.desc: To the east behind the temple is this Shinto shrine devoted to protecting the Buddhist temple in a typically Japanese arrangement. The fairly plain shrine is not much to look at, but is notable as the focal point of the Sanja Matsuri festival (see Do).

spots.name: Chingodō Shrine
spots.desc: If you turn left before the Hōzōmon gate and head west for a few hundred meters, this quiet shrine is on your left. The shrine is dedicated to the Japanese raccoon god tanuki, notably primarily for its big flask of sake and gigantic testicles (at least when depicted as a statue).

spots.name: Dembō-in Temple
spots.desc: This temple next to Sensō-ji, to which it belongs, has a spectacular Japanese garden. While generally closed to the public, it opens for exhibitions most years from roughly mid-March to early May. Other than the small garden, which is best in the cherry blossom (sakura) season, the exhibition also features some of the temple's cultural treasures. The entrance is close to the five-story pagoda…

spots.name: Sanja Matsuri
spots.desc: Organized at Asakusa Jinja yearly on the third weekend in May, this is Tokyo's largest festival (matsuri) and attracts up to 2 million spectators. The main event is a procession known as Daigyōretsu, when traditional performers and musicians parade through the streets, while on the next two days portable shrines (mikoshi) are carried to and from the temple for purification.

spots.name: Asakusa Samba Carnival
spots.desc: Held on the last Saturday of August. The street parade, which features thousands of participants from all over Japan, is held in the afternoon around Sensō-ji, and there are some stage shows in the evening. The event started in 1981, it's the biggest party of the year for the many Japanese-Brazilian residents of Tokyo.

spots.name: Nakamise
spots.desc: This busy covered shopping arcade leads from the Kaminarimon gate to the temple, selling all sorts of Buddhist paraphernalia as well as assorted tourist kitsch. This is one of the best places in Tokyo to buy souvenirs (the other being the Oriental Bazaar in Omotesando), but more expensive items such as swords and kimono are likely to be of inferior quality. Slightly nicer crafts, rather than…

spots.name: Kagetsudo
spots.desc: This place has been making "melon pan" since 1945, and they haven't changed the decoration. It is a buttery and milky small cake with a crispy sweet crust.

spots.name: Naruto Taiyaki
spots.desc: Freshly grilled taiyaki, a traditional sweet waffle in the shape of a lucky fish, with your choice of red bean, sweet potato or custard filling.

spots.name: Nishiyama Sweets
spots.desc: After an exhausting day visiting the temples, grab some hot steamed dumplings outside, or step inside for traditional desserts such as oshiruko (grilled rice cake in a sweet-bean porridge) or cream an-mitsu (gelatin cubes in molasses with candied fruit and ice cream). This very simple shop serving tea and sweets has been in business since 1852.

spots.name: Sansada
spots.desc: Over 150 years of history. Try their tempura and soba set! Or the fresh deep fried flour/batter at the front of the restaurant. You can smell them from a mile away, because they use sesame oil.

spots.name: Aoi-Marushin
spots.desc: Good tempura in a convenient location, with fifty years of history behind it.

spots.name: Benizuru
spots.desc: Ludicrously fluffy pancakes served in wobbly stacks of three, with a selection of sweet and savoury toppings. Extremely popular among the Instagram crowd, the only way to get a guaranteed seat is to queue up in person before 8:30am and pay a ¥1000/person deposit. No English sign, but English menu available.

spots.name: Daikokuya
spots.desc: One of Tokyo's most famous tempura restaurants, opened in 1887. Be prepared for extremely long queues during meal times. An English menu is available on request.

spots.name: Komagata Dozeu
spots.desc: Another local institution, Komagata has been serving up loach hotpot (dojō nabe) for over 200 years. Small, bony and slimy, loach was the working man's alternative to eel, then as now an expensive luxury. It's a bit of an acquired taste -- "tofu with bones" is a common description -- but it's very Asakusa and you can ladle on green onion and shichimi spice to add some flavor. Tatami seating…

spots.name: Torijin
spots.desc: Lurking in the dingy/atmospheric "mole alley" under Tobu Asakusa station, this friendly joint serves up yakitori grilled chicken skewers and, incongruously, a limited menu of Italian favorites. Try the tsukimi tsukune, a giant chicken meatball served with a raw egg for dipping.

spots.name: Tonkatsu Tōyama
spots.desc: Classic tonkatsu pork cutlets deep-fried to perfection, with your choice of fatty rōsu or leaner hire. Limited but extremely popular lunch menu (expect to queue for up to an hour), dinner menu has more options like katsu curry and katsudon.

spots.name: Amitatsu
spots.desc: One of the longer-running operators, with set meals of sashimi and tempura and daily departures sailing a loop from Asakusa to Odaiba and back.

spots.name: Sushi Isshin
spots.desc: This tiny 8-seater restaurant has had a Michelin star for 13 years running thanks to its uncompromisingly old-school Edo-style sushi, prepared with seasonal seafood and akasu red vinegar made from sake lees. Reserve well in advance.

spots.name: Kamiya Bar
spots.desc: The home of the Denki Bran cocktail, this was Japan's first Western-style bar when it first opened in 1880 and remains a truly local institution. The ground floor is a large beer-hall-like bar, the second is a Western-style restaurant, and the upper floor serves Japanese food. Find a seat at one of the shared tables, buy your tickets at the counter, and join in the fun. Beware the oddly limited…

spots.name: Asakusa Naniwaya
spots.desc: Asakusa Naniwaya branch the original of Taiyaki Naniwaya Sohonten (Azabu Jyu-ban). You can enjoy green tea and coffee at the cafe in the shop, with all handmade Japanese sweets.

spots.name: Sumitomo Collection
spots.local: 泉屋博古館, Sen-oku Hakuko kan
spots.desc: Since the 19th century, the Sumitomo family has collected art objects, such as bronzes, ustensils and paintings, mostly from Japan and China.
spots.price: ¥520, ¥310 for students, free for children under 15

spots.name: Tokyo city model
spots.desc: A photo-realistic model of downtown Tokyo, with every real-life building photographed and its photo glued onto its 1:1000 scale model. Can be seen by appointment.

spots.name: Fujisoba
spots.desc: Small buckwheat noodle place. Healthy and popular with budget-conscious office workers.

spots.name: TETSU
spots.desc: Dip cold noodles into tasty thick hot soup, this is tsukemen! Free soup refill. If your soup gets cold, ask for the spectacular soup heating iron.

spots.name: Bangkok
spots.desc: A lunchtime legend. Pad thai special on Thursdays (¥980) is divine.

spots.name: yelo
spots.desc: Not really hungry? Go for shaved ice with toppings like you've never seen before. Try the tiramisu, watermelon or organic carrot mascarpone.

spots.name: Atelier de Joel Robuchon
spots.desc: The first overseas venture of the eponymous Paris-based Michelin-starred chef. Each dish is a work of art almost as breathtaking as the price tag, as courses cost ¥2900–12,800 — still a steal by Tokyo gourmet standards. Reservations by telephone only.

spots.name: Fukuzushi
spots.desc: Sushi place. Set menus are available, and their ¥3000 lunch set is excellent. Dress code: No sleeveless for men.

spots.name: Roku Roku
spots.desc: This complex of six restaurants on the sixth floor is a good choice if price is not an issue. You can choose between sushi, steak, Japanese and Chinese, and will be looking at upwards of ¥5000 per head on the bill.

spots.name: Sushi Saito
spots.desc: Described as somewhat of a hidden gem, this three Michelin star restaurant run by renowned "sushi maestro" Takashi Saito. With just eight seats, reservations should be made early.

spots.name: Bar Quest Roppongi
spots.desc: Serves a selection of Aussie lagers including VB, Crown Lager and Coopers, cocktails and meat pies. A big-screen TV and a wide range of music played by DJs provide ongoing entertain­ment. You can also kick back Australian-style along the U-shaped bar.

spots.name: Motown
spots.desc: Up a flight of stairs to the left of TGI Friday's. No cover except for special events, drinks are reasonable and the staff is English friendly. Popular among expats for its smaller size and music selection, you can often find groups or solo western businessmen (and women) on expense accounts into the wee hours of the morning. Does get crowded at times, so go early if you actually want enough…

spots.name: Odeon Club
spots.desc: Mix of hip-hop and techno. one of the most popular after hours nightclubs open from 22:00 until 12:00 the next day

spots.name: Ameyoko
spots.desc: A packed shopping bazaar full of stalls selling almost anything you can imagine. It runs roughly south of Ueno station along the inside of the JR Yamanote line tracks to Okachimachi station. If you are looking for a more typically "Asian" market street in Tokyo, with bargaining expected and friendly vendors trying to out-shout each other, this is it. Definitely a good place for souvenirs for…

spots.name: Okina An
spots.desc: One of the most authentic soba places in Tokyo. The owner keeps the place clean but has not renovated anything since the Showa era. Note the cash register from the 1960s and the museum-worth tea hearth. Try negiseiro, which is buckwheat noodles with tempura-style soup. Put the onions and some wasabi in your soup, then put a bit of soba into your soup and slurp it. When you're done, pour the…

spots.name: Yayoiken
spots.desc: Cheap and cheerful grills served on a hot teppan iron plate, with all the rice you can eat. Plastic food models plus a coupon machine with pictures make ordering easy.
spots.price: Morning sets from ¥350, full meals from ¥580

spots.name: Juraku
spots.desc: An affordable restaurant popular for families. Serves omelettes, hamburg steaks among other Western and some Japanese dishes. No credit cards accepted.

spots.name: Ueno Seiyōken
spots.desc: Opened in 1877, this was one of the first Western restaurants in Japan, serving French cuisine befitting its stature.

spots.name: Tōrindō
spots.desc: A little off the beaten track but just a short walk from the Tokyo National Museum, this traditional shop serves tea ceremony tea (¥450) without the ritualized fuss and delectable Japanese desserts (from ¥150) to go with them.

spots.name: Tasuichi (plus one)
spots.desc: Down the street from the 0101(Marui) department store is an extremely small but very friendly stand-up bar. They serve good food, have cheap drinks, speak some English, and are very friendly to foreigners. A great place to go if you are traveling by yourself, know some very basic Japanese and want to make friends with a local or two, but this is not a club. The surrounding area is filled with…

spots.name: The Warrior Celt
spots.desc: Known locally as the hangout for a few good beers in a typical Irish pub atmosphere. Expat crowd as well as Japanese drinkers. Say you found the place off Wikivoyage for a little something special.

spots.name: Yametsuhime Shrine
spots.desc: The shrine was built in the mountains where the mountain goddess Yame Tsuhime is said to reside according to the Nihon Shoki. The city is named after her. It is said to have existed here for 1300 years.

spots.name: Yame-Fukushima Historic District
spots.desc: A historic preservation district of white-walled storehouses from the Edo, Meiji, and Taisho periods.

spots.name: Bike rental
spots.desc: Rent a scooter or motorbike and just cruise around the island to admire it's beautiful nature and discover tiny beaches where you can hop off and go for a swim. The best way to travel on the island.

spots.name: Jidoriya
spots.desc: This place is ideal if you have to wait for the ferry or if you have a big appetite coming from the ferry. You get great value for your money with a starter (e.g. sashimi), your own little stone grill with chicken, salad, boiled beef, rice, and a dessert. Friendly, local atmosphere.

spots.name: Westerners Café
spots.desc: This little café by the road is owned by two retired people from Kobe who are mad about cowboys. It is filled with pictures, paintings and ephemera of the Wild West. The owner, dressed as a cowboy, will gladly receive you. They serve two types of freshly ground coffee and Indian tea. Relaxed atmosphere.

spots.name: Joyama Park
spots.desc: It is a park made using the old castle site, and you can see a panoramic view of the city when you go up.

spots.name: Eguchihama Seaside Park
spots.desc: Located in Higashi-Ichikicho, this beach park faces the East China Sea. It opens as a beach in the summer and is also the venue for marine sports activities such as surfing.

spots.name: Tokushige Shrine
