spots.desc: A golden statue of a woman named Tatsuko jutting out of Lake Tazawa. According to legend, Tatsuko was a woman who lived in Innai (present-day Yuzawa). After praying for 100 days and 100 nights that she would stay beautiful forever, the goddess Kannon came to her and told her "Eternal beauty comes from drinking from the northern lake, but it cannot be granted to humans" and urged her to think hard…

spots.name: Mount Katamae Forest Park
spots.desc: A nature park with trails featuring edible plants. There is also a viewpoint where you can look out over Lake Tazawa.

spots.name: Cycling around the Lake Tazawa (Lake Tazawa Renta Cycle, in Kyōei Palace)
spots.local: 田沢湖周回サイクリング (田沢湖レンタサイクル, 共栄パレス内)
spots.desc: Loop around lakeside the Lake Tazawa. Up and down the not very flat road. Approximately 20 km around, takes 2 - 3 hr.
spots.addr: 148, Haruyama, Tazawa, Tazawako 田沢湖田沢字春山148

spots.name: Tazawako Beer
spots.desc: It is a local beer. The brewery has a restaurant offering French and Italian cuisine.
spots.addr: Waseda, Sotsuda, Tazawako, 田沢湖卒田字早稲田

spots.name: Seiyoken
spots.desc: This ramen shop serves many kids of ramen. It also has some rice dishes. The staff are friendly, and will chat if you like.

spots.name: Blue Pond
spots.desc: This is the most popular pond in the "12 Lakes" (十二湖 Jūniko) area of the city on the edge of the Shirakami-Sanchi. As the name suggests, it's known for its vibrant blue color. In the autumn, people say that the yellow leaves that fall on the lake look like gold-leaf on blue porcelain.

spots.name: Furofushi Onsen
spots.local: 不老ふ死温泉 Furōfushi Onsen
spots.desc: The daytripper fee gives you access to three different onsen, however, they have different hours of operation, so pay attention to their hours. The Kogane no Yu (黄金の湯) open from 09:00-17:00 located in the Honkan features 2 indoor baths of different temperatures. There are large glass panels with views of the sea. The Furofushi no Yu (不老ふ死の湯) located in the Shinkan has the most facilities, with a…

spots.name: Itayanagi Chapel
spots.desc: Christian chapel, with a cafe and Christianity-related bookstore.

spots.name: Bodaiji Temple
spots.desc: Bodaiji Temple (菩提寺, also referred to as Entsuji), run by the Soto Zen sect, is built around a number of volcanic cauldrons (Jp. jigoku, literally "hells"), bubbling in all sorts of unnatural shades from canary yellow to blood red. There are also many, many offerings to the souls of the dead scattered around the area, including tiny Jizo statues wearing bibs and piles of pebbles built (or so they…

spots.name: Gankake
spots.desc: A large boulder overlooking the sea that is known for its view from the top. It is also a popular swimming spot and has changing room facilities available. It can be found on the way to Hotokegaura.

spots.name: Christ's tomb
spots.desc: according to legend, the final resting place of Jesus Christ. This legend is engraved on a large stone plaque at the burial site. The story states that during Jesus' young life, that period of time where not much is written about him in the Bible, Jesus was living in Japan and learning Shinto philosophies that he mixed in with Judaism. Then, when Jesus was going to be crucified, his identical…

spots.name: Tsuru-no-mai Bridge
spots.desc: This "dance of cranes" bridge is a feature of the park, which locals are fond of pointing out as Japan's longest all-wooden bridge. The bridge is not particularly old, but its natural structure and the lake and Mount Iwaki in the background make it a good spot for photos. It was built using locally produced timber and traditional building techniques.

spots.name: Crane Nature Park
spots.desc: Wild cranes were said to have existed here during the Edo Period, but decreased until Japan had no more of its signature bird over time. The cranes raised here were donated from China and Russia. In spring it is possible to see young hachlings.

spots.name: Tsurunosato Furusatokan (former Kawamura residence)
spots.local: 鶴の里ふるさと館（旧川村家）
spots.desc: Near the lake is a very old traditional Japanese-style house, which has been well-preserved and worth a look. There is also a large play area nearby with an enormous, dangerous-looking slide, and a large globe with many flags around it in tribute to Tsuruta's efforts towards internationalization.

spots.name: Onsen
spots.desc: A man-made onsen is connected with the park. If you go, be sure not to forget to use a pair of indoor slippers, which can be found to the left of the main entrance. Hand soap is provided, but a full onsen kit is recommended. Overall, there is nothing really special about this onsen, but it's a nice enough place.

spots.name: Tsugaru Dialect Competition
spots.desc: Every year in June or July a competition is held at the town hall in which foreigners create skits in the local dialect. NHK (a national news network) has covered the competition.

spots.name: Arujya
spots.local: 道の駅つるた 鶴の里あるじゃ
spots.desc: You would be missing out if you did not stop by at Arujya, the roadside station (michi no eki) for Tsuruta, which is not only fascinating because the restroom building is designed (like most things in the town) in the shape of cranes, but is also where you can taste some wonderful Steuben grape whipped ice-cream. It is delicious! Also to be found are lots of fresh vegetables and great food…

spots.name: Tamamatsu-dai
spots.desc: A small park with a monument to villagers who went off to war, and also to a pine tree, Tamamatsu. To find Tamamatsu, stand among the monuments and look up at the trees (away from the sea), you look for pine with branches that form a circle shape. This tree was supposedly a landmark to those in centuries past traveling from Hokkaido by boat. The park itself is not particularly well maintained…

spots.name: Summer Craft School
spots.desc: This small arts and crafts fair takes place in a quaint old school building by the sea, now the village Culture and Folklore Museum (文化伝承館). In addition to the dusty artifacts piled in the hallway, for one weekend in August the wooden gym is filled with cute handmade treasures, antiques, and traditional crafts. Coffee and lunch are available, and hands-on workshops are held throughout the weekend.

spots.name: Yomogi Hot Spring
spots.desc: Hot spring bath. After your soak, stop by the cute country ice cream stand among the vegetable gardens across the street.

spots.name: Hiking
spots.desc: Most of the village land is mountains. Hike to Kurotaki waterfall or climb Okura-dake. Be aware that there have been alleged bear sightings, and there are definitely monkeys.

spots.name: Tamamatsu Beach
spots.desc: Picnic, barbecue, or wade in the waves. There's a festival here in August with events for kids, performances, and grilled scallop samples. Be smart about swimming; this beach has a history of drownings.

spots.name: Marche
spots.desc: In the summer, you can buy the touted local tomatoes at this produce market by the sea. They also sell Yomogita's gourmet ketchup, yomogi (mugwort) tea, rice, and other local produce. There's also a cafeteria serving ramen, ice cream, and picnic food for beachgoers.

spots.name: Tamamatsu Shokudo
spots.desc: Katsudon, teishoku, and other hearty lunches for locals and travelers alike.

spots.name: Yomotto
spots.desc: A roadside station (michi no eki) selling local produce (including tomatoes) and edible souvenirs from around the prefecture. They also serve ramen - the signature Yomotto ramen has scallops and sea urchin in it.

spots.name: Mori Kashiten
spots.desc: The village's main sweet treat: Mori's fry balls. Deep fried dough rolled in sugar, filled with sweet bean paste. Take some for the road.

spots.name: Noguchi Hideyo Memorial Museum
spots.desc: A bacteriologist who is credited with discovering the agent that causes syphillis and doing research that led to the creation of a yellow fever vaccine. His childhood home, where he suffered burns that led him to pursue a medical career, is located on-site. Along with learning about Noguchi, the museum also features exhibits to educate people about bacteriology.

spots.name: Kokeshi Vending Machine
spots.desc: Known as the "world's only kokeshi vending machine", you can buy Nakanosawa Kokeshi from 2 local artisans at any time of day.
spots.addr: In front of Konishi Shokudo Restaurant

spots.name: 89 Diner
spots.desc: A traincar that has been converted into a restaurant. They have steak, sandwiches, and pasta as main dishes. Their crepes are also popular.
spots.hours: Weekdays from 11:00, Weekends from 09:00 - Closing time is when they sell out. Closed We-Thu

spots.name: Hayama Shrine
spots.desc: The town's main Shinto shrine, also known as Number 33, the thirty-third shrine in a pilgrimage route that goes across Japan.

spots.name: TEPCO Decomissioning Archive Center
spots.desc: The 2011 Fukushima nuclear power plant disaster happened just north of Tomioka. The plant and surroundings are unsurprisingly off-limits to visitors, but the plant operator maintains a documentation center in town where you can learn about the plant, disaster and the aftermath.

spots.name: Chūson-ji Temple
spots.desc: Hiraizumi's largest and most famous temple, renowned particularly for its Golden Hall (金色堂 Konjikidō) — which, unlike Kyoto's Golden Pavilion, is housed inside a large glass case. True to the name, the shrine inside is elaborately decorated with golden lacquer and mother-of-pearl, with three Buddha images.

spots.name: Mōtsu-ji Temple
spots.desc: The second of Hiraizumi's two large temples, known for its Heian-era Pure Land Garden (浄土園 Jōdo-en) dating to 800 AD. The garden seems downright un-Japanese in its liberal use of wide, grassy spaces — but most of the open spaces have scattered rocks and are marked with small posts in the middle, indicating the locations of destroyed temple buildings.

spots.name: Takkoku no Iwaya Bishamon-dō
spots.desc: A nice cave temple. It is the 5th incarnation of the temple since it was established in 801. It is dedicated to Bishamon the god of war, but was called Iwaya Bishamondo — a place to pray for peace. Also at this site is the Ganmen Daibutsu a giant stone carving of Buddha, but only the head remains after an earthquake destroyed the body. The ride to the temple is enjoyable in itself with nice…

spots.name: Kanjizaiō-in Ato
spots.desc: Built by Fujiwara Motohira's wife, it was originally a large garden. A fire destroyed it in the 16th century but many of the structures were rebuilt. Today, it's more of a park, although there are still some preserved elements that remind you it was once a garden.

spots.name: Muryōkō-in Ato
spots.desc: This used to be a temple, but all that remains is the temple's pond.

spots.name: Yanaginogosho Iseki
spots.desc: This is the site of the former palace. Although no structures remain, the pond and foundations still give visitors an idea of how grand the palace once was. Excavations are still being done.

spots.name: Yanaginogosho Museum
spots.desc: Yanaginogosho Iseki is often closed to the public, so the museum provides a way for visitors to learn about Hiraizumi's history and the former palace.

spots.name: Ryoei Sushi
spots.desc: Ryoei Sushi is the type of place you might just walk out of if you'd wandered in. There are several disconnected video game tables from the 1980s, and the owner is an old woman who moves very slowly and at first glance appears to be not particularly interested in having guests, at least at lunch time. There is no menu, just a bunch of sets listed on the wall. Three nigiri (sushi roll) sets, and…

spots.name: Kanzan-tei
spots.desc: A restaurant in the grounds of Chusonji Temple serving soba, udon, pizza, and desserts.

spots.name: Ryusendo Cave
spots.desc: A Japanese national monument and one of three largest caves in Japan.
spots.addr: 岩手県下閉伊郡岩泉町岩泉字神成1番地1

spots.name: Kanran-tei Pavilion
spots.desc: It was built in Kyoto by famed Shogun Toyotomi Hideyoshi. It was moved to Matsushima by Date Tadamune in 1645 and is the largest Momoyama-style tea house in Japan. An excellent place to stop for a ¥200 cup of tea (traditional Japanese sweets included) and a view of the Matsushima coastline.

spots.name: The Museum Matsushima
spots.desc: The museum contains three separate collections; the Orgel Collection of music players, the Segawa Collection of fashion from 1870-1960, and the Kitahara Toy Collection, featuring a variety of old, nostalgic toys.

spots.name: Godaido Hall
spots.desc: A picturesque building built on its own peninsula overlooking the bay, it is a well-known symbol of the city. It was founded 807 and the current structure dates back to 1604.

spots.name: Yajiro Kokeshi Village
spots.desc: The primary place to purchase Yajiro Kokeshi, they also have a small exhibit about the local kokeshi. Artisans also work here, and they also offer kokeshi-painting opportunities.

spots.name: Cat Shrine
spots.desc: It is a steep hike uphill from the port, past the last few houses (and an abandoned school) and then a short distance into the forest. The path is not well marked (unless you read Japanese). It has a small gate and shrine covered in offerings and cat figurines.

spots.name: Miyagi Zao Kokeshi Museum
spots.desc: Features over 5500 kokeshi (simple wooden dolls with no arms or legs), making it the largest kokeshi museum in Japan. It features the local Togatta Kokeshi along with all other varieties. Artisans also work here, so it's possible to watch them make kokeshi when they are present.

spots.name: Okama Crater
spots.desc: Named Okama after local cooking pots, it's known for its striking blue-green caldera lake.

spots.name: Sato Ryuhei Kokeshi Shop

spots.name: Mokume

spots.name: Towadako Ferries
spots.desc: You can take a boat tour from Yasumiya (休屋) around Lake Towada (45 minutes) or to Nenokuchi (50 minutes). Both cruises have a recorded guide (in Japanese) and show the beautiful rugged coast around the lake. Between late April and late November only.

spots.name: Lake Towada
spots.desc: Lake Towada, or Towada-ko, is Honshu's largest volcanic caldera lake and also the country's third deepest lake. The area nearby is dotted with dense forests and waterfalls, and is the top tourist draw in all Tohoku.

spots.name: Oirase River
spots.desc: The upper reaches, known as literally as the Oirase Stream (奥入瀬渓流 Oirase-keiryu) or as the Oirase Gorge, are famously scenic, featuring constant-flowing water since this is the drain of Lake Towada, and numerous waterfalls.

spots.name: Lake Towada Winter Stories Festival
spots.desc: This annual February festival features fireworks every evening, light displays, snow sculptures, food stalls and hot wine. You can drink in an igloo bar where drinks are served in glasses made of ice. Many local inns and hotels offer shuttle service to and from the festival site.

spots.name: Towada Art Center

spots.name: Shinbashi Steam Locomotive Square
spots.desc: Historic steam locomotive displayed in the middle of the square. A popular meeting point. During the year end holiday season, the train is lit up with colorful lights with light and sound shows throughout the day.

spots.name: Jin Homura Art Museum
spots.desc: The modern art of Jin Homura's works featured in a traditional farmhouse is an interesting combination of old and new that enhances the art, as well as bringing new intrigue to the houses and architecture themselves. It has a completely different atmosphere from the various preserved farmhouses scattered about that merely contain artifacts.

spots.name: Gassho-zukuri Minkaen
spots.desc: A collection of historic farmhouses moved here from other areas of the village in order to preserve them. Some of them date back to the 18th century. The buildings contain artifacts and objects used by the past residents as well as information about the history of the buildings and surrounding area.

spots.name: Kanda House
spots.desc: A well-preserved farmhouse that always has its fire lit. The second floor has similar artifacts as others in the village. Many visitors enjoy the traditional cat carrier. The third floor offers a good look at the inner construction of the house along with nice views of the rest of the town from the windows.

spots.name: Wada House
spots.desc: This is the largest of the farmhouses in Ogimachi. It contains some artifacts used during its heyday. For those fans of ‘Higurashi no Naku Koro ni’ the Wada residence is Shion and Mion’s home

spots.name: Nagase House
spots.desc: The house is well-known for its 11-meter length which comes from single trees used as horizontal beams inside the house. The house dates back 250 years when the Nagase family worked as doctors. The artifacts inside include medical objects, and things used in daily life.

spots.name: Shirakawa-go no Yu
spots.desc: A convenient hot spring for day visitors located right in the historic area. It's especially popular in the winter to warm up after wandering around town in the cold. Hotel rooms also available.

spots.name: Shiramizu no Yu
spots.desc: A hot spring for day travelers. It's a large area with a variety of indoor and outdoor pools to soak in and relax.

spots.name: Shirakawa-go Light-Up
spots.local: 白川郷ライトアップ Shirakawa-gō raito-appu
spots.desc: The winter light-up event in Ogimachi is a popular event held in January and February where the town is lit up at night. The pictures of the town lit up at night from the Shiroyama Viewpoint is arguably the most iconic winter (snowy) view in the nation. The event used to be open to everyone (and was held on more nights), but it is extremely popular and neither the town nor the roads leading to it…

spots.name: Tonkatsu Fumiya
spots.desc: The restaurant specializes in pork cutlets. You can choose the quality of pork and different sauces.

spots.name: Soba Wakimoto
spots.desc: All of the soba noodles are made and served in the same day. They also have grade 4 and 5 Hida beef.

spots.name: Stargazing tours
spots.desc: Guided stargazing at the top of a snowy mountain. Make sure to bring warm clothing! Website only in Japanese.

spots.name: Kappabashi Bridge
spots.desc: The suspension bridge is the symbol of Kamikochi. If you're there early enough in the morning (between 17:00 and 06:30), you may see the local monkeys make their morning crossing from one side of the bridge to the other.

spots.name: Atera Valley
spots.desc: A 15-km scenic valley that is known for its emerald green waters.

spots.name: Nojiri-juku
spots.desc: A station along the Old Nakasendo Road, it was the second longest in the Kiso Valley after Narai-juku. Some buildings have been preserved but much of the old post town no longer exists. It is known today for the 7 hairpin curves in the road that were used as a defense against attacks.

spots.name: Joshoji
spots.desc: The oldest of Kiso's three holiest temples, the current temple dates back to 1600 after being moved here from the previous post town which was abandoned and moved after constant flooding. It has a nice zen garden and houses the "Josho Daruma" made of Kiso cypress.

spots.name: Suhara-juku
spots.desc: The 39th station of the Nakasendo Road, it is known for the "water boats", carved-out boat-shaped logs on the sides of the streets that hold water for the villagers to use.

spots.name: Kitchen Kuranbo
spots.desc: A restaurant with a variety of dishes such as pizza, omelettes, and Shinshu salmon.

spots.name: Awashimaura Village Museum
spots.desc: On display are ancient wooden fishing boats and fishing gear, Jomon pottery and stone tools that tell the history of the island.

spots.name: Hotokezaki Observatory
spots.desc: Observation deck with views of coastline, often called the best sunset spot on the island.

spots.name: Awashima Farm
spots.desc: Awashima used to have many horse stables but only one now remains.
spots.price: ¥200 per minute if staff are pulling your horse, ¥2000 for farm tour, ¥100 per minute for lessons and independent riding

spots.name: Awashimabaitenkumiai
spots.desc: Souvenir store with fishing gear, locally harvested seaweed and sweets.

spots.name: Shop Kinbei
spots.local: おみやげ きんべい
spots.desc: Shop with local seaweed, dried octopus and other souvenirs. The only store on the island's eastern side.

spots.name: Cafe Sosodo
spots.desc: Awashima's most fashionable cafe, serving cutlet, curry and croquette.

spots.name: Mikayoka
spots.desc: Serves the islands specialities of Wappani and Sashimi along with ramen

spots.name: Ryokan Memorial Hall
spots.desc: Built in 1965 to commemorate the 200th birthday of Buddhist monk Ryōkan. Various documents and personal items are on permanent display.

spots.name: Echigo Izumonsaki Tenryo-no-Sato Village
spots.desc: The main attraction is the History Hall, which contains representations of Tokugawa era life.

spots.name: Gogo-an
spots.desc: Ryōkan's hermitage for more than twenty years of his life and the place where many of his well known poems were composed.

spots.name: Shinjo-juku
spots.local: 出雲街道新庄宿 Izumokaido Shinjō-juku
spots.desc: Shinjo was one of the stops along the Izumo Pilgrimage Route (Izumo Kaido) that connected Himeji to Izumo where people would visit Izumo Shrine. The Shinjo-juku, also known as the Kishiro-tei (木代邸) is the former wakihonjin used during the Edo Period. Daimyo from Matsue once stayed here.

spots.name: Shinjo History and Folk Museum
spots.local: 新庄村歴史民俗資料館
spots.desc: The museum building is a historic site, built as a residence during the Edo Period. It houses objects and artifacts from the town with displays about its history. Because the town is small and does not get a lot of tourists, reservations (which can be made by phone) are necessary to enter.

spots.name: Gaisen Cherry Blossom Road
spots.desc: Shinjo is most known for its cherry blossoms, the Gaisen cherry blossoms that align its historic street. These are some of the latest-blooming cherry blossoms in the region blooming around mid-April. The cherry blossoms were planted here in 1905 after Japan's victory over Russia in the Russo-Japanese War, so they are aptly named gaisen-zakura, Triumphant Cherry Blossoms.

spots.name: Mount Kenashi
spots.desc: A mountain popular for hiking, nature, and pure water. It is known for its beech forest and Asian fawnlilies. From the summit, you can see Mount Daisen and the Hiruzen Highlands.

spots.name: Meruhen
spots.desc: Meruhen is known for its gyumochidon, with the famous local himemochi for ¥650. All of the typical donburi are also available.

spots.name: Aka'iwa Seigan-kyo
spots.desc: Aka'iwa Seigan-kyo (gorge of red boulders and greenery) is a magnificent gorge whose walls soar in a spectacular contrast of red and blue rocks, some of them immense and others oddly shaped.

spots.name: Tenkawa Grand Benzaiten Shrine
spots.desc: A Shinto shrine for arts and crafts. An annual festival is held on 16 through 17 July every year, where noh is performed on the stage.

spots.name: Dorogawa Eco Museum Center
spots.local: 洞川エコミュージアムセンター
spots.desc: Introduces the natural resources of this area. Admission is free. Opens 10AM to 5PM. Closed on Wednesdays and winter months (December through March). Located at 784-32, Dorogawa, Tenkawa.

spots.name: Gallery Honobono
spots.desc: A library offering materials of folkways of this area. Exhibits an engine for US B29 bombers. Located at 674-1, Dorogawa, Tenkawa.

spots.name: Mount Omine
spots.desc: A sacred mountain and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Climbing the mountain is famously forbidden to women, although the ban has no legal force.

spots.name: Sanjogatake Historical Museum
spots.desc: Offers Buddha statues made of gold. Admission fee: ¥300. Located at 492-1, Dorogawa, Tenkawa.

spots.name: Hirano Old City
spots.desc: A rare surviving example of a medieval moated city that was rebuilt in the early Edo period with a grid-patterned layout. While most of the moats were filled in during modern urban development, the district preserves its historical atmosphere through its orderly grid of streets lined with traditional Edo-period machiya and numerous historic temples and shrines.

spots.name: Kire Moated Settlement
spots.desc: Explore Osaka City's best-preserved moated settlement. This townscape retains the traditional form of a moated settlement dating back to the Middle Ages.

spots.name: Katana Museum
spots.desc: Small sword museum attached to Masumian, with displays and sword polishing demonstrations.

spots.name: Cotton City Museum
spots.desc: Museum in the kura of the registered Ebisui House, showing tools used in yarn production.

spots.name: Hirano-gō Summer Festival
spots.desc: The largest danjiri festival in Osaka, and among summer festivals it ranks second only to the Tenjin Festival in scale. Rooted in the Heian-period “Gion-e” tradition, which shares its origins with Kyoto’s Gion Festival, it attracts as many as 300,000 visitors from across Osaka to experience the raw energy of the danjiri floats and the sacred dignity of the mikoshi procession. Held July 11–14.

spots.name: Kozushima Hot Spring Center
spots.desc: Public bath. saunas, jacuzzis, indoor hot spring facilities, and a vast open-air bath. Swimsuits required for open-air bath only.

spots.name: Akazaki Shiokaze Wooden Trail
spots.desc: Wooden walking course reaches of the Akasaki coast on the north side of the island.

spots.name: Matsugashita Miyabiyu
spots.desc: This outdoor hot spring has two pools -- a shallow area with benches for soaking your feet, and a deeper area for your entire body. The water is yellowish, which can stain bathing suits and towels. There's a change room nearby, and bathing suits are required.

spots.name: Ashitsuki Onsen
spots.desc: This outdoor hot spring has fairly clear water, but water temperature varies with the tide. At times it can be only lukewarm, in which case Matsugashita Miyabiyu is a good alternative. There is a change room nearby, and bathing suits are required.

spots.name: Jinata Onsen
spots.desc: This outdoor hot spring is next to the ocean. Some areas of the hot spring are too hot, but if you move closer to the ocean, you can probably find a pool with reasonable temperature. This onsen is at the bottom of a gorge, and is rather isolated. At night, bring a flash light to see the stairs down the gorge. There is a change room at the top of the stairs, quite far from the onsen.

spots.name: Shikinejima Onsen Ikoi no Ie
spots.desc: The only indoor hot spring on Shikinejima. There are 2 large single-sex baths, showers, vending machines, and an area to relax.
spots.hours: 10:00-22:00, closed Mondays, closed on some holidays

spots.name: Wander
spots.desc: Rent a motorbike, a bicycle, or walk and explore the island. A mountain bike costs ¥1,000 per day, but some tops are only accessible walking. Just look around for shops which have bicycles in the front, or ask the owners of your ryokan. You can easily cycle around the entire island in less than a day.

spots.name: Tomari beach
spots.desc: The beaches are often quiet, as few people are on this island (except during "long" holidays, such as Golden or Silver Week). Tomari Beach is very popular with tourists in the summer months - here the water is clear and snorkeling is possible.

spots.name: Fish
spots.desc: Hire rods from local stores, and ask locals for advice on where to perch yourself.

spots.name: Kayak
spots.desc: Rent a kayak, for instance on Oura Beach, and explore the area.

spots.name: Kanbiki Mountain
spots.desc: Climb the 99 m for a spectacular view on the neighboring islands. Continue to the West to enjoy the thick forest.

spots.name: Restaurant Daishi
spots.desc: A restaurant with standard Japanese fare: ramen and rice dishes. Also serves coffee and beer.
spots.addr: 東京都新島村式根島２８２ー２

spots.name: Cook at Kamanoshita campsite
spots.desc: There are BBQ stoves at the Kamanoshita campsite, so why not cook the fish you caught?

spots.name: Yodobashi Camera
spots.desc: A famous Japanese department store selling computers, components, cameras, household appliances, and pretty much anything electronic.

spots.name: Yuzawaya
spots.desc: A handicraft shop adjacent to the station. There are two floors of crafting materials. The dedicated shopper may find interesting souvenirs on the fabric floor.

spots.name: Onao
spots.desc: A nice selection of traditional Japanese paper and related souvenirs. The website has some English info about papers and their shops.

spots.name: Baobab: World Kitchen Y Musica
spots.desc: Food and music from the Caribbean, South America, Africa, and Asia.

spots.name: Bubuka
spots.desc: The abura soba served at this ramen restaurant is a welcome break from the usual salty and soupy ramen. Actually ramen not soba, abura soba is served with no soup, but does include the usual green onion, slice of pork, etc. An interesting addition is raw egg (nama tamago). Look for the store with the line in front — it is a popular place.

spots.name: Kichijoji Satō
spots.desc: Famous for its ball-shaped deep-fried mincemeat cutlets (menchi katsu, ¥300 apiece) which you can get as take-out, and there's usually a long line of customers spilling out into the shopping arcade. Has a steakhouse upstairs.

spots.name: Harmonica Quina
spots.desc: In the Harmonica Alley, across from the Kichijoji Station, there is a little shop serving the uniquely Okinawan dish called taco rice. Taco meat and all the usual taco toppings, all over rice. Surprising and tasty!

spots.name: Bloomoon
spots.desc: This restaurant has an eclectic selection of Asian food and international interior decorations. The bizarre mixture of furniture from various countries and of assorted ages makes the mind boggle.

spots.name: Hachijuhachiya
spots.desc: This restaurant serves western-style vegetarian and vegan sandwiches and salads. Oddly, the atmosphere is more reminiscent of a coffee shop near a college than a restaurant. Lights dangle from long cords from the ceiling and hover just above the table surface.
spots.addr: 御殿山1-2-1 御殿山デュープレックスR'S 2階

spots.name: Iseya
spots.desc: This yakitori (grilled chicken) tavern is a Kichijoji institution, first opening in 1928. The interior scene could be straight out of a 1950s black-and-white movie, full of raucous salarymen drowning their troubles in tall glasses of beer. This is the smaller branch shop; the main shop, housed in a marvelous old wooden building from 1953 to 2006, reopened as the base of a modern apartment tower…

spots.name: Jiima
spots.desc: This restaurant is small — only room for 20. However, the meat and fish are quite good, and the young and energetic wait staff make for a worthwhile visit.

spots.name: La Befana
spots.desc: An Italian restaurant serving pasta and pizza. The restaurant can get packed on Friday and Saturday nights, at which time reservations are recommended.

spots.name: Monk's Foods
spots.desc: Buddhist ascetics and quirky jazz pianists alike will feel at home at this cozy "slow food" restaurant. The fare is organically-grown, mostly vegetarian/vegan home-style Japanese. When you sit down, the owner will almost certainly ask if you can read the Japanese-only menu, if you look like you can't. If that's the case, just pick one of the three daily specials — vegetarian, fish, or…

spots.name: Richouen
spots.desc: This is a very large yakiniku place. It has patchwork architecture and tasty meat.

spots.name: Shimanchu Shokudo Niraikanai
spots.desc: Okinawa-themed restaurant and bar. Head downstairs for the Hawaiian-themed bar Jingle-Jangle.

spots.name: Unatetsu
spots.desc: This is a sushi restaurant that specializes in eel, as its name indicates.

spots.name: Village Vanguard Diner
spots.local: ヴィレッジヴァンガードダイナ―
spots.desc: A burger and beer joint with a large variety of burgers and international drinks. Run by Village Vanguard, a chain of variety/bookstores.

spots.name: Cat Cafe Calico
spots.desc: Enjoy the company of this cafe's 15 cats as you sip your coffee or tea. An outlet for cat lovers who don't or can't keep cats at home, this cafe was covered in news wire reports in late 2007. Has another branch at Shinjuku.

spots.name: Tsuru's Original Roast Beans
spots.local: 自家焙煎 珈琲散歩
spots.desc: Beans roasted to order, nicely-made lights sweets and a blend coffee to rival them all. Quiet, bright and popular.

spots.name: Cheeky
spots.desc: Formerly the annex of Warp, now independent. Musicians such as Inushiki and Latyr Sy gather there, and collaborate until the brink of dawn. Time spent there is to experience musical and artistic genius.

spots.name: Alvorada
spots.desc: A cozy Brazilian-style luncheonette and bar with good food and live music.

spots.name: Yankee Town
spots.desc: This izakaya has a unique style. There is a barbecue pit that can be used by a large group of people. The owner has many interesting stories about the island. Expect occasional live music from local musicians.

spots.name: Yebisu Brewery Tokyo
spots.desc: A mildly interesting permanent exhibition covering the brewing process in general and the history of Japan Beer Brewery Company which developed Yebisu beer, and which is now a part of Sapporo Breweries. There is even a Virtual Brewery Adventure to try.
spots.price: Entry is free, and you can sample 6 types of beer for ¥400 each if so inclined. Alternatively there are guided…

spots.name: Yebisu Garden Place
spots.desc: Has its fair share of boutiques. The Beer Museum's souvenir shop deserves a special mention.

spots.name: Kabuto
spots.desc: Charcoal grill (sumibiyaki) restaurant that looks way more expensive than it actually is. Not a bad choice just for drinks either, which start at ¥400 for a draft beer.

spots.name: Buri
spots.desc: A small standing bar with many high quality varieties of sake available in cup-size bottles: great for tasting several from all over Japan. All sake is initially served cold, but the staff will warm each cup to your desired temperature.

spots.name: Liquid Room
spots.desc: One of Tokyo's best-known and oldest-running nightclubs, although it used to be in Kabukichō before 2004.

spots.name: What The Dickens
spots.desc: An extremely popular British pub in the heart of Ebisu. Fairly expensive (anything imported costs close to ¥1000), but has one of the best selections of British beer and cider in town.

spots.name: Ippo
spots.desc: A small restaurant on the second floor of an unassuming building behind the Ebisu Station; it features fresh fish and a large selection of sake. The menus are in Japanese but the staff speaks English.

spots.name: Hatakeyama Collection
spots.desc: Outstanding collection of artwork from around Northeast Asia in this small museum surrounded by manicured grounds. Excellent ceramics and items related to tea ceremony. Some exhibits change seasonally.

spots.name: Naitoh Shoten
spots.desc: This local liquor shop carries a good selection of domestic and imported beverages. Visitors looking for colorful and fun souvenirs might try their huge selection of decorative one-cup sake. One-cup is a brand name of cheap sake, but better quality brewers have started making these attractive 180 ml packages where the cup can be saved and reused. Naitoh offers one of the larger selections in the…

spots.name: Chin Mar Ya
spots.desc: This local fast-food chain started here and serves good, cheap, and spicy maboudofu or Szechuan-style spicy tofu. Though the original restaurant closed in 2022, there are two other locations in Gotanda. Take out also available.

spots.name: 7025 Franklin Avenue
spots.desc: Excellent burger restaurant with a bit more of an upscale decor, including a quiet and comfortable garden in this converted house. A bit pricier than some hamburger restaurants, but very good. No credit cards are accepted.

spots.name: Bar Arara
spots.desc: Reasonably priced Spanish food and wine in a small restaurant open to the sidewalk in season.

spots.name: Bar Blast
spots.desc: This basement bar is not a dive, but trying to be a little cooler than other bars in the neighborhood. See website for online reservation form. ¥500 table charge if just stopping in for a drink.

spots.name: Ribera Steakhouse
spots.local: ステーキハウス リベラ
spots.desc: Reasonably priced steaks with great character. Think C&W meets pro-wrestling. Hank Williams on cassette and photos of Andre the Giant and The Rock. The walls are covered with autographed photos of K1 and other fighters eating steaks here. Look for the giant photo of Hulk Hogan tucking into a steak. Yokuzuna Akebono has been a regular here for years.

spots.name: The Grafton
spots.desc: Though a bit out of the way this Irish pub is a good place for the standards: fish and chips, Guinness, and football.
spots.addr: Shinagawa-ku, Nishi-Gotanda 2-26-5 Ito Building III, B1

spots.name: Karasumori Shrine
spots.desc: Small Shinto shrine tucked between the commercial buildings surrounding Shinbashi station. Built during the Heian period to commemorate a victory by Fujiwara no Hidesato.

spots.name: Shiogama Shrine
spots.desc: Small Shinto shrine with a surrounding park in the middle of a quiet residential neighbourhood. It is a remnant of a Date samurai clan household.

spots.name: Yurikamome elevated train
spots.desc: Take the Yurikamome elevated train across the bay bridge from Shimbashi station to the bayside Odaiba district, and take in the scenic view of the metropolis, including a giant Unicorn Gundam robot statue. A great experience during the day or night. Each of the train provides a large window with a clearer view. Good for also visiting the famous Fish Market at Toyosu. 16 stations in all from…
spots.price: max ¥390 each way; \820 one day pass

spots.name: New Shinbashi Building
spots.local: ニュー新橋ビル (NEW しんばしビル on entrance)
spots.desc: Building filled with shops catering to the salarymen that work in the offices nearby with the nickname "Oyaji-biru (middle-aged men building)". There are restaurants, menswear stores, massage parlors, and discount ticket stores (kinken shops) inside.

spots.name: Tamiya Plamodel Factory
spots.local: タミヤプラモデルファクトリー
spots.desc: Official shop of Tamiya, famous manufacturer of plastic model kits, "mini 4WD" slot racers and RC cars. Large slot racing course on the second floor.

spots.name: Don Blanco
spots.desc: Tucked away among Korean hostess bars, a cozy joint with some of the most authentic Mexican food you're likely to find in Japan -- the owner makes regular trips to Mexico. Excellent selection of tequilas, home-made tortillas, and lucha libre wrestling masks for guests.

spots.name: Advertising Museum Tokyo
spots.local: 広告とマーケティングの資料館, kōkoku to māketingu no shiryōkan
spots.desc: A small modern museum of the history of advertising in Japan, run by Japan's biggest ad company Dentsu. Probably the most interesting section is war-time propaganda, with posters exhorting the populace to grow pumpkins and apply for permits before listening to the radio. Most exhibits annotated in English.

spots.name: Old Shinbashi Railway Station
spots.local: 旧新橋停車場, Kyū-shinbashi Teishajō
spots.desc: This faithful reconstruction of the Tokyo terminus of Japan's first railway is built on the site of the original and even showcases the few remaining bits. The inside, however, is now given over to several expensive restaurants and cafés.

spots.name: Panasonic Shiodome Museum of Art
spots.local: パナソニック汐留美術館
spots.desc: This small museum has only a tiny permanent collection, but houses changing exhibitions.

spots.name: Nittele Shop
spots.desc: Stocks a vast variety of TV-related goods; much will be unfamiliar to the non-resident, but there's a pretty good selection of Studio Ghibli items too.

spots.name: 3333 Stone Steps
spots.desc: These are the most stone steps in Japan. In November, there is a challenge to climb these steps. Access is by car, or bus from the Kumamoto City Bus terminal. Paid parking is available. The nearby restaurants are open seasonly. Water is available along the climb, but food is only sold at the base of the stairs. Stone markers exists every 100 steps to mark progress. At the top, there is a scenic…

spots.name: Mine tour
spots.desc: Two-hour tours of mine, two times a day, including a ride on the mine "trolley" train. Intended for Japanese speakers. Book at least one day in advance.
spots.price: ¥3170/1580 adult/child, plus ¥900 for a "miner's bento" for morning tours only.

spots.name: Mount Tara
spots.desc: Mount Tara is one of the tallest mountains in Kyūshū. It is surrounded by the Tara mountains.

spots.name: Angela Beach
spots.desc: Perhaps the prettiest beach on the island, with good snorkeling. Sea turtles can often be spotted here. Public toilets, but no other facilities.

spots.name: Atoa Shokudo
spots.desc: Simple eatery without a fixed menu, they'll cook whatever is available. Dinner only.

spots.name: Ikoidokoro Iriijo
spots.desc: The best (and only) drinking hole on the island, more like drinking in someone's house than a regular izakaya. Beer, awamori and simple dishes of whatever is available that day.

spots.name: M-Air Kiteboarding
spots.desc: A huge kite in the sky and a board (usually) in the water with a crazy-ass fool in the middle.

spots.name: Maenohama Beach
spots.desc: Right in front of the ferry terminal and village, the beach is protected by breakwaters and thus not particularly picturesque, but good for swimming. Beware of currents further out in the channel.

spots.name: Shimanakahama Beach
spots.desc: Small but picturesque beach on the north side, flanked by coral rocks. The reef is very close to the beach, close enough that swimming at low tide is hazardous.

spots.name: Yarahama Beach
spots.desc: The longest beach on the island, on the west side. The best spot on the island for watching the sunset.

spots.name: Oyasumidokoro Azateya
spots.local: お休み処 あざて家
spots.desc: Next to the ferry terminal, offers Yaeyama soba, Japanese staples like curry rice and oyakodon, and cold draft beer.

spots.name: Nishi no Hama
spots.desc: Not much in the way of a beach, but it's a spawning ground for sea turtles during summer nights. The turtles are a protected species, of course, so viewing them is possible only under strictly regulated conditions.

spots.name: Kuroshima Research Station
spots.desc: Studies mostly sea turtles, and plenty of juvenile specimens can be viewed in tanks. There are also sharks and local fish, as well as exhibits on local life on the island. Nighttime excursions to view the sea turtles are available for ¥1,500.

spots.name: Iko Pier
spots.desc: Walk far out (354m) on the old access pier over the beautiful blue lagoon and see views of Iriomote across the water. The scenery is nicer at high tide.

spots.name: Nakamoto Beach
spots.desc: Doesn't have turtles, but the reef is a quite good snorkeling spot. It seems to only be officially open for swimming during low tide, when the lagoon becomes completely separated from the sea. During other times there can be strong currents, so be careful. Shower facilities are available next to the beach, as well as the visitor center next to the research center.

spots.name: Teshima Art Museum
spots.desc: The museum, which resembles a water droplet landing on concrete, was created by Ryue Nishizawa. It has only has 1 exhibit: Matrix, by the artist Rei Naito. Silence and bare feet are required.

spots.name: Les Archives du Coeur (Heart Archives)
spots.desc: Listen to the heartbeats of people who have visited here and at other installations around the world. You can then make a recording of and listen to your heartbeat! Your heartbeat may then be played for future visitors.

spots.name: The Setouchi Triennale aka Setouchi International Art Festival
spots.desc: The festival takes place over several islands in the Seto Inland Sea. Works of contemporary art are installed throughout the islands. The festival is held every 3 years. It consists of 3 sessions in each of the spring, summer, and fall. The next festival is being planned for 2022.

spots.name: San-jo Jinja
spots.desc: This shrine is in the center of Ochiai Hamlet (not along the road, but accessed by walking path from every direction) and the site dates back to the Edo era. Surrounded by towering cedar trees, the doors of the shrine usually remain closed, but the structure is of traditional wooden style and is a calm, cool spot to take a break during a warm summer afternoon. Adjacent to the shrine is a small…

spots.name: Nagaoka-ke
spots.desc: It is a thatched roof farmhouse and one of the oldest still standing structures in Ochiai. A culturally protected building, it has been cleaned up nicely for visitors to walk through and see the interior. With its floor hearths, paper doors, and antique chests, it's a nice place to relax and view the valley. Local information is available here. It is in the center of Ochiai along the hamlet road…

spots.name: Nakochi (Life Share Cottage)
spots.desc: It's about three or four minutes up the path from San-jo Jinja (to the right/northeast) or from the road just above. Nakochi is a cafe and event space situated in a restored traditional farmhouse. Usually only open on weekends and national holidays, it's a good place to take a break and enjoy a meal or cup of tea while exploring Ochiai hamlet. The house has nice views through the valley and is…

spots.name: Ochiai-toge
spots.desc: If you follow the road up through the hamlet, and then continue heading up for another 20 to 30 minutes by car, you will reach Ochiai-toge (Ochiai Mountain Pass). At 1520 m, it is the highest driving road in the Iya valley (and actually 4 m shy of the highest driving point in the entirety of western and southern Japan) and offers fantastic views of the southern ridge line, peaks, and valley floor…

spots.name: Chiiori House
spots.desc: A mountain-side thatch-roofed, traditional Japanese farmhouse, restored at exorbitant cost by way of public tax money and described in Alex Kerr's books Lost Japan and Dogs and Demons (where he complains extensively about Japan's misappropriation of public money for private use). Sadly, for those who remember, Chiiori's previous days as a drop-in spot, cultural experience workshop, and volunteer…

spots.name: Mt. Tsurugi
spots.local: 剣山, Tsurugi-san, also known locally as Ken-zan, sometimes spelled 'Turugi'
spots.desc: (1955 m) It is Iya's most popular hiking destination and the 2nd tallest in Shikoku (#1 being Mount Ishizuchi). One of Japan's "100 Most Famous Mountains", the name may mean "Sword Mountain", but this is a singularly inaccurate description of this gently rounded fell, and you can even take a chairlift up most of the way (¥1000). From the chairlift terminal, it's a half-hour climb to the summit.…

spots.name: Mt. Miune
spots.desc: Another popular trip, but less crowded and maybe prettier than Mt. Tsurugi. At 1893 m, locals say it is the best hike to see the autumn foliage, but it's nice any season. The main trail starts at the hamlet of Nagoro (follow signs) with lower and upper parking areas (the upper area follows the crumbling road about 1.5 km, not recommended if you love your car) and takes about 2½ hours up. Miune…

spots.name: Mt. Tenguzuka
spots.desc: This tall, pyramid shaped mountain peak has fine 360° views from its 1812-m pointed top. Along the ridge below the peak itself, a broad expanse of sasa (short bamboo grass) fields curve gently over the mountain top, allowing for a fairly flat long walk around the area (eventually the path here just goes down the other side of the mountain). A very nice mountain hut is nearby in the opposite…

spots.name: Mt. Yahazu
spots.desc: On the other side of the valley, Mt. Yahazu peak can be accessed from Ochiai-toge 落合峠 (Ochiai mountain pass). The summit is about a 2- to 2½-hour hike from the parking area near the pass top (if going up from Ochiai, the path would be on the right). This is fairly steep, but the panoramic views from the peak top are fantastic as this is the highest point on the northern side of the valley (1848…

spots.name: Ochi-hage
spots.desc: For those looking for a little less effort but a rewarding mountain experience (and who have a car), Ochi-hage (1683m) is only a 30-40 minute hike from Ochiai-toge (Ochiai mountain pass) and visible from the road here (take the path going to the left on the pass top if heading up from Ochiai, the opposite direction of the Mt. Yahazu trail). The beginning of the path is a gentle climb through the…

spots.name: Hotel Iya Onsen
spots.desc: The pretty river-side bath smells of sulfur, but the temperature is not very hot (nice in warm weather, but only just manageable on a colder day). The indoor bath up at the hotel is basic and sparse. The cable car down takes nearly 15 minutes each way, so if you just miss its departure or the car is full, you might need to wait 40-45 minutes before getting in the bath.

spots.name: Hikyō-no-Yu Hotel
spots.desc: The large indoor baths are elaborate and refreshing (by far the best indoor baths in the valley), but the outside stone-lined pools don't offer as nice of a view as elsewhere.

spots.name: Hotel Kazurabashi
spots.desc: The indoor bath is minimal, but the stone-lined outdoor baths up the mountain via the short cable car are award-winning. Overlooking the valley and designed with charming rustic appeal, there are men's and women's baths, and a mixed-sex bath. Small, traditional wood heated baths in private huts are also available for additional cost by reservation, but allow for an experience of cooking oneself…

spots.name: Iyashi-no-Onsenkyo
spots.desc: the indoor and outdoor baths here are thorough enough, and mostly made of local cypress wood. A good option if coming from one of the mountain hikes or if visiting the double Oku-Iya vine bridges. Views are better from the ladies' side.

spots.name: La Fôret Tsurugi
spots.local: ラ・フォーレつるぎ山
spots.desc: This small hotel's simple baths in a quiet secluded setting are the closest to the Mt. Tsurugi trail head area.

spots.name: Jazz Concert
spots.desc: An annual jazz concert that includes a buffet dinner of various local foods is held the first Saturday night of October starting at 18:00 at the large thatched roof Bukeyashiki house on top of the hill far above Kyojo in Higashi Iya. Tickets can be bought at the door and run about ¥4,000-5,000. The event runs till about 21:00. See listing for Bukeyashiki under "See (other)" for directions.

spots.name: Kakashi-matsuri
spots.desc: On either the first or second weekend of October (usually) the small hamlet of Nagoro hosts a small festival to celebrate the scarecrow artwork of Ayano Tsukimi. With food vendors, workshops, and some performances, this very local affair is open to anyone. See the "Scarecrow Village" listing under See for more info.

spots.name: Yukigassen
spots.desc: ("Snowball Fight Competition") It has become a major event at a time when few visit the valley. Not simply a free-for-all, this event is team-based and participants often practice for months to coordinate their skills in the tightly ruled sport. There are several classes of participation including children, women's, men's, and 'just for fun' leagues, and the winners of the main event get to…

spots.name: Mt. Ryugatake
spots.desc: Within neighboring Matsuogawa Valley, go about 20 minutes up Rt 140/149 from Deai past the Matsuogawa Onsen (a fairly desolate road through the narrow valley). The huge 4-km-long Ryugatake cliff face here is famous for its awesome red maples that explode up this impending wall. It begins just past the public restroom along the roadside.

spots.name: Iya Gorge
spots.desc: The entirety of the gorge, from Deai to central Nishi-Iya, has lots of brilliant leaves and several viewpoints to enjoy them.

spots.name: Manpu Gorge/Ryugugake Park
spots.desc: Drive or walk along the old road here (that bypasses the tunnel) and then stroll across the wire suspension footbridge into the park around Ryugugake Cottages for a splendid autumn view through the valley.

spots.name: Oku-Iya Kazurabashi
spots.desc: The isolation in the forest here is great for feeling immersed in the colors, and the dual vine bridges lurking in the bounty only add to the other-worldliness.

spots.name: Mt. Miune
spots.desc: Known as the locals' favorite mountain for autumn leaves, the colors only add to the rewards of the hike.

spots.name: Mt. Tsurugi
spots.desc: In early October a week long maple leaf festival is held here (though it isn't much of a "festival"), as the mountainside is the first in the valley to explode with color.

spots.name: Senkichi
spots.desc: If looking for somewhere special, this soba noodle restaurant also serves various other local specialties, including rice dishes, tempura, and fish. It's easily spotted by the ninja climbing up the outside of the building (If coming from Oboke, you see the ninja only after passing the entrance, so u-turn and go back 50 m). Inside it's beautifully decorated with rustic style furniture, old house…
spots.hours: Open for lunch, closed in winter. Closed Thursdays

spots.name: Iya-bijin
spots.desc: A large restaurant and hotel perched on the side of the valley in a new (but traditional looking) building, offering fine views and lots of local specialties. Known for its soba.

spots.name: Onomiya
spots.desc: This small pub along the main road is instantly recognizable due to being painted like an old style orange and yellow bus (it's also the site of the Kazurabashi Taxi and Bus Tour). Though mostly set up as a drinking place with lots of side dishes, there are also some main meals to be had and its open for lunch and dinner. Not your typical tourist fare or clientele, but you'll surely be welcomed.…
spots.hours: 11:00-21:00 (or later if customers present), closed Wednesdays

spots.name: Mori-no Kuma-san (The Forest's Bear)
spots.desc: If you've had your fill of soba, or are just looking for a light snack or creamy gelato, then this is the place to head. With a nice woodsy feel, you'll find a variety of hot sandwiches, fries made with local potatoes, fruit smoothies, and even waffles drenched in Iya honey. Free Wi-Fi brings you momentarily back into the modern world, and the owner can speak a bit of English to help you along…

spots.name: Kimura Cafe
spots.local: 古民家喫茶 きむら
spots.desc: Set in the valley's oldest recorded house (and thus regarded with historic protection) the Kimura family house is a great place to soak up the traditional lifestyle while enjoying some tea. The over 300-year-old thatched roof house has twin sunken fire hearths around which you are served and is styled the way of days gone by. Tea sets (or coffee) come with a sweet pastry and cost ¥700. It's…

spots.name: Kakunodate Castle Ruins
spots.desc: Pile of old castle ruins. Castle tower does not remain, only stone wall remains.

spots.name: Dakigaeri Valley
spots.desc: Valley with sheer Tama River along. Autumn leaves is great. Promenade is placed.

spots.name: Cherry Blossom
spots.desc: There are 400 Prunus yedoensis (ソメイヨシノ) trees on the embankment of Hinokinai River spans 2 km, and 150 Prunus pendula (シダレザクラ) trees in Samurai town street.
spots.hours: Best time to see late-Apr - early- May.

spots.name: Festival of Kakunodate
spots.desc: Will be held on 7 to 9 September every year. Festival has a history of 350 years. Many floats to move the town. People traditional dancing to continue behind the floats. When floats run into each other on the street, claiming the priority in the way that they hit each other floats.

spots.name: Fire and Snow Festival
spots.local: 火振りかまくら Hiburi Kamakura
spots.desc: In a sort of purification ritual, people whirl flaming pieces of straw on a string above their heads. Onlookers can participate if they like. If so, a hat covering one's hair is a good idea.

spots.name: The Sasara Dance of Kakunodate
spots.desc: "Sasara" is the local dialect for the traditional Lion Dance. The name comes from the sasara - wooden instruments played during the dance. The dance's origins go back four hundred years, when the new lord Stake, arriving in exile from the south, had the dance performed in advance of his procession in order to drive away malevolent spirits. Now it is part of local O-Bon celebrations (mid-August)…

spots.name: Rice Paddy Art
spots.local: 田舎館村田んぼアート
spots.desc: The rice field murals in Inakadate Village have made news around the world. See them for yourself from June to early October. There are two murals, one viewable from the tower at the village office, and the other from a tower near roadside plaza Yayoi no Sato (道の駅弥生の里). There's a shuttle between the two sites.

spots.name: Mori no Naka no Kajuen (Orchard in the Forest)
spots.desc: Admission gets you a knife, a basket, and permission to eat as much fruit as you want straight from the orchards. It's an additional cost to take fruit home. They grow raspberries, peaches, cherries, plums, strawberries, grapes, pears, walnuts, and others.... but no apples. The fruits in season are posted on the website.

spots.name: Tsugaru Kanayamayaki
spots.desc: Shop and learn about pottery made from local Kanayama mountain clay. Check out the sculptures (outside and upstairs) made by visiting artists and take a peek at the kilns. The gallery staff insists beer and even water taste better served in kanayamayaki cups. You can make your own pottery too, but it takes several months to fire. The restaurant serves everything on kanyamayaki dishes, 10:00 to…

spots.name: Kitayamasaki Cape
spots.desc: The village's No.1 tourist spot with 200m high cliff and 8km wide along Sanriku coast. The locals call here as "Alps of the Sea" because of the vivid landscapes. There are three observation decks in the park area (although they offer pretty much same views) as well as staircases down to the shore. The park area consists of a large car park, giftshops, lodges and restaurants. There are also a…

spots.name: Unosu Cliff
spots.desc: Similar to Kitayamasaki apart from the distinctive waveline which attract many seabirds especially cormorant. The name "Unosu" means "cormorant's nest.

spots.name: Shii-no-Ohashi Bridge
spots.desc: Located along National Road 45, which crosses high on deep valley. Many people had to walk across lengthy roads with steep hills before the bridge being built. Today, you can admire the valley view and the sea in horizon from top of the bridge. There is a gift shop selling local products, especially "Tanohata Ice-cream" which is quite popular for visitors.

spots.name: Dainichibō Temple
spots.desc: Offers a priest's remains and various other interesting trophies. English is not well spoken and no pamphlet is available. However, everybody will be nice and comforting while showing you around.

spots.name: Chūrenji Temple
spots.desc: Offers another Buddhist priest who starved himself to death while praying. Though this one is said to have been a criminal before becoming a priest.

spots.name: Jizokura
spots.desc: A jizo shrine built into the side of a mountain. It is said that the monk who discovered Hijiori Onsen lived here. When you visit, you will likely find 5 yen coins hanging from the rocks. This is due to a legend that if you can thread paper through any of the holes in the rocks that your wish will come true.

spots.name: Shikamura Rice Terraces
spots.desc: It's listed as one of Japan's Top 100 Rice Terraces. The views of the rice terraces with the surrounding mountains is a popular photo spot.

spots.name: Suzuki Kokeshi Shop
spots.desc: A shop where Hijiori kokeshi are made and can also be purchased directly from their maker.

spots.name: Okura Shokudo
spots.desc: A ramen restaurant with spicy tanmen, Chinese ramen, and miso ramen. They also have beef bowls (gyudon) if you don't want ramen.

spots.name: Otogitei Kofu
spots.desc: Hotel with restaurant.

spots.name: Taisho Pond
spots.desc: Very nice pond with dead trees and view on the mountains

spots.name: Iwade Kannon
spots.desc: An Edo Period temple built into the cliffside

spots.name: Inaho
spots.desc: A local soba restaurant outside of Atera Forest Spa Kiso.

spots.name: Kanon-ji
spots.desc: Awashima's main temple, home to an Itabi, an ancient stupa.

spots.name: Makihira
spots.desc: Former horse pasture turned bird watching area.

spots.name: Otohime no Yu
spots.desc: Large onsen in the centre of town.

spots.name: Kamome Shokudo
spots.desc: Shokudo with various soba dishes

spots.name: Zensaburo
spots.desc: Shokudo with large menu, features local ingredients

spots.name: Izakaya Menko
spots.desc: Izakaya with various bar snacks

spots.name: Ryusenji Temple
spots.desc: A Shingon-sect temple with a water spring.

spots.name: Snow Park Dorogawa
spots.desc: A ski resort.

spots.name: Hirano Hommachi Dōri Shopping Arcade
spots.desc: Retro covered shopping street in the Hirano Old City.

spots.name: Dive Nangoku
spots.desc: Spoken languages Thai, English & Japanese.

spots.name: Oura beach
spots.desc: Another beach a bit further, also with toilets.

spots.name: Kichijoji Art Museum
spots.desc: Information is only available in Japanese.

spots.name: RAG TAG
spots.desc: Vintage clothes shop for popular brands.

spots.name: Capricciosa
spots.desc: An Italian-style chain restaurant.

spots.name: Warp
spots.desc: A live house with recording studios available for booking.

spots.name: Star Pines Cafe
spots.local: スターパインズカフェ
spots.desc: A large club and live house. 2 floors and stage.

spots.name: HUB
spots.desc: An English-style pub with locations throughout Japan.

spots.name: Good Day Books
spots.desc: Moved to Gotanda.

spots.name: Hiiragi
spots.desc: A famous Taiyaki shop.

spots.name: Kimu Katsu
spots.desc: A cutlet shop. The special cheese cutlet is recommended.

spots.name: The FooTNiK
spots.desc: A British pub where there's always football on the telly.

spots.name: Sapporo Beer
spots.desc: You can try a lot of beer at a low price.

spots.name: Ne Quittez Pas
spots.desc: High-end French cuisine.

spots.name: Shiodome City Center
spots.desc: Glass tower full of trendy restaurants and shops.

spots.name: Ikeshima Chuo Kaikan
spots.desc: Spartan lodging at the community hall.

spots.name: Agarihama
spots.desc: The beach closest to the village.

spots.name: NatureLand Kayaks
spots.desc: Offers kayaking and snorkeling tours

spots.name: Matsuogawa Onsen
spots.desc: The simple baths are in a traditional setting.

spots.name: Sakura no Sato
spots.desc: Located in the Samurai town.
spots.price: Bowl of rice topped with chicken and eggs used the Hinaijidori (比内地鶏を使った親子丼) ¥1575. Inaniwa Udon ¥840

spots.name: Tairadate beach
spots.desc: Near Tairadate light house.

spots.name: Hijiori Morning Market
spots.desc: A daily market where locals sell vegetables.

spots.name: Kotobukiya
spots.desc: A soba restaurant.

spots.name: Koganeyama Shrine
spots.desc: This shrine is the reason most Japanese come here. The shrine originally dates to the 8th century, However a major fire destroyed most of the buildings during the Meiji period. Following that a team of hundreds of woodworkers were brought to the Island, where they spent 15 years building one of the most exquisitely carved pavilions in Japan. Legend has it that those who visit the shrine three…

spots.name: Preservation Area
spots.desc: The preserved area of Magome runs beside the Nakasendo, most tourist sites are in this area and cobblestone streets connect the area. The photogenic streets are one of Magome's biggest tourist draws, and it is a good idea to spend time absorbing the rural atmosphere of the area. Be aware that people still live in the traditional buildings of the area.

spots.name: Old Official Bulletin Board
spots.desc: Just off the Nakasendo, this board was where the shogun would post his orders during the Edo Period.

spots.name: Shimizuya Museum
spots.local: 清水屋 資料館, Shimizuya shiryōkan
spots.desc: Small museums with artifacts from when Magome served as a post town.
spots.hours: 08:00 to 17:00, 08:30 to 16:30 from December to March

spots.name: Tsuchimaya Shiryokan
spots.desc: Small museum remembering Toson and displaying artifacts of his family, it also features artifacts from the Meiji Era, which was when most of his early works were published
spots.hours: 09:00 to 18:00, closed irregularly during winter, check website for dates

spots.name: Wakihonjin Museum
spots.local: 馬籠脇本陣史料館, Wakihonjin shiryōkan
spots.desc: The wakihonjin served as the post town's secondary inn after its honjin, there is now a small museum recounting Magome's history as a post town and features various artifacts from the Edo Era.

spots.name: Walk the Magome-Tsumago Trail
spots.desc: Simply follow the Nakasendo north out of Magome and in about 7 km one will arrive at the next post town Tsumago, the trail is still well preserved and an enjoyable trip.

spots.name: Kawakamiya Magome branch
spots.desc: Founded in 1864, this traditional sweet shop is one of the oldest in Magome, most famous for their chestnut sweets like Kurikinton, a common souvenir from the area.

spots.name: Magomekan
spots.desc: Magome's largest souvenir shop serving various dishes like udon and curry.

spots.name: Shimizuya
spots.desc: Snack store with many bean snacks and other souvenir snacks.
spots.hours: 09:00-16:00 on weekdays, 11:00-15:00 on weekends and holidays

spots.name: Simo-oogiya
spots.desc: Selling straw folk crafts like toy horses and bags, also sells rice crackers. Only takes cash.

spots.name: Usagiya
spots.desc: Senbei (rice cracker) shop with a very large variety with many different flavours.

spots.name: Yaoya
spots.desc: Souvenir shops with local folk crafts, they also sell a few snacks including preserved red turnips.

spots.name: Keiseian
spots.desc: Soba hand milled by local grandmothers. They only accept cash and there is no English menu.

spots.name: Haginoya
spots.desc: Kaiseki restaurant using fresh ingredients specializing in tempura and fish.

spots.name: Masuya
spots.desc: Restaurant making fresh soba, their most popular dish is soba served with fresh Ena Chicken. Only takes cash.

spots.name: HillBilly Coffee Company
spots.desc: Cafe making coffee inspired by the flavours of the Kiso Valley, also has a small selection of pastries.

spots.name: Yomogiya
spots.desc: An old house of Toson, now functions as a tea-house that also serves coffee and snacks.
spots.hours: 10:00-16:30, only open on weekends during January and February

spots.name: Mt. Nishi-Hotakadake
spots.desc: This 2,908 m peak is part of Mt. Hotakadake, and climbing it is relatively easy thanks to the cable car from Shin-Hotaka which takes you halfway up.
spots.price: Cable car ¥1500 one way, ¥2800 round trip, ¥300 large packs

spots.name: Kado Isaburō Museum and Tsujiguchi Hironobu Museum
spots.local: 角偉三郎美術館 and 辻口博啓美術館 respectively
spots.desc: The Kadoi side is devoted to lacquerware, while Tsujiguchi is a master confectioner trained in the French tradition, whose delicacies can be sampled in the cafe (no ticket required).

spots.name: Yumoto no Hiroba
spots.desc: The central point of town, this is the spot where the hot spring bubbles up and is shunted off into all the hotels via a proudly displayed if rather unsexy set of pipes and pumps. It's surrounded by a small park, and there's also a spot to boil your own eggs in spring water (15-20 minutes).

spots.name: Showa Era and Toy Museum
spots.desc: A museum focusing on toys from yester-year, as far back as the early Meiji period, and on daily life in the Showa era of Japan.

spots.name: Wakura Fireworks
spots.desc: Wakura hosts a spectacular fireworks show twice a year. There's a winter show on the second Sunday in January, and a summer show on the first Thursday in August. With an impressive display of over 1,500 fireworks, it's worth checking out. As parking fills up quickly, make sure you either get there early, or don't drive.

spots.name: Wakutamakun Park
spots.desc: A small-ish park good for a stroll and good for spotting the many different Wakutama-kuns, which are the mascot characters of Wakura Onsen. Children will have a fun time here.

spots.name: Darumaya Souvenirs
spots.desc: A souvenir shop which doubles up as a cafe. A convenient place to stock up on different kinds of mochi!

spots.name: Janome Sushi
spots.desc: The "Snake's Eye" is a friendly family-run sushi joint specializing in local Noto delicacies. The top seller is akanishigai (赤ニシ貝, ¥500), a chewy mollusk found exclusively in Nanao Bay, but you won't miss much if you skip it. Instead, try their seasonal nigiri set (四季限定にぎり shiki-gentei-nigiri, ¥2000), which gives a good sampling of the best seafood Noto has to offer.

spots.name: Taiwanese Restaurant
spots.desc: Home-style Taiwanese meals. Try the braised pork rice and soup dumplings.

spots.name: Noto Milk
spots.desc: Ice cream, gelato, frozen yogurt, milk tea and coffee, all made from locally sourced milk.

spots.name: Le Musee de H
spots.local: ル ミュゼ ドゥ アッシュ
spots.desc: Beautiful looking cakes, pastries and desserts. Many items on the menu are seasonal.

spots.name: Kamidonya Shiryokan
spots.desc: History museum in a building from the Edo period. It is maintained with the same techniques that were used in the Edo Period. Various tools and document from the area are on display
spots.hours: 10:00-17:00, closed at 16:00 in March and Novermber

spots.name: Nakamura Residence
spots.desc: Home of the former Nakamura family, a family of merchants who used to be one of Narai's richest families during the Edo Period. The house functions as a museum and showcases a traditional Edo Era residence.
spots.hours: 09:00 to 17:00 from April to November, closes at 16:00 from December to March

spots.name: Shizu Shrine Festival
spots.local: 鎮神社まつり, Shizujinja matsuri
spots.desc: Narai's main festival, a musical procession descends from the shrine to Narai station via the main road playing traditional music for the town's residents and its many visitors.

spots.name: Nagiso Town Museum
spots.local: 南木曽町博物館, Nagiso-chō hakubutsukan
spots.desc: Contains information on the areas history, the preservation of row houses and data about row houses throughout the country. The Museum is in the towns Wakihonjin which has been preserved since the Edo Period, Wakihonjins were smaller inns that served wealthier travellers
spots.price: ¥600 by itself, ¥700 for a combo ticket with the Honjin

spots.name: Honjin
spots.desc: The primary of the post-town during the Edo-Period, although it has been restored it still looks like it's from the late-Edo Period.
spots.price: ¥700 for combo ticket with the Nagiso town museum (Wakihonjin)

spots.name: Tsumago Castle Grounds
spots.desc: Ruins of a sixteenth century castle with views of Tsumago from the top.

spots.name: Old Bulletin Board
spots.desc: The place where the shogun's announcement were decreed. Those with the ability to read some Japanese may be able to read some of the shogun's warnings and prohibitions.

spots.name: Koi Rock
spots.desc: This rock was said to used to look like a Koi fish that greeted travellers walking the Nakasendo, due to it earthquakes it has now fallen over and its resemblences no longer remains but it is still popular with domestic visitors and considered and of the symbols of Tsumago.

spots.name: Walk the Magome-Tsumago Trail
spots.desc: Simply follow the Nakasendo south out of Tsumago and in about 7km one will arrive at the prior post-town Magome, the trail is still well preserved and an enjoyable trip. It is usually walked while starting in Magome and you will have to go against the crowds and face a small uphill incline

spots.name: Walk the Nakasendo to Nagiso
spots.desc: If you follow the Nakasendo north out of Tsumago and you will soon reach Nagiso station. It is not as well preserved as the Magome-Tsumago section but still pleasant.

spots.name: Shinya
spots.desc: Goheimochi shop in the south of the town. Probably the best place to get this Kiso Valley speciality.

spots.name: Kongoya
spots.desc: Shop specializing in soba served with grilled fish, due to limited seating large groups should reserve ahead

spots.name: Kojitsu Coffee
spots.desc: Cafe with many options for both food or drink, it also sells alcohol.

spots.name: Kiyosato Highland Park (Sun Meadows)
spots.desc: This highland does business during summer as a beautiful flower garden. It does business as a Kiyosato ski area, and a lot of skiers visit there during winter season.

spots.name: Roadside Station Minami Kiyosato
spots.desc: This place is service area. A fresh local vegetable can be bought, and it can enjoy oneself over the barbecue.
spots.addr: 760, Nagasawa, Takane town, Hokuto city, Yamanashi

spots.name: A Museum of Art
spots.desc: A Museum of Art was built by Tanaka Haruhiko in 1985. Tanaka Haruhiko also make some homemade jewelries. The jewelries are sold in the museum shop.
spots.addr: 2-1-1, Kiyosatonomori, Takane town, Hokuto city, Yamanashi

spots.name: Moeginomura
spots.desc: This small village was made for sightseeing. There are many gift shops and a small merry-go-round. This place is surrounded by a forest, so you can enjoy relaxation there. And there are famous for music box pavilion. You can make your original music box there. Every season, this village is crowded.

spots.name: Yatsugatake Kiyosato Ham Studio
spots.desc: This ham store is very popular. Especially their in-house made Vienna sausage is well-known and very popular. You can eat pizza baked in a stone oven.

spots.name: Yatsugatake beer Touchdown
spots.desc: This beer called Touchdown has 5 types. Dunkel and Premium Rock Bock are two type of Touchdown. These beer won by Japan Alcoholic Drink Competition Beer Section.

spots.name: Wakaebisuya chaya
spots.desc: Dating from 1724 and once the largest chaya (brothel/geisha house) in the Inland Sea, which employed over 100 women. Famous for the gruesome legend of the Ohaguro Incident (お歯黒事件), where a courtesan called Yae Murasaki poured boiling tooth-blackening paste (o-haguro) made from iron filings down an attendant's throat. A blackened handprint left by the poor girl in her death throes is said to still…

spots.name: Ippōji-san Observation Deck
spots.desc: The highest point on the island, with great views across the area on a clear day.

spots.name: Inujima Seirensho Art Museum
spots.desc: An art museum that was built in the ruins of a former copper refinery. The refinery was built in 1909 and shutdown in 1919 after a decline in copper prices. The art was inspired by the late novelist Yukio Mishima, a controversial figure who opposed Japan's modernization and movements away from its culture and traditions. The abandoned copper refinery is symbolic of how modernization at the…
spots.hours: ¥2,060 (includes admission to Inujima Art House Project and Seaside Inujima Gallery)

spots.name: Inujima Art House Project
spots.desc: 5 galleries constructed of material from the island, including parts of abandoned houses.
spots.hours: 10:00-16:30, closed Tue, closed Tue-Thu in winter
spots.price: ¥2,060 (includes admission to Inujima Art House Project and Seaside Inujima Gallery)

spots.name: Setouchi Triennale aka Setouchi International Art Festival
spots.desc: The festival takes place over several islands in the Seto Inland Sea. Works of contemporary art are installed throughout the islands.

spots.name: Shiraishi Odori
spots.desc: This is the biggest event on the island. These dances are performed in honor of those who died in the Genpei Wars. There are 13 dances performed over the three days.

spots.name: San-chan's
spots.desc: The only real restaurant on the island, serving simple Japanese beach fare such as curry noodles and fried rice, along with alcoholic beverages. English menu. If planning on having dinner there on a weeknight, it may be best to let them know ahead of time; they may otherwise close early. They can also arrange barbecues.

spots.name: Senyakuto
spots.desc: The first bath developed in the area. It's extremely simple without any of the typical small showers or taps for washing. Just scoop water from the pools.

spots.name: Yakushiyu
spots.desc: A short walk up the main street. This Meiji-era (1872) building is highly ranked by the Japan Onsen Association. The upstairs is a relaxing place to take a break.

spots.name: Power Beach
spots.desc: Casual beach side cafe serving American inspired food (think nachos, burgers, ice cream etc.). It has a great view of the Seto Inland Sea, indoor and outdoor seating, English menus, and a very friendly English speaking staff.
spots.hours: Wed-Sat 11:00-16:00; Sun 11:30-16:00, closed Mondays and Tue

spots.name: Kasahara Honey
spots.desc: Modern cafe specializing in locally-made honey and serving pastries, coffee, tea, and sweets among other things. English menu available

spots.name: Cafe Misaki
spots.desc: Cafe with a nice view serving delicious pancakes, Japanese curry, and pizza among other things. Has an English menu and English speaking staff. Can get busy during the weekends.
spots.hours: Wed-Fri 11:00-17:00, Sat Sun 11:00-17:30, closed Mondays and Tue

spots.name: Setouchi Jams Garden
spots.local: 瀬戸内ジャムズガーデン
spots.desc: Quaint cafe specializing in locally made jam but also serving drinks and sweets. Indoor and outdoor seating available.

spots.name: Tachibana-ya
spots.desc: Old school ramen restaurant run by the same husband and wife for decades. It is legendary among ramen connoisseurs in Yamaguchi Prefecture due to its unique take on ramen, they use iriko-dashi (dried infant sardines) in the base of the broth. There is no English menu, it is cash only, and smoking inside is allowed so it may seem intimidating to the average Western traveler. However, if you can…

spots.name: Osamuraijaya Hikoemon Oshima-honten
spots.local: お侍茶屋 彦右衛門 大島本店
spots.desc: Restaurant with a large menu serving good quality Japanese food. One of the few places open for dinner on the island.

spots.name: Kawai Sushi
spots.desc: Good sushi restaurant with friendly service, although no English menu. Open for lunch and dinner most nights.

spots.name: Crest of the Wave Tateishi
spots.local: クレスト・オブ・ザ・ウェイヴ 立岩
spots.desc: Kaiseki restaurant for a good price considering the high quality of the food. The chef was trained in top of the line restaurants in Kyoto and is very friendly.

spots.name: Hidaka Kombu
spots.desc: Kelp (Kombu), which is harvested in this region, is famous as the "Hidaka Kombu". In summer, harvested kelps can be seen being sun-dried on beaches.

spots.name: Pork Bowl
spots.desc: Pork bowl with sightly bigger pork. Obihiro is originated, it is possible to eat in Tokachi whole area.

spots.name: Kinosaki Onsen Ropeway
spots.desc: A cable car located a short walk from the station that offers scenic views of the town and the Sea of Japan. At the summit, visitors can find Onsenji Temple, a historic site with over 1,300 years of history, and the Miharashi Terrace Café for panoramic views and coffee.
spots.addr: 806-1 Yushima, Kinosaki-cho, Toyooka City, Hyogo Prefecture, 669-6101

spots.name: Kinosaki Bungeikan（文芸館）
spots.desc: A small literary museum dedicated to Naoya Shiga and other authors associated with Kinosaki. Permanent exhibitions cover the Shirakaba literary movement, and visitors can also try traditional straw crafts or nostalgic Japanese toys. Ask them about Engeki Quest.

spots.name: Satono-Yu
spots.desc: It is the first bathhouse that you see when exiting the train station. As of April 1, 2024, Satono-Yu is temporarily closed for long-term renovation. Please check the Visit Kinosaki website for reopening updates.

spots.name: Jizo-yu
spots.desc: It is located inside an interesting concrete building with roomy ceilings and offers public baths and rentable private baths.

spots.name: Yanagi-yu
spots.desc: Only opens in the afternoon (15:00), so it is best to plan a few visits to the other bathhouses first. Its waters are said to be especially helpful for healing wounds.
