spots.name: Ichino-yu
spots.desc: It is praised as the best bathhouse in Japan. Its architectural style and well thought out decoration make it a popular and as a result, very busy bathhouse that is very popular with tourists.

spots.name: Goshono-yu
spots.desc: It is perhaps the prettiest out of all seven bathhouses. The traditional garden and facade welcomes you into both indoor baths and very elaborate outdoor baths, that are especially fascinating with snowfall.

spots.name: Mandara-yu
spots.desc: With architecture inspired from temples, the bath might remind you of the mighty Buddhist temples that you saw in Kyoto, although at a much smaller scale. This is another bathhouse that opens late (3pm).

spots.name: Kono-yu
spots.desc: This is the bath where the legendary storks bathed in the waters to heal their wounds. It is the most down key, but also the most relaxing public bath house.

spots.name: Shinsen-en Garden
spots.desc: Although cherry blossom-viewing and festivals can be seen all over Japan today, Shinsen-en Garden is where the very first organized cherry blossom viewing festival took place.

spots.name: Nijō-Jinya
spots.desc: A private residence, Nijo-Jinya is a former samurai house. Tours discuss the roles of samurai and the dangers experienced during that time period. The house features unique trap doors and escape routes used by samurai and former residents to escape fires and attacks. Guided tours are available in Japanese by a family member of the current residents. You are welcome to bring an interpreter.

spots.name: Kyoto International Manga Museum
spots.local: 京都国際マンガミュージアム, Kyōto Kokusai Manga Myūjiamu
spots.desc: Housed in an old elementary school building, the museum holds over 300,000 manga-related items ranging from rare Meiji-era publications to the works of contemporary artists. One of its main attractions is the so-called "Wall of Manga": a vast collection of some 50,000 volumes arranged on shelves running along the building's corridors. Much of the collection is in Japanese, but there is a sizeable…

spots.name: Shōseien Garden
spots.desc: Shosei-en Garden was commissioned by Prince Minamoto no Tōru. He designed the Ingetsu Pond to resemble the Shiogama Coast in Miyagi Prefecture. During the Tokugawa Period the garden was given to Higashi Hongan-ji Temple, restoring the old sections and adding on to the garden. It's a stroll garden with buildings dating back to the 19th century.

spots.name: Mibu-dera
spots.desc: Founded in 991 CE, Mibu-dera is a Buddhist temple. The temple has Setsubun celebrations in February which draws large crowds. It's free to visit the grounds, however, a small museum and garden have an admission fee.

spots.name: Kyoto Railway Museum
spots.desc: An expansive and modern railway museum with over 50 historical Japanese rollingstock, primarily used in service by JR West and its predecessor, JNR. Three Shinkansen models are on display, along with an extensive collection of preserved steam locomotives, including one you can ride. Many informative displays and exhibits of railway technology, operations and systems line a three story main…

spots.name: Kyoto Aquarium
spots.desc: A modern aquarium with a wide variety of sea life such as small and large Fish, Garden Eels, Dolphins, Seals, and Giant Salamanders. The Aquarium also includes a small Japanese style garden, two cafes, and a gift shop. The whole facility is wheelchair and pram accessible with elevators and ramps.

spots.name: Nishijin Textile Center
spots.desc: While visitors may just go to the museum to see the history of Nishijin Textiles, you may also want to try dressing up as a geisha or trying your hand at weaving. You need reservations for each activity, and separate fees are charged for each activity. As of Aug 2023, kimono shows are suspended.
spots.price: Weaving costs ¥1,800 adult (¥1,500 for students) and dressing up as a geisha costs ¥10,000

spots.name: Kōbō-san Market
spots.desc: On the 21st of each month, Tō-ji hosts a large flea market on and around the temple grounds. It's like a one-day festival, with long rows of food vendors joining an odd assortment of sellers — everything from elegant Japanese crafts and rare plants to piles of old postcards, photos, movie posters, and appliances from decades past.

spots.name: Gallery Gado
spots.desc: Gallery Gado sells modern woodblock prints (ukiyo-e) with traditional themes. The gallery also has catalogs of the work of artists who are maintaining this art form. All prints are authentic woodblock prints.
spots.price: Postcard-sized prints ¥800, medium-sized prints ¥2,000-3,000, large prints for more

spots.name: Junkudo
spots.desc: A huge bookstore with big selection of English books and magazines.

spots.name: Musashi Sushi
spots.desc: One of the oldest kaitenzushiya (conveyor belt sushi) restaurants in Kyoto. All of the sushi is handmade, though it may take a while to see something new float by. Fortunately, the seats surround the chefs, so you can request whatever you want if you don't see something you like.

spots.name: Kappa Sushi (on Pontocho)
spots.desc: A reasonably-priced (for fresh sushi) restaurant. They have an English menu which is, unfortunately, inferior to the Japanese menu. Specials change daily, but are generally on the pricey side. Sit at the sushi bar, and eat well-apportioned nigiri off of banana leaves with your fingers. Not a bad place to try real o-toro for ¥800 a plate.

spots.name: Shofukutei
spots.desc: One person udon nabe for ¥1,100. Green soba or udon noodles for as cheap as ¥400.

spots.name: Shishin Samurai Cafe & Bar
spots.desc: The place proclaims that an increase of food production, food self-sufficiency, and the decrease of food waste can prevent war. This cafe serves local Japanese foods as much as possible to increase food self-sufficiency and sustainability. In addition this cafe uses 5% of its gross sales to aid homeless people and orphans who are suffering from a lack of food. Furthermore, this cafe aims to…

spots.name: Siam
spots.desc: A tiny but wonderful Thai curry restaurant. The food is delicious, reasonably priced and spice levels are indicated on the menu. Relax in a soft-lit room decorated with exotic paintings from Bali, while the friendly staff prepare your meal right in front of you. An English menu available.

spots.name: Fuka
spots.desc: This old shop makes the best nama-fu manju (wheat gluten filled with sweet bean paste) in Kyoto and supplies many sweet shops and restaurants throughout the city. There might not be enough supplies to sell over the counter, so it is best to arrive early.

spots.name: Tengu
spots.desc: A chain izakaya offering their own beer and good shared food with occasional seasonal specials.

spots.name: Anil
spots.desc: A nice Nepalese restaurant with a great atmosphere and awesome food. The dahl, cheese nan and momo dumplings are highly recommended.

spots.name: Torikizoku
spots.desc: Torikizoku is the most popular yakitori chain in Kansai. There are several locations in Kyoto - most convenient for travellers is in Kawaramachi/Shijo, just before the bridge, or between sanjo and shijo, on kiyachou-dori. The yakitori is delicious, comes in generous serves and is very cheap. It's very popular with both locals and expats, and is always busy. Try to come before 19:30 to secure…

spots.name: Apollo
spots.desc: If hipster izakaya didn't exist before, Apollo has invented it. Izakaya style with a clean, laid back environment consisting more of hip and arty locals instead of an older "regulars" crowd. Beautiful interior with a center garden and private dining rooms, or you can sit at the bar or in the more casual tables upstairs. Chefs prepare a mix of salads, grilled foods and fried foods from seasonal…

spots.name: Tuzuri
spots.desc: Quiet Japanese place specialising in traditional home cooking dishes (called obanzai).
spots.addr: Matsubara Dori, just west of Karasuma

spots.name: Nijiya
spots.desc: Cozy vegan izakaya with only counter 7 seats. As of March 2024, they had to temporarily stop taking reservations due to popularity, and serve customers in order of arrival.

spots.name: Pontochō
spots.desc: One of Kyoto's most traditional nightlife districts, the restaurants here run the gamut for super-exclusive geisha houses to common yakitori bars. Many have pleasant open-air riverside terraces. Rule of thumb is, any establishment with a menu and prices outside is OK, but others are best skipped.

spots.name: Mishima-tei
spots.desc: If you have a yearning for sukiyaki, and your pockets are deep, you must visit Mishima-tei at the junction of Teramachi-dori and Sanjo-dori. Here you will be bowed in and shown to your own private tatami room by your personal kimono-clad hostess. There, having helped you to order, she will prepare your sukiyaki feast on the hotplate set between you. Order the "premium beef", and the richly…

spots.name: Ing
spots.desc: No night in Kyoto is complete without the requisite after hours visit to all-night Ing (a.k.a., "Box Bar," or "the office"). Proprietor Hako-san will keep bringing you the booze, and he's happy to join you for a drink when offered. Food there is always an option - tofu salad & potato pizza are good for the price (¥600). Get ready for Rolling Stones, competitive Jenga, sharing tables with odd…
spots.price: Sapporo sells at ¥600 each shareable bottle

spots.name: Sake Bar Yoramu
spots.desc: From the unusual to the standard, this sake bar has both an impressive selection of traditional Japanese rice wine. Even more impressive is the barkeep and owner, who's from Israel, who can translate your preferences in wine into sake. Well-aged sake is available, busting the myth that sake does not age. Traditionally-brewed sake ranging from slightly cloudy to yogurt-like may also be available.
spots.hours: Tue-Sun 18:00-00:00, closed first Sun of the month

spots.name: Nikki's Bar
spots.desc: This is a nice little bar ran by a gregarious Nepalese guy named Nikki. It's got a great bunch of regulars and new customers are always warmly welcomed. It's just north of Hamid's Kebab shop. Mixed drinks and beer run ¥700 per drink and shots are ¥500. It's a little hard to find because it's on the 8th floor. If you can't find it ask the folks working at Hamid's.

spots.name: Sugar Trip
spots.desc: A ritsy cocktail bar with a variety of drinks from the standard beers to champaigne and cava. Most people come for one of the many cocktail varieties that this bar is famous for.
spots.price: Original cocktails sell for ¥700-750, Smoothie cocktails for ¥900, Beer for ¥650-700, tonic ¥700

spots.name: A bar
spots.desc: A hard-to-find (on 2nd floor) izakaya close to the Shijo/Kiyamachi corners, makes a great start to the evening. Food is good and reasonable - daily sashimi specials and fried goods, especially. You share long tables with foreigners and locals alike; a friendly thing to do would be to pour beers for your neighbors and Suei-san, the proprietor.

spots.name: Pub Africa
spots.desc: Although many think this is an Africa-themed bar, there is nothing very African about it. If there's a football match from home that you need to catch, they'll show it here, and they have cheap Asahi jugs. Beers half off during Happy Hour. Also, their fooseball table is very well kept. Across from the Hub, infra.

spots.name: K-ya
spots.desc: Classy beautiful off the beaten path bar that caters to locals more than tourists. The owner is one of Japan's best bartenders. Staff wear tux's ala Rainbow Room in New York. The vibe is upscale yet casual. It overlooks a beautiful Japanese garden. Cocktails range from classics like Moscow Mule to their own specialities. Tasty amuse bouche come with each round of drinks. Service is wonderful.

spots.name: Milan's Bar
spots.desc: A fun little bar tucked away down a back alley on the west side of the canal. The alley is just south of Karaoke Paradise, and the sign for Milan's read just Mil-N Bar. Located on the 2nd floor, it's a cozy, cave-like interior, but Milan, the Nepalese proprietor, is gregarious and always has a funny tale to tell.

spots.name: The Hub
spots.desc: Lots of TVs for sports, cheap beer (¥700/pint) (especially with a ¥500 membership) and more expensive imports; food, however, is mediocre. This is basically the headquarters for English-speaking tourists and gaijin residents for happy hour. Happy hour (17:00-19:00) discounts cocktails only. If you want some inside information about where to go, where to eat, what to see, etc., ask a group here.…

spots.name: McLoughlin's
spots.desc: Presided over by the most amiable owner/chef Tadg McLoughlin. Quality beers, domestic and foreign (including microbrews). The staff are friendly and speak English. Live music on weekends. Giant screen TV (Mr. McLoughlin being a rugby fanatic), darts, foosball and a great view of east Kyoto. Happy hours are 17:00-20:00.

spots.name: Teradaya
spots.desc: It was here at this inn where Ryōma Sakamoto, a famous samurai who wanted to overthrow the Tokugawa, was injured in an attack, although he escaped. Some pictures, his handgun, and other historical artifacts are viewable inside.

spots.name: JRA Kyoto Racecourse
spots.desc: For those interested in horse races, Kyoto's racecourse is the biggest and most significant in the Kansai area.

spots.name: Riverboat Cruises
spots.desc: A peaceful ride down the canal past all of the historic sake breweries. It's a unique experience that is both scenic and affordable.
spots.hours: Call to make a reservation to schedule your ride. No tours are offered on Mondays
spots.price: ¥1000 for adults, ¥500 for elementary school and younger

spots.name: Ryomakan
spots.desc: An interesting souvenir shop dedicated to the famous samurai Ryoma Sakamoto. Inside you'll find some of the typical tourist souvenirs, like Ryoma Sakamoto keychains, but there are also some interesting and unique finds. Those looking to purchase swords may find that this shop sells more authentic swords than those in Kyoto's larger tourist spots.

spots.name: Uosaburo
spots.desc: A pricey restaurant serving local Kyoto cuisine with a variety of set options.

spots.name: Ramen Factory Kyoto
spots.desc: Ramen Factory Kyoto consists of the Ramen Restaurant (for eating - tabemasu) which offers different types of ramen such as Miso, Shoyu (Soy sauce), Shio (Salt) and Ramen Experience (for experience - taiken) which is the only restaurant in Japan where you are able to make original ramen from scratch by your hand and enjoy its deliciousness. Ramen Factory has the root from “Menbakaichidai” which is…

spots.name: Gekkeikan
spots.desc: Founded in 1637, this local sake brewing company remains popular among Japanese even today. Many of the old breweries still exist and visitors can tour Gekkeikan and visit the attached museum to get a glimpse of how the sake is made.

spots.name: Osaka Museum of Housing and Living
spots.local: 大阪くらしの今昔館 Ōsaka kurashi no Konjaku-kan
spots.desc: Step back in time as you walk through this life-sized reproduction of an Osaka neighborhood from the 1830s. The street contains re-creations of a public bath (you can borrow a yukata, or cotton kimono, to wear as you stroll around), as well as various shops and merchants' living quarters. There's also a section displaying detailed dioramas of Osaka after the Meiji Period. English-language audio…
spots.price: Adults ¥600, free for junior-high students, kids, and seniors

spots.name: Japan Mint and Mint Museum
spots.desc: It's not widely known even by people from elsewhere in the country that Japan Mint is headquartered in Osaka. For Osakans, Sakura-no-tōrinuke (桜の通り抜け, cherry blossom tunnel road) is a synonym for this facility, attracting a large number of visitors (close to 1 million in just 7 days) during a limited, planned week in mid-Apr. A must-see if you are fond of nature and happen to drop into Osaka…

spots.name: Osaka Shiki Musical Theater
spots.desc: Home of the Shiki Theatre Company, proposing plays and musicals.

spots.name: Hankyu Sanban-gai
spots.desc: The large shopping areas filled with a variety of shops from cages to brandname boutiques.

spots.name: Herbis Plaza ENT
spots.desc: Boutiques of famous brands inside and outside Japan, gourmet restaurants.

spots.name: Snack Park
spots.desc: Offers okonomiyaki, takoyaki and a few surprises like doteyaki (どて焼き) — stewed beef sinew.

spots.name: Tsuruhashi Fūgetsu
spots.desc: Good okonomiyaki as well as yakisoba, with extra toppings (egg, cheese, etc.). The restaurant overlooks Umeda. There's an English menu.

spots.name: En (Umeda)
spots.desc: En is one of the most atmospheric and tastiest izakayas in Osaka, with branches in Umeda and Namba. The interior is beautiful and food is delicious and reasonably priced. En also has a large range of Japanese sake and has an English menu.
spots.price: Food will cost ¥2000-2500 per person, drinks start from around ¥500

spots.name: Torikizoku
spots.desc: Torikizoku is the most popular yakitori chain in Kansai, and can be found near most major stations in Osaka. The food is delicious, comes in generous serves and is very cheap. It's very popular with both locals and expats, and is always busy. Try to come before 7:30PM to secure seats.

spots.name: Harukoma honten
spots.desc: Sushi restaurant located in the Tenjinbashisuji shopping street. Whenever they are open, there is a line outside, mainly composed of locals, so be prepared for a wait of an hour or more.

spots.name: Explosion
spots.desc: Osaka's most popular and largest (albeit still not very big) gay club. They hold special events on Fridays and Saturdays, some of which are men-only and occasionally women-only, so check their website to make sure that you will be able to enter on the day you plan to visit. Foreigners sometimes get discounts or extra free drink coupons, so bring identification (especially if you are of Asian…

spots.name: Sam and Dave
spots.desc: Popular international dance club with a meat-market vibe. Two locations in Osaka.

spots.name: Kamigata Ukiyoe Museum
spots.desc: (上方浮世絵館) A rather small museum in Nanba dedicated to ukiyoe, Japanese woodblock prints. The interior of the museum looks a bit like an adobe house. It may be most interesting to someone already familiar with the art, as the information inside mostly Japanese only.

spots.name: Sumo Spring Grand Tournament
spots.desc: The Osaka Tournament of Japan's national sport, sumo wrestling, is usually held mid-March annually at Osaka Prefectural Gymnasium. Check for schedules and ticket availabilities at the official Nihon Sumo Kyokai homepage.

spots.name: The Silver Ball Planet
spots.local: ザ・シルバーボールプラネット
spots.desc: Pinball arcade featuring over 100 retro, classic & modern pinball machines. ¥100 per play (3 balls) typically, but some are as cheap as ¥10

spots.name: Tamago-yaki stand
spots.desc: Best for a snack, this outdoor stall offers a hard-to-find and delicious treat called tamago-yaki, fried egg atop a wide flat sembei cracker with sauce and a variety of toppings available. Much tastier than it sounds.

spots.name: Tsuruhashi Fūgetsu
spots.desc: Good okonomiyaki and yakisoba, with extra toppings (egg, cheese, etc.). The restaurant overlooks Umeda. There's an English menu.

spots.name: Tako Tako King
spots.desc: This takoyaki place has very friendly staff. Look for the big red octopus wearing a crown.

spots.name: Torikizoku
spots.desc: Torikizoku is the most popular yakitori chain in Kansai, and can be found near most major stations in Osaka. The food is delicious, comes in generous serves and is very cheap. It's very popular with both locals and expats, and is always busy. Try to come before 19:30 to secure seats.

spots.name: Ajinoya
spots.desc: Some of the best okonomiyaki in Osaka, and they're so proud of it they prepare it for you from start to end, making a good choice for the casual visitor as well. The "A set" (¥5,900) includes no less than four styles and will leave four people stuffed to the gills. Very popular, so join the queue early, and beware that ordering here is once and done: you can't add on more later.
spots.addr: Namba 1-7-16 現代こいさんビル2F

spots.name: Harijyu
spots.desc: Shabu-shabu or sukiyaki in Japanese tatami rooms. No reservations are taken except for large groups, so arrive early at nights (18:00 or so) to be sure you get a room without waiting.

spots.name: Kani Dōraku
spots.desc: Now a nationwide chain, but this is the original -- although there are three branches around Dotonbori alone! Easily identifiable by the giant mechanical crab waving its pincers about, and as you might guess, the speciality here is crab. The menu runs to pages and pages of ways to prepare the crustaceans, ranging from sushi to hotpots to gratin, but perhaps the most Japanese way is to order…

spots.name: Bar Kama Sutra
spots.desc: Small cozy karaoke bar is almost impossible to find but well worth the effort. Foreign and English-speaking Japanese staff, and over 130,000 songs to choose from. The owner, Richard, is a long term resident of Japan and is a wealth of information on what to do and see in the area, where to stay and even where to find work. (No "u" in e-mail address is correct, or: richosaka@gmail.com.)

spots.name: Blarney Stone
spots.desc: This pair of Irish pubs have a laid-back atmosphere, friendly staff, and a decent happy hour.

spots.name: HUB
spots.desc: This British pub chain is at many locations around Osaka, including along Midosuji street in Shinsaibashi, in Namba, and in Chayamachi (Umeda, east side of Hankyu station and walk north a little). HUB serves as a meeting place for many expats as well as Japanese locals. Get there early for happy hour discounts on cocktails (17:00-19:00).

spots.name: G Physique
spots.desc: One of Osaka's most popular gay and lesbian bars among foreigners.

spots.name: Club Life
spots.desc: Great place to listen to Hip Hop, R&B, Reggae and all black music. Beside playing the latest music, you can also listening the old school classics. Enjoy a wide range of drinks to get you in the party mood or help you relax.
spots.addr: Gold Center Building B1F 2-8-12 Higashi Shinsaibashi

spots.name: Club Pure
spots.desc: Extremely crowded dance club. The crowd is around 25-30% international. Be sure to bring your passport, as the ID check here is atypically rigorous. The closest subway station is Namba Station, which is about 5-10 min walk. No dancing is allowed in the club.
spots.price: Cover ¥4000 men, ¥2500 women; includes unlimited drinks but don't lose your cup

spots.name: Open Air Museum of Old Farmhouses
spots.local: 日本民家集落博物館 (nihon minka shūraku hakubutsukan)
spots.desc: Ryokuchi park is lovely, and in it is a museum of a dozen old Edo period farmhouses, moved across country and lovingly reconstructed. Also on display are tools, furniture, and the like. You can go to Himeji-jo or the old palace in Kyoto and see how the rulers lived, but come down here to see how the people lived. Thanks to the efforts of a volunteer from Australia, they have a great new…

spots.name: Nagai Stadium
spots.local: ヤンマースタジアム長居
spots.desc: Nagai Stadium is the home of the professional soccer team Cerezo Osaka.

spots.name: Taiyoshi Hyakuban
spots.desc: Most of the "restaurants" in the area are really brothels in disguise (since prostitution is illegal in Japan), but this extravagant century-old brothel is a Tangible Cultural Property that has been turned into an actual restaurant open to the public. Specialities include hot pot dishes like sukiyaki and yosenabe.

spots.name: Kumano Hongu Taisha
spots.desc: A Shinto shrine in the mountains with a giant torii. Designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

spots.name: Tsuboyu
spots.desc: A 1300 year old hot spring, considered to be one of the oldest in the nation, it is listed as part of the World Heritage Site Kumano Kodo Pilgrimage Route as it was frequented by pilgrims traveling on the Old Kumano Road (Kumano Kodo). To access the bath, you must get a timed usage ticket from the ticket office and be ready to enter from the time on your ticket.

spots.name: Child nature park
spots.desc: This big park is loved by the young and the old alike. There is a pond, whose water was used for cooking at the battle of Tsurugamine in 1202. The pond was enlarged for irrigation in 1700. It is a habitat for "genjibotaru" (Nipponoluciola cruciata, a variety of firefly) and registered as one of Yokohama City's natural monument. In spring, cherry blossoms are very beautiful.

spots.name: Zoorasia
spots.local: よこはま動物園ズーラシア
spots.desc: It is a zoo. There are many animals, including rare species like Okapi, which has a face of giraffe and body of zebra.

spots.name: Choshoji Temple
spots.desc: Sōtō sect temple. Many people visit there on New Year's Eve to strike the temple bell toll. Everyone can participate after waiting in a long line. Amazake (sweet drink made from fermented rice) is served on the occasion for free.

spots.name: Central fitness club
spots.local: セントラルフィットネスクラブ
spots.desc: Central fitness club is a gym. You can enjoy many kinds of sports. For example, tennis, squash, golf, sauna bath, pool, etc. But, it is a little expensive. It costs ¥5000-8000.

spots.name: Ukki-tsuushin karaoke
spots.local: うっきー通信カラオケ
spots.desc: It takes 5 minutes to walk from the station. There are from big to small room. And, you can eat many foods in there.

spots.name: Kirari
spots.desc: (きらり) It is rice ball shop. It takes 1 minute to walk from station. There are many kinds of rice balls. All rice balls are very delicious. There are miso soup in there. It is delicious, too.

spots.name: Yamada Denki LABI Shinagawa Oi-machi
spots.desc: A large-scale home electronics store chain with the biggest duty-free store franchise.

spots.name: Tonkatsu Mitake
spots.desc: The shopkeeper is The baseball player Ichiro's fan. A courteous service, a shop with a very welcoming hospitality.

spots.name: Manraien
spots.desc: Many celebrities frequently visit Chinese cuisine. However, lunch is for commoners.

spots.name: Bird Sanctuary Center
spots.desc: In line with the park's goals as a bay habitat preserve, nearly a third of the park is maintained as a Sea Bird Sanctuary. The area attracts bird lovers and photographers who are free to roam the area, except the marsh areas which are restricted. At the center is a Sea Bird Center with information on the local birds.

spots.name: Nippori Fabric Town
spots.desc: Any lover of crafting and sewing needs to visit Nippori Fabric Town. Fabric Town has about 90 shops from Nippori Station to Nippori Chuo Street. Here you'll find wonderful fabric in any print you could want and any sewing notion you'll ever need.

spots.name: Akasuimon
spots.desc: The Red Floodgate may be of little interest to the casual tourist, but involves a pleasant walk in a riverside park. Tokyo is low-lying, and depends on floodgates and levees to avoid inundation. The historic red flood gate is no longer used, replaced by the larger (but less attractive) blue gates to the east.

spots.name: Asukayama Park
spots.desc: Asukayama Park is the first park in Japan. It has about 650 sakura trees, planted by the Japanese political leader Yoshimune Tokugawa (1684-1751). People drink and eat under them when the cherry blossoms bloom in spring. There are also some museums in the park (combined website). The paper museum shows the history of paper and has a library. The Shibusawa museum is about the famous Japanese…

spots.name: Market of the cock
spots.desc: It is the Japanese traditional festival that have continued from Edo period. Held in November on the days of the cock by Ootori shrine in Nerima - 5th, 17th and 29th in 2024. There are many kinds of booths. For example, Chinese foods, grilled chicken, apricot candy, big cotton candy and so on. You can eat those foods and enjoy this traditional atmosphere.

spots.name: United cinema Toshimaen
spots.local: ユナイテッド・シネマとしまえん
spots.desc: This cinema has 9 screens and special seats that have more beautiful sound than normal seats. It can accommodate about 2372 spectators. There are some shops, you can buy foods, for example, popcorn and ice cream, drinks and goods of movies. Prices are ¥1,800 for adults, ¥1,500 for university and high school students, ¥1000 for junior and senior, ¥900 for infants (from 3 years old).

spots.name: Warner Bros Studio Tour Tokyo - The Making of Harry Potter
spots.desc: Opened in June 2023, it is the first Harry Potter studio tour in Asia.
spots.price: Adults ¥6300, child ¥5200. Tickets must be purchased in advance

spots.name: Niwa-no-yu
spots.desc: A large, upscale sento adjacent to Toshimaen which features indoor and outdoor baths, Roman steam rooms, Finnish saunas, a large indoor pool (bring your bathing suit), and an upstairs area with food, drinks, massages, and relaxation chairs (food, drinks, and massages cost extra). Children not permitted.

spots.name: Stage Up
spots.desc: A karaoke parlor with a performance stage near Toshimaen station. When you enter the room, choose your favorite songs and sing it. If you look for a song and put its number to the karaoke machine, music without a voice is being played so you can sing with music. And you can eat many kinds of foods and drink.

spots.name: Jūjō-Ginza
spots.desc: This covered shopping street is as good a way as any to see how every-day people shop and what they buy.

spots.name: Cartagena
spots.desc: A cozy and friendly spot where you can dance and drink. It is probably the first Latin bar in Nerima. The owner is a lady who once lived in Colombia; she speaks English and Spanish. There is a salsa event on weekends.
spots.price: Beer, rum and others start at ¥500

spots.name: Koiki Shrine
spots.desc: A shrine built in 1226 by Michizane Sugawara to console himself after having to leave his wife and child in the capital. The shrine contains the oldest known stone carvings of a married couple in Japan. It is known today for the stone heart on its torii gate.

spots.name: Samurai Street
spots.desc: While many small towns in the Japanese countryside advertise samurai streets or houses that lead to disappointment, Chiran's collection of samurai houses is quite good and the street makes a nice stroll in spring or autumn.

spots.name: Kuroki Goshoato
spots.desc: The house where Emperor Antoku and his descendants are said to have lived. Exhibits are limited to a few musty scrolls claiming to record the genealogy.

spots.name: Sakamoto Onsen
spots.desc: A natural seaside hot spring where the water bubbles out at 50°C, which is too hot to bathe in -- except during and after high tide, when seawater is mixed in, making the temperature bearable! At high tide, water depth can reach 1.5 m, so it doubles as a heated pool as well.

spots.name: Amakusa Shiro Memorial Hall
spots.desc: Exhibits about the Shimabara Rebellion. Amakusa Shiro was responsible for leading the rebellion against the Tokugawa Shogunate. The museum has 13 exhibits that tell the story of Christianity in Japan from its arrival in 1549 to its suppression.
spots.hours: 09:00–17:00 (closed at 16:35 during summer and 16:20 during winter)
spots.price: Adults ¥600, Junior High school students and younger ¥300, infants and toddlers free

spots.name: Club Noho Salt
spots.desc: Small cafe, museum and shop selling hand-kneaded Noho salt, which is also available in flavors including curry, yuzu, and chilli.

spots.name: Unpenji Temple
spots.desc: This is temple 66 of the 88 Temple Shikoku Pilgrimage on a mountain top in the western part of town, near the border of Shikoku-chuo City (aka Kawanoe). To access, drive out westward from the town center on route 192 about 10-15 minutes, then follow the signs (in English) for the turn off on the right side. Drive a winding road up the mountain or park at the bottom of the mountain to hike the…
spots.addr: On a mountain top along the Tokushima-Kagawa Prefectural border

spots.name: "Frespo" Shopping Center
spots.desc: This large one-floor shopping center is in the same parking area as the bus station, and includes a substantial supermarket, ¥100 shop, drug store, clothes store, and a home center (DIY/hardware store). Some camping supplies can be found here. Most stores are open 09:00 to 21:00 (home center is open till 19:30).

spots.name: Oboke and Koboke Gorge
spots.desc: The gorge formed by the Yoshino River is quite spectacular. The steepest and most rugged sections lie in the area between JR Koboke Station to the north and Tosa-Iwawhara Station to the south (with JR Oboke Station in the middle). Aside from rafting, pleasure boat tours are operated out of the Hotel Mannaka, offering views from within the gorge but without the need to get wet. The gorges can also…

spots.name: Youkai
spots.desc: Japanese youkai (mythical monsters) are known to all, with their quirky ways and unique characteristics. Some are fun, some spooky, and others just plain weird, they are the sources of popular legends and have greatly influenced manga (comic book) and animation sub-cultures. As it goes, the area around Oboke/Koboke is actually the original home to many of these monsters (there are hundreds if not…

spots.name: Monster Museum
spots.desc: A monster museum. Large carvings of various monsters can be seen along roadsides in the area. More information, including maps, is available at the Michi no Eki.

spots.name: Youkai Festival
spots.desc: This popular festival is held every November, with lots of costumes and events. It's great for kids and serious otaku.

spots.name: Happy Raft
spots.desc: Arranges half/full-day rafting trips from ¥5500/10000, mostly mid-spring to mid/late autumn (lunch included for full day). Canyoning is offered as well. A very chilled out group of experienced guides are here who seem to like having a good time. Good English is spoken by all the staff. Located just near Tosa-Iwahara station. Station pick-up from Oboke is also available. Cafe and accommodation…

spots.name: Go!Go! Adventure
spots.desc: Operated in conjunction with the Momonga Village Guesthouse, half and full day rafting trips are available either with or without lunch. Prices for half day start at ¥4000, and full day starts at about ¥9000

spots.name: WestWest
spots.desc: The largest and newest of the rest areas, it includes a 7/11, a cafe & ramen restaurant, a souvenir shop, and a Mont Bell outdoor store with various hiking, camping, and rafting gear. Adjacent to the main building is a soba noodle restaurant (see section "Eat").

spots.name: Oboke-kyo River Cruise Rest Area
spots.desc: This large rest area is operated by the Hotel Mannaka and has a vast range of local souvigners across the road (beside the river) from the hotel. This is from where the river cruises depart (See Do for river cruise information).

spots.name: Furutani Food Shop
spots.desc: A fairly well stocked grocery store with fresh food, packaged goods, and alcohol. Convenient to anyone staying near or passing through the center of town.

spots.name: Boke-Mart
spots.desc: It is a small, normal grocery store, and probably the best place to stock up in the area, especially if heading into Iya Valley.

spots.name: The Woody Rest
spots.desc: Local soba and udon are served along with a variety of Japanese sets. The menu is in English and the owner's charming wife speaks English decently as well. Lots of good travel info available.

spots.name: WestWest
spots.desc: In this large rest area are a 7-Eleven convenience store, and two restaurants:

spots.name: Momiji-tei
spots.desc: A soba and noodle restaurant housed within a beautiful restored thatched roof farmhouse with garden, offering views of the river and gorge.

spots.name: Tazawako Ski Area
spots.desc: Located at the foot of the Mt. Akita-Koma. View of Lake Tazawa is great.
spots.addr: 73-2, Shimotakano, Obonai, Tazawako 田沢湖生保内字下高野73-2

spots.name: Mount Akita-Koma
spots.desc: This mountain is an active volcano, and the highest mountain in Akita prefecture. View of Lake Tazawa from the top is wonderful. Roadway through to 8Gōme (80% on the mountain) parking. Climbing to the top from 8Gōme takes about 2 hours round trip.

spots.name: Mount Nyūtō
spots.desc: The name of the mountain means "nipple". It was named from the shape of the mountain as seen from the Akita side is similar to the female breast. There are alpine plants and wetlands near the top. Climbing 4 - 5 hr round trip to the top from Kuroyu Onsen in Nyuto Onsen. After climbing, you can take a tired by hot spring.

spots.name: Tsurunoyu
spots.desc: The lodge offers lunch for everyone, dishes including noodles, set menus and vegetable hotpot.

spots.name: Shirakaba no Yu
spots.desc: Spa complex featuring the largest outdoor tub (rotenburo) in Tohoku, indoor pool and sauna. Directly connected to the Holiday Inn, also served by the Area Shuttle.

spots.name: Lawson
spots.desc: This otherwise unremarkable convenience store near the station is notable as the only independent shop around. Sells the usual range of meals, snacks and liquor.

spots.name: Marudai Shokudo
spots.desc: A time warp to the Showa era, this humble eatery in the no man's land between the village and the highway serves up freshly cut soba, with foraged mushrooms (in season) as well as ramen and rice bowls. Cash only, no English menu.

spots.name: Appi Plaza Food Court
spots.desc: The only semi-reasonably priced option in the ski resort, this food court catering squarely to skiers has half a dozen stalls offering ramen, curry rice, Indian, pizza and more, with plenty of seating. The food is expensive and average for Japan, but at least the portions are generous. Packed at lunch, but most stalls close up shop by 4pm even on weekends, when it's theoretically still open for…

spots.name: Little Rabbit
spots.desc: Australian-style coffee, burgers, curry rice and craft beer. The only cafe in Appi that opens early and stays open late.

spots.name: House Appi
spots.desc: Bakery-cafe selling their own pastries, bread, salads and similar light fare. This is IHG's in-house supplier and you'll find their products at the cafe & restaurants at the resort as well.

spots.name: Aburitei
spots.desc: Izakaya specializing in robatayaki ("primitive grilling", per English menu). The menu is short but well selected, tasty, and not too extortionately priced if you avoid the wagyu.

spots.name: 19. Brewpub
spots.desc: A Colorado style microbrewery transplanted into Japan, this cozy pub has burgers, chili and ten beers on tap.

spots.name: Taki no Yu
spots.desc: A small traditional old wooden bathhouse with waters blended from two springs, one milky white, the other clear. Several pipes create artificial waterfalls, which are comfortable to sit under.

spots.name: Skiing
spots.desc: Several ski resorts operate in the winter, especially around the hot spring resort of Onikōbe.

spots.name: Kokeshi
spots.desc: Naruko is one among many places to claim to have originated this cylindrical wooden doll, emblematic of Tohoku. The Japan Kokeshi Museum is in Naruko, and some 80 craftsmen work there full-time.

spots.name: Sobadokoro Kobana
spots.desc: A basic noodle joint, locally known for its free-range chicken namban (southern barbarian) style.

spots.name: Komachi no Yu
spots.desc: Rustic little outdoor spring, separated into men's and women's sides, but with no facilities — even payment is on the honor system. Alas, even though it's next to the river, there are no river views from inside.

spots.name: Onogawa Public Ski Course
spots.local: 米沢市営小野川スキー場
spots.desc: With one ski lift and a single easy 500-m downhill run, this isn't exactly Shiga Kogen, but at that price you can't really complain. Ski lodge/restaurant open only weekends.

spots.name: Ryuge Shokudō
spots.desc: Cozy, smoky little den at the south edge of town, where locals come to slurp their noodles. Try the two local specialities, mamemoyashi ramen (with bean sprouts) and nameko-miso ramen (with slippery nameko mushrooms), and any of the tofu dishes freshly made by the tofu shop next door.

spots.name: Tengendai Ski & Trekking
spots.desc: Ski resort right next to Shirabu, with 7 courses covering 6000m. Ski and snowboard rental available.

spots.name: Warabe no Sato History and Culture Museum
spots.local: わらべの里歴史と文化の美術館
spots.desc: A museum consisting of five buildings collected and over 1000 artifacts collected by a single man, Yaheiji Okazaki. Emperor Meiji stayed in one of the buildings, and imperial objects and items from Yamagata Castle's former lords are featured among many others.

spots.name: Zao Onsen Dairotemburo
spots.desc: An open-air hot spring (rotemburo) in an atmospheric forest enclave in the mountainside. It easily sets itself apart from other onsen in the country and consistently receives high ratings among visitors.

spots.name: Zao Onsen Ski Resort
spots.desc: Zao is Tohoku's largest ski resort and has been a popular ski destination for decades. The area features 32 lifts and a variety of options for skiers from first-timers to pros.

spots.name: Zao Juhyo Festival
spots.desc: Even if you're not interested in skiing, Zao's Ski area attracts winter visitors for its famous juhyo, better known as "Snow Monsters". Of course there are no real monsters; the "snow monsters" are created by the heavy amount of snow covering the trees. The festival season begins in late December and continues through early March. There is a Light-Up on specific days during the event, including…

spots.name: Notoya Kobo Eijiro
spots.local: 能登屋 工房 栄治郎
spots.desc: The shop was founded by the renowned kokeshi artist, Okazaki Ikuo as the place to purchase his kokeshi. He is among the most famous of the Zao Takayu kokeshi artists, and the shop features the widest selection of kokeshi with many sizes to choose from. It also offers some kokeshi from other artists, including those from other schools, so if either the artist or school are important to you…

spots.name: Tanaka Kokeshiya
spots.desc: A shop selling Zao Takayu kokeshi from some of the prominent local artists. There are also other kokeshi and souvenirs. They also offer a paint-your-own kokeshi experience for a fee until 5PM.
